It is unfitting because the Holy Ghost is never described as being less than the Father.
It is fitting only if the Holy Ghost assumes a human nature like the Son did.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because human nature requires learning about invisible things through visible ones, it was appropriate for the Holy Ghost to be sent in a visible manner.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, what is the specific role of the visible mission of the Holy Ghost?
options: To serve as a visible sign that points to the gift of sanctification.
To act as the author who directly creates sanctification in believers.
To demonstrate that the Holy Ghost is superior to the Son in power.
To replace the need for the invisible mission of the Holy Ghost.
questions.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes the roles, stating the Son is sent as the author of sanctification, while the Holy Ghost is sent as the sign of that sanctification.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that angels, not the Holy Ghost, are the ones sent visibly?
options: He argues that the visible creatures were formed by angels to signify the Holy Ghost.
He agrees that the angels are the primary agents of the visible mission.
He claims that the Holy Ghost assumed the visible creatures into His own person.
He states that visible appearances are impossible because they belong only to prophecy.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the fifth objection, Aquinas explains that while angels formed the visible creatures, they did so to signify the Person of the Holy Ghost, not themselves.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, who sends a divine person?
options: The entire Trinity, because all three persons cause the effect of the mission.
Only the specific person from whom the sent one eternally proceeds.
Only the Father, since He is the ultimate source of all divinity.
The person being sent, acting independently of the others.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that while the sent person proceeds from a specific principle, the act of sending involves the effect of the mission, which is caused by the whole Trinity.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main reason for saying the whole Trinity sends?
options: Because human beings can also participate in sending the Holy Spirit.
Because the sender is defined by causing the visible or invisible effect of the mission.
Because authority over the sent person belongs equally to all three divine persons.
Because Augustine explicitly stated that the Son sends Himself alone.
questions.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes between the principle of origin (which is specific) and the principle of the effect (which belongs to the whole Trinity), concluding the latter defines 'sending'.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that a man could send the Holy Ghost?
options: He agrees that men can send the Spirit through the power of grace.
He claims the Holy Ghost is never sent by anyone.
He argues that only the Father has the authority to send.
He rejects it because men cannot cause the effect of grace.
questions.explanation: Aquinas refutes the idea that a man can send the Holy Ghost by stating that humans lack the power to cause the effect of grace, which is required for sending.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the origin of all existing things?
options: Some beings exist without a cause, just like a person can lack whiteness.
Only necessary things are created by God; others exist on their own.
Mathematical objects prove that not all beings need an efficient cause.
Every existing thing is caused by God as its source of being.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that 'every being in any way existing is from God' because all beings participate in being, which must be caused by the one who possesses being essentially.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why all things must come from God?
options: Necessary things do not require causes, so God is the cause of contingent things only.
God is the only being that possesses existence essentially, while others only borrow it.
Plato argued that unity must come before multitude in all physical objects.
God is the greatest in heat, so He causes all other forms of warmth.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that God is 'essentially self-subsisting Being,' whereas all other beings exist by 'participation,' meaning they do not have being in themselves but receive it from God.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that mathematical proofs do not use efficient causes?
options: The objection is wrong because all sciences must use the same type of cause.
Mathematics deals with mentally abstracted objects, not real things that need physical causes.
God is the cause of mathematical truths, but not of the physical objects they describe.
Mathematical proofs are invalid because they do not follow Aristotle's rules of logic.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas explains that mathematics treats objects as 'abstracted mentally,' whereas in reality, everything has an efficient cause in proportion to its being.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether primary matter is created by God?
options: Primary matter is eternal and was never created by any cause.
Primary matter is created by God, the universal cause of all being.
Primary matter exists independently of God as a separate first principle.
Primary matter creates itself through natural processes like condensation.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since God is the cause of things as beings, He must cause not just their forms but also the underlying matter itself.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why God must create primary matter?
options: Matter is purely potential and therefore cannot exist without being acted upon by a purely actual being.
Ancient philosophers failed to understand that matter is actually a form of divine energy.
God is the cause of existence itself, so He must cause everything that contributes to a thing's being, including matter.
Matter is the passive counterpart to God's active power, so they must be two equal, uncreated principles.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that the cause of things considered as 'beings' must be the cause of all aspects of their being, which includes primary matter.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that God and matter are opposing principles, neither from the other?
options: He suggests that passion and action are identical, so the distinction between God and matter is false.
He claims that matter is actually active, not passive, so it is similar to God in nature.
He argues that the first passive principle (matter) is the effect of the first active principle (God).
He states that God and matter are indeed two separate, uncreated principles that oppose each other.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas explains that since every imperfect thing is caused by a perfect one, the first passive principle is caused by the first active principle.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the source of the perfect models for all created things?
options: God is the only first source of these models for everything.
Nature creates its own models without any divine input.
Separate, self-existing species exist independently of God.
The models are found in the minds of human scientists.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that God is the first exemplar cause of all things and that the types of all things exist in the divine wisdom.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas argue that the divine mind must be the source of these models?
options: Because human minds are too weak to design complex forms.
To ensure created things receive specific and distinct forms.
Because the Bible explicitly lists the designs for every animal.
Because God is physically similar to the creatures he makes.
questions.explanation: He argues that an exemplar is needed so the effect can receive a determinate form, and this determination is reduced to divine wisdom.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that creatures are too different from God to be like Him?
options: Creatures are like God because they have the same physical shape.
Creatures are like God because they reflect the ideas in His mind.
Creatures are like God because they share the same biological species.
Creatures are like God because they possess independent self-existence.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas compares a material house to the house in an architect's mind, stating creatures represent the divine idea.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether God is the final cause of all things?
options: No, because acting for an end implies a need that God does not possess.
No, God acts only as an efficient cause, not as a final cause for creation.
Yes, but only for intelligent beings who consciously choose to desire God.
Yes, God is the final cause because His goodness is the goal all creatures seek.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that divine goodness is the end of all things, meaning God is the final cause because creatures seek to acquire perfection which is a likeness of His goodness.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, what is the main reason God acts as the First Agent?
options: To ensure that primary matter exists, which is the true first principle of reality.
To satisfy a natural need, as all agents must act to achieve a missing end.
To communicate His perfection and goodness to others, not to gain anything for Himself.
To acquire the form of the things He generates, completing His own nature.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that the First Agent acts only to communicate His perfection (goodness), unlike imperfect agents who act to acquire something they lack.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that God cannot be the final cause because acting for an end implies need?
options: The objection is valid for God, so He is not the final cause of inanimate objects.
God acts for an end only when He creates intelligent beings who can recognize Him.
God has a need to create, but it is a spiritual need rather than a physical one.
Acting from need applies only to imperfect agents; God acts freely to share His goodness.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 1, Aquinas states that acting from need belongs to imperfect agents who are both agent and patient, whereas God acts only for His own goodness.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the definition of creation?
options: Creation means making something new out of pre-existing materials.
Creation is the bringing forth of all being from absolute nothingness.
Creation involves improving existing things to a higher state.
Creation is a process that requires a material cause to start.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that creation is the emanation of all being from a universal cause, meaning it proceeds from 'nothing' (no being) rather than from any pre-existing matter.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why creation comes from nothing?
options: Because God is too powerful to rely on any physical materials.
Because no being could exist before the first universal cause.
Because Augustine explicitly defined creation as starting from zero.
Because 'nothing' is a more noble starting point than matter.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since creation is the origin of all being from the first principle, it is impossible for any being to have existed before this emanation.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that 'from' implies a material cause?
options: He says the preposition 'from' here indicates sequence, not material origin.
He states that the objection misunderstands the definition of a statue.
He argues that 'nothing' can act as a material cause in this case.
He claims that material causes are irrelevant to the act of creation.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas explains that the preposition 'from' in this context signifies order or sequence (like morning coming before midday), not a material source.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether God can create anything?
options: It is necessary to say that God created all things from nothing.
Creation is impossible because there is an infinite distance between being and nothing.
God cannot create because ancient philosophers proved nothing comes from nothing.
God can create, but only by shaping pre-existing natural materials.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that it is not only possible but necessary to affirm that all things were created by God from nothing.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main reason for concluding that God must create from nothing?
options: Because change always requires a subject, and nothing exists before creation.
Because if God used pre-existing matter, that matter would not be caused by Him.
Because ancient philosophers were wrong about the nature of movement and time.
Because God is a craftsman who needs raw materials like wood to work with.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that if God acted on something already existing, that thing would not be caused by Him; since God is the cause of all being, He must bring things into existence from nothing.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that creation involves crossing an infinite distance between being and nothing?
options: He argues that there is no infinite medium between nothing and being.
He claims that being and nothing are actually the same thing in different forms.
He states that creation is a slow process that takes an infinite amount of time.
He agrees that the distance is infinite, but God's power is stronger than distance.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 4, Aquinas rejects the idea of an infinite medium between nothing and being, calling it a false imagination derived from viewing creation as a change between forms.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about the nature of creation within the created thing?
options: It is a real physical substance added to the creature.
It is a medium that exists separately between God and the creature.
It is a real relation connecting the creature to its Creator.
It is a temporary accident that changes the creature's essence.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that creation places something in the thing created according to relation only, specifically a real relation to the Creator as the principle of its being.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas argue that creation is only a relation and not a change?
options: Because there is no medium between the Creator and the creature.
Because the creature is the subject of the creation process.
Because God creates without movement, leaving only relation when motion is removed.
Because creatures are made from pre-existing material through movement.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that creation is not made by movement or change because it does not come from something pre-existing; when movement is removed, only relation remains.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that creation cannot be a medium between God and the creature?
options: He says creation is a medium only in the active sense, not the passive.
He agrees that creation is not a medium and rejects the term entirely.
He claims the creature is the medium, not the act of creation.
He argues that since creation signifies change, it acts as a medium between them.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas states that because creation is signified as a change, and change is a kind of medium, creation is also signified as a medium.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, who or what are properly called 'created things'?
options: Matter alone, since it is the underlying substrate of all physical objects.
Abstract concepts like 'being' itself, rather than individual objects.
Only things that exist as independent, complete entities in their own right.
Forms and accidents, because they are the principles that make things be.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that 'being' properly belongs to subsisting things (independent entities), so only these are truly 'created,' whereas forms and accidents are merely 'concreated.'

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main reason for saying creation belongs to subsisting things?
options: Natural generation produces matter, which is the primary component of creation.
Composite things are more complex than simple things, requiring more divine power.
Creation is a form of making, and making aims at the being of a thing.
The book De Causis states that the first creature is being itself.
questions.explanation: He reasons that to be created is to be made, and making is directed toward a thing's being, which properly belongs only to things that subsist (exist independently).

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that composite things are not created because they come from parts?
options: Creation refers only to the addition of a new form to pre-existing matter.
The objection is correct; only simple, non-composite substances are truly created.
Creation brings the whole composite into being simultaneously with all its parts.
Composite things are not created, but only their individual parts are created separately.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas clarifies that creation is not building from pre-existing parts, but bringing the entire composite entity into existence along with all its principles.

questions.q: What is Aquinas’s final conclusion regarding who can create?
options: God creates alone, but He can give creatures the power to create indirectly.
Only God can create, and no creature can do so even with God's help.
Perfect creatures can create because they can make things like themselves.
Any being with enough power can create since created things are finite.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that it is impossible for any creature to create, either by its own power or instrumentally, because creation is the proper act of God alone.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why only God can create?
options: Material things cannot create because they need to touch or move existing matter.
Creation brings existence into being from nothing, which is the most universal effect.
God is the only being that is infinite, so only He can make finite things.
Creating from nothing requires more power than making something from its opposite.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that 'being itself' is the most universal effect, and therefore it must come from the most universal cause, which is God.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that creating from nothing is easier than changing existing matter?
options: He states that the contrary resists less than nothing, making creation simpler.
He argues that nothing resists the creator, so no special power is actually needed.
He claims that finite effects always require finite power, regardless of the source.
He says the power needed depends on the mode of being made, not just the result.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas explains that the maker's power is measured by the mode of production; creating from nothing shows infinite power even if the effect is finite.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, is the act of creating something unique to one specific Person of the Trinity, or is it shared?
options: It is unique to the Holy Spirit alone.
It is unique to the Son alone.
It is common to the entire Trinity.
It is unique to the Father alone.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that creating belongs to God's essence, which is shared by all three Persons, so it is common to the whole Trinity.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main reason for saying creation is not proper to just one Person?
options: Because creation flows from God's essence, which is shared by all three Persons.
Because the Father creates independently of the Son and Holy Spirit.
Because creation is an accidental property rather than an essential one.
Because the divine Persons are too similar to have distinct creative roles.
questions.explanation: He states that since every agent produces its like, the principle of action is the agent's being (essence), which is common to the three Persons.

questions.q: In his reply to Objection 2, how does Aquinas explain the order among the Persons regarding creation?
options: The Father creates first, then the Son, and finally the Holy Spirit acts last.
The Holy Spirit is the primary cause, with the Father and Son assisting.
There is no order because all three Persons act simultaneously and identically.
The Son receives nature from the Father, and the Spirit from both, establishing an order.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that while the power is common, it belongs to them in an order: the Son receives from the Father, and the Spirit from both.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether creatures bear a trace of the Trinity?
options: Only rational creatures bear a trace of the Trinity.
Every creature necessarily bears a trace of the Trinity.
No creature bears a trace because the Trinity is invisible.
Creatures bear an image, but never a trace, of the Trinity.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that while rational creatures have an 'image' of the Trinity, 'in all creatures there is found the trace of the Trinity.'

questions.q: Why does Aquinas argue that every creature contains a trace of the Trinity?
options: Because smoke represents fire, and all creatures are effects of God.
Because every creature possesses intellect and will, mirroring the Son and Holy Spirit.
Because the Trinity directly creates only rational beings, not irrational ones.
Because every creature has substance, form, and order, which reflect the divine persons.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that substance reflects the Father, form reflects the Son (Word), and order/relation reflects the Holy Spirit (Love), constituting the trace in all creatures.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that finding a trace in every property leads to an infinite regress?
options: The trace is found only in the will, which is not divisible.
The trace applies only to the creature as a whole, not to every part.
Properties do not exist in creatures, so they cannot have traces.
The infinite regress is acceptable because God is infinite in nature.
questions.explanation: In Reply 2, Aquinas clarifies that a creature is a 'self-subsisting thing' and the trace is ascribed to the whole being, not to every individual property within it.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the relationship between creation and natural processes?
options: Creation happens simultaneously with every act of nature and art.
Nature creates the forms directly without any prior divine action.
Creation is a prerequisite that exists before nature begins its work.
Creation and nature are two separate, unconnected processes.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that creation does not enter into the work of nature but is presupposed to it, meaning it must happen first.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why nature does not create forms directly?
options: Forms are too powerful to be produced by natural agents.
Matter is too unstable to hold any form in place.
Natural agents lack the power to produce anything from nothing.
Forms are not independent things, so they cannot be made or created.
questions.explanation: He states that forms do not exist on their own; therefore, they are not 'made' or 'created' but are 'concreated' with the composite thing.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that nature's products must be creatures or it is heretical?
options: Heretics are wrong to claim that nature's products are not creatures.
Nature's products are created directly by God, bypassing natural causes.
Nature's products are creatures because they rely on already-created principles.
Nature's products are not creatures, so the objection is invalid.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the fourth objection, he explains that nature operates only on the assumption of created principles, making its products creatures.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's conclusion regarding whether the universe always existed?
options: It is impossible to prove by reason that the universe had a beginning.
The universe must have always existed because God is eternal.
The universe definitely began to exist at a specific moment in time.
The universe exists eternally because it is incorruptible.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that while the world began to exist by God's will, this fact cannot be demonstrated by reason alone; it is an article of faith.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas believe we cannot prove by reason that the world had a beginning?
options: Aristotle proved that the world is eternal, and Aquinas agrees with him.
Human reason is too weak to understand the concept of time.
God's will is free, so He did not have to will the world to exist eternally.
The world is necessary because God is the sufficient cause of all things.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that since God's will is not necessitated to will anything except Himself, it is not necessary for the world to be eternal, making its beginning a matter of divine choice, not logical necessity.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that a beginning of the world implies a 'vacuum' (empty space) existed before it?
options: He states that a vacuum is possible if it is caused by God's power.
He agrees that a vacuum existed but says it was not empty of God.
He argues that space and place did not exist before the world was created.
He claims that God filled the vacuum with spiritual beings before creating matter.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 4, Aquinas explains that 'vacuum' implies a space capable of holding a body; since there was no place or space before the world, there was no vacuum.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether the world had a beginning?
options: It is a matter of personal opinion that varies depending on the philosopher's view.
It is a fact that can be proven with absolute certainty using logical reasoning alone.
It is a truth known only through faith, not through human demonstration or science.
It is a philosophical error because the world must have existed from all eternity.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that the newness of the world is held by faith alone and cannot be proved by any demonstration.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why the world's beginning cannot be proven by reason?
options: The world is too old for any human to have witnessed its actual creation.
The essence of things is universal and does not include specific limits of time or place.
Logical arguments are only useful for proving things that happen in the present moment.
God's will is too complex for human minds to understand or investigate in any way.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because the essence of a thing is abstracted from 'here' and 'now', it cannot be demonstrated that a specific thing did not always exist.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that an eternal world would mean an infinite number of days passed before today?
options: He states that time is an illusion and therefore the concept of passing days is invalid.
He argues that between any specific past day and today, the number of days is finite.
He claims that days did not exist until God created the sun and moon recently.
He agrees that an infinite number of days makes the existence of the world impossible.
questions.explanation: In his reply to Objection 6, Aquinas explains that passage is from term to term, and between any chosen past day and the present, there is only a finite number of days.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding when God created the world?
options: Creation occurred before time began to exist.
The world has existed forever and has no beginning.
Creation happened at the very start of time, not before it.
Time was created separately after the physical world.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that 'In the beginning' refers to the beginning of time, meaning heaven and earth were created together with time itself.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas argue that creation happened at the beginning of time?
options: Because time, matter, and spiritual beings were all created simultaneously.
Because the physical world existed before time started flowing.
Because God needed time to measure the process of making things.
Because evil things were created before good things in time.
questions.explanation: He states that four things—corporeal matter, the highest heaven, time, and angelic nature—were created together, so creation coincides with time's start.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that creation implies a 'before' and 'after' which cannot exist at time's indivisible start?
options: Creation is not a movement with duration, so it does not require a 'before' and 'after'.
The 'before' and 'after' refer to God's eternal plan, not physical time.
Creation happened slowly over a long period before time began.
Time is divisible, so the beginning of time actually contains many moments.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas clarifies that the Philosopher's rule about 'before' and 'after' applies to movement, but creation is not a movement.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, where does the variety and difference of things in the universe ultimately originate?
options: From the deliberate intention of God.
From the random movement of matter alone.
From the inherent nature of matter seeking form.
From secondary spiritual beings created by God.
questions.explanation: Aquinas rejects the ideas that matter or secondary agents cause diversity, concluding instead that it comes from God's intention.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main reason for rejecting the idea that secondary agents (like first intelligences) cause the diversity of things?
options: Because secondary agents are too simple to understand complexity.
Because only God has the power to create being from nothing.
Because matter prevents secondary agents from acting effectively.
Because God forbids secondary agents from creating anything.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that creation belongs to God alone, and since diverse things require creation, they must come from Him, not secondary causes.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that God, being one, must produce only one effect?
options: The one effect is so large it appears as many.
God produces one effect that then splits into many.
God is actually many things disguised as one.
God acts by will and intellect, allowing for multiple effects.
questions.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes God as a voluntary agent acting by intellect, unlike natural agents that act by a single fixed form.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether inequality in the world comes from God?
options: Inequality exists because God is just and must give unequal things to unequal beings.
Inequality is not from God but resulted from the free choices of rational creatures.
God created all things equal initially, and inequality arose later due to sin.
God’s wisdom is the direct cause of the inequality found among different kinds of things.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that just as God's wisdom causes the distinction of things, it is also the cause of their inequality, rejecting the idea that it stems from sin or free will.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why God creates a hierarchy of different kinds of things?
options: Because it is necessary to show that God is the best agent by making the best parts.
To punish souls that turned away from God, resulting in the creation of bodies.
Because different forms require different levels of perfection to arrange species in degrees.
Because God is one, and unity naturally leads to the creation of equal things.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that formal distinctions (different species) require inequality because forms vary like numbers, creating a natural arrangement where some species are more perfect than others.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that the best agent should make all parts equally best?
options: He agrees that God should make all things equal to reflect divine unity.
He argues that the whole is best if parts are unequal, like an eye in an animal.
He states that equality is the first effect of unity, so God must start with equality.
He claims that inequality is only relevant for rewards, not for the creation of things.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas explains that a whole is best when its parts are proportioned to it, not when every part has the same dignity, using the example of an animal's eye.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the number of worlds?
options: There is only one single world.
The number of worlds is unknown.
God could create many worlds but chose not to.
There are many worlds created by God.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly concludes that the order of created things shows there is only one world, rejecting the idea of multiple worlds.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main reason for believing there is only one world?
options: Matter can only exist in one specific location.
All created things are ordered together into a single unified system.
God's power is limited to creating only one universe.
Creating many worlds would be too wasteful of resources.
questions.explanation: He argues that because all things come from God, they relate to each other and to God in a single order, forming one world.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that 'many good things are better than a few'?
options: He argues that an endless number lacks a definite goal or end.
He states that other worlds would physically collide with ours.
He says that nature cannot produce more than one world.
He claims that God prefers quality over quantity in creation.
questions.explanation: In Reply 2, Aquinas states that material plurality tends toward infinity, and since infinity opposes the notion of a definite end, God does not intend it.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether evil is a nature?
options: Evil is a positive force that exists alongside good.
Evil is a distinct genus, separate from being and goodness.
Evil is a nature, but only in the realm of moral actions.
Evil is not a nature; it is simply the absence of good.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that evil signifies the absence of good and is neither a being nor a nature.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for saying evil is not a nature?
options: Because every nature seeks its own being, and being is inherently good.
Because Aristotle claimed that evil is merely a logical category.
Because evil cannot act on its own to corrupt good things.
Because the universe would be imperfect if evil were a real nature.
questions.explanation: He argues that since every nature desires its own being and perfection, and being is good, evil cannot signify being or any nature.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that evil acts (by corrupting good) and therefore must be a being?
options: He argues that corruption is not a true action in the philosophical sense.
He admits evil acts but says it is a weak form of being.
He says evil acts formally as a lack, like whiteness makes things white.
He claims evil only acts when joined to a good nature.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 4, Aquinas explains that evil acts 'formally' as a privation or corruption of good, similar to how whiteness acts to make something white.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether evil exists in created things?
options: Evil is a positive substance that exists alongside good things in the universe.
Evil is found in things, specifically as a failure or lack of expected goodness.
Evil does not exist because God always creates only the best possible things.
Evil is not found in things because it is too distant from existence to be real.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that evil is found in things as a 'privation,' meaning it is the failure of a thing to possess the goodness it ought to have, rather than a positive entity.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why evil must exist in the universe?
options: God made evil to punish humans for their disobedience and moral failures.
Evil is necessary to balance out the good, ensuring that neither side dominates.
The universe is more perfect if it includes a range of beings, some of which can fail or corrupt.
Nature is imperfect and therefore inevitably produces evil alongside good things.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that the perfection of the universe requires inequality and variety, including corruptible beings that can fail in goodness, which allows for the full realization of all grades of goodness.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that God always makes the best, so there should be no evil?
options: God makes the best whole universe, which includes some parts that can fail for the greater good.
God makes the best in every single part, but evil arises from human misuse.
God allows evil because He is distant from existence and cannot control all things.
God does not make everything; nature makes the imperfect parts where evil is found.
questions.explanation: In his reply to Objection 3, Aquinas states that God makes what is best for the whole universe, not necessarily for every single part, and the whole is better if some parts can fail.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether evil exists within good?
options: Evil is completely separate from good and has no connection to it whatsoever.
Evil is a positive substance that exists independently of any good thing.
Good and evil are identical, so they cannot be distinguished from one another.
Evil is found within good, because good serves as the underlying subject for evil.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that evil is in good as its subject because evil is a lack of good in something that is capable of having it.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas argue that the subject of evil must be good?
options: Because evil is a missing quality in something that exists, and all existing things are good.
Because good and evil are opposites that must always be found together in nature.
Because evil is a physical substance that needs a physical container to exist.
Because good is the only thing powerful enough to contain and control evil effectively.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since every actual being is good, and evil is a lack in a being, the thing lacking the good (the subject) must itself be good.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that evil cannot be in good because they are opposites?
options: The rule about opposites does not apply to spiritual matters like good and evil.
Evil is in a good subject, but not in the specific good that is missing.
The objection is wrong because evil is not a real thing, so it has no subject.
Good and evil are not actually opposites, but rather different types of existence.
questions.explanation: Aquinas clarifies that while evil is in a good subject (like an animal), it is not in the specific good it lacks (like sight).

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether evil completely destroys good?
options: Evil always destroys the entire good because good and evil are direct opposites.
Evil destroys the good entirely, leaving nothing behind in the subject.
Evil can never completely consume good, though it may diminish some aspects of it.
Evil consumes good only if the good is infinite, which created goods are not.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that 'Evil cannot wholly consume good,' distinguishing between goods that are destroyed, those that remain, and those that are merely diminished.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why evil does not destroy all good?
options: He distinguishes between different types of good, noting that the underlying subject always remains.
He claims that evil is not a real thing, but merely the absence of good.
He asserts that good is uniform and indivisible, so it cannot be partially removed.
He argues that good is infinite and therefore cannot be exhausted by finite evil.
questions.explanation: Aquinas categorizes good into three kinds, emphasizing that while some good is destroyed, the 'subject' of evil (the underlying substance) always remains intact.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that good is uniform and thus wholly taken away by evil?
options: The objection is wrong because evil does not actually take away good, it only hides it.
Good relates to different things; it is diminished where it touches action but remains where it touches the subject.
Good is infinite, so even if it is uniform, it can never be fully consumed by evil.
Good is not uniform; it is composed of many separate parts that evil can only remove one by one.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas explains that good is a medium between subject and act; it is diminished regarding the act but remains regarding the subject.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether evil is adequately divided into pain and fault?
options: The division is adequate, but only for evils found in beings with free will.
The division is superfluous because all evil is essentially just pain.
The division is incorrect because temptation is a third category of evil.
The division is inadequate because it ignores defects in non-living things like stones.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that pain and fault adequately cover all evil in 'voluntary things' (rational creatures with will), but do not apply to irrational creatures or mere natural defects.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas claim that evil in rational creatures takes the form of either pain or fault?
options: Because rational creatures are more complex than stones, so they suffer more physical damage.
Because God punishes rational creatures more severely than irrational ones for their defects.
Because rational creatures can feel temptation, which is distinct from both pain and fault.
Because rational creatures have a will, so losing their natural integrity feels like pain against their will.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that because good is the object of the will, the loss of natural integrity (form) is against the will (pain), and the failure of voluntary action is a fault.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that temptation is an evil that is neither pain nor fault?
options: He says temptation is not an evil at all, but merely an opportunity to practice virtue.
He argues that for the tempter, temptation is a fault, and for the tempted, it is not a fault unless they consent.
He asserts that temptation is a pain for the tempter and a fault for the person being tempted.
He claims temptation is a pain because it causes anxiety before the sin occurs.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 3, Aquinas explains that temptation is a fault for the one tempting, but not a fault for the one tempted unless they change internally (consent).

questions.q: According to Aquinas, which is the greater evil: fault (moral wrong) or pain (suffering)?
options: They are equal evils since both involve a lack of good.
Pain is worse because it deprives us of God's vision.
Fault is the greater evil because it corrupts the will.
Pain is the greater evil because it harms the person directly.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that fault is worse because it involves a disordered act of the will, which is the source of moral evil, whereas pain is merely a privation of goods.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's primary reason for claiming that fault is worse than pain?
options: Fault opposes the good of action, while pain opposes the agent.
Fault makes a person evil, while pain does not make a person evil.
Pain is only physical, while fault affects the soul permanently.
God causes pain as punishment, but never causes moral fault.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that one becomes evil through the evil of fault (a bad will), but being punished or suffering pain does not make a person evil in themselves.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that fault is like merit and pain is like reward?
options: He states that merit and fault are unrelated concepts.
He says merit is actually worse than reward, so fault is worse.
He argues that pain is intended to help us avoid fault.
He claims that reward is not truly good for the agent.
questions.explanation: In Reply 1, Aquinas explains that unlike merit which aims at reward, fault is not intended for pain; rather, pain is brought about so that fault may be avoided.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether good can cause evil?
options: Good directly causes evil because all beings are inherently good.
Good can cause evil, but only as an accidental side effect rather than a direct aim.
Evil has no cause at all, so the question of good causing it is invalid.
Good cannot cause evil because a good tree never produces bad fruit.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that while good is the cause of evil, it is not a direct cause but an accidental one, meaning evil results as a side effect of a good action or power.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why good can be the cause of evil?
options: Evil is a lack of good, and only existing things, which are good, can act as causes.
Nature is fundamentally defective, forcing good things to create bad outcomes.
Evil is a positive force that requires a strong good agent to bring it into existence.
Good and evil are the same thing, so one must necessarily produce the other.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that evil is the absence of good, and since only beings (which are good) can be causes, good must be the cause of evil, albeit accidentally.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that a good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit?
options: He argues that trees are not moral agents, so the biblical metaphor does not apply to human actions.
He states that the objection is wrong because evil fruit is actually a type of good.
He says the 'evil tree' refers to a bad will, so a good will does not produce morally bad acts.
He claims that good trees can produce evil fruit if the soil is poor and deficient.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas cites Augustine to clarify that the 'evil tree' represents a bad will, meaning a good will does not produce morally evil acts.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether God is the cause of evil?
options: God causes neither the evil of punishment nor the evil of fault.
God causes the evil of punishment but not the evil of moral fault.
God is the direct cause of all evil, including moral wrongdoing.
God is the cause of moral fault but not of physical suffering.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that God is the author of the evil which is penalty (punishment) but not of the evil which is fault (sin).

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for saying God is not the cause of moral evil?
options: Moral evil does not exist in reality, only in human perception.
God possesses perfect goodness and lacks any defect to cause moral failure.
Moral evil is caused solely by demons, not by God or humans.
God created the universe without any possibility of failure or defect.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that moral evil arises from a defect in the agent, and since God is perfectly good with no defect, He cannot be the cause of such evil.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the biblical objection that God 'creates evil'?
options: He claims the scripture is metaphorical and should not be taken literally.
He states that God creates evil only when humans fail to pray.
He argues the scripture refers to the evil of punishment, not moral sin.
He asserts that the scripture means God creates the potential for evil.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas clarifies that the biblical passages refer to the evil of penalty, not the evil of fault.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the existence of a single supreme evil that causes all other evils?
options: There is a supreme evil that exists alongside the supreme good.
There is a supreme evil, but it is weaker than the supreme good.
There is no such thing as a supreme evil or first principle of evil.
There is a supreme evil, but it only causes accidental evils.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that 'there is no one first principle of evil, as there is one first principle of good,' rejecting the idea of a supreme evil entirely.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for why a 'supreme evil' cannot exist?
options: Evil is too weak to sustain itself as a primary cause.
Evil is merely an illusion created by human misunderstanding.
Evil is the absence of good and requires a good subject to exist.
God's goodness is too powerful for any evil to be supreme.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that evil is a privation (lack) of good and can only exist 'in good as in its subject,' meaning it cannot exist essentially or supremely on its own.

questions.q: In his reply to the objection that contraries must have contrary causes, how does Aquinas explain the relationship between good and evil causes?
options: Good and evil are separate forces that never interact with each other.
Contraries do not need a common cause because they are independent.
Contraries share a common nature of being, leading to one common first cause.
The cause of evil is always stronger than the cause of good.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 1, Aquinas states that contraries agree in the nature of being, so we must ultimately trace them back to 'one first common cause.'

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about whether an angel is made of matter and form?
options: An angel has no matter and no form, being pure act.
An angel is composed of both matter and form.
An angel is made of neither matter nor form, but of a different substance.
An angel is made only of form, with no matter.
questions.explanation: Aquinas rejects the idea that angels have matter; he says they are purely immaterial forms.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for rejecting matter in angels?
options: Matter would require angels to be finite, contradicting their nature.
Matter would make angels corporeal, which they are not.
Matter would make angels less than God, which is impossible.
Matter cannot be divided, so angels cannot have it.
questions.explanation: He argues that matter would make angels corporeal, which contradicts their purely immaterial nature.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to Objection 3, which says form is act and angels are not pure act?
options: He says angels are pure act, just like God.
He says angels have both act and potentiality, not just act.
He says angels are made of matter, so act is irrelevant.
He says angels have form but no act at all.
questions.explanation: In his reply he notes angels have act and potentiality, showing they are not only pure act.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about the total number of angels?
options: Angels exist in a number far greater than any material quantity.
Angels exist in the smallest possible number to reflect God's unity.
Angels are limited in number to match heavenly body movements.
Angels are as numerous as the different species of physical things.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because angels are more perfect than material things, they are created in a much greater excess of multitude than physical objects.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why angels are so numerous?
options: Angels need to be numerous to move all the heavenly bodies effectively.
Angels must be numerous to distinguish themselves from human nature.
God creates more perfect things in greater excess to perfect the universe.
Each angel corresponds to a specific ray of divine goodness received.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that since God intends the perfection of the universe, more perfect things are created in greater excess, meaning incorporeal beings outnumber material ones.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that angels cannot be numerous because they have no physical bodies to divide?
options: Angels are numerous because they are made of a subtle, invisible physical substance.
Angels are numerous because they are copies of the many different human souls.
Angels are numerous because they are created to replace the movements of stars.
Angels are numerous because they are divided by distinct forms, not physical matter.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas explains that angelic number comes from the distinction of their forms, not from the division of continuous physical bodies.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether angels belong to different species?
options: Angels differ in species only if they have different material bodies or physical forms.
All angels belong to a single species because they share the same spiritual nature.
Angels of the same hierarchy belong to one species, but different hierarchies are distinct.
Every individual angel constitutes a unique species, so no two angels share the same species.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since angels are not made of matter, they cannot be distinguished merely as individuals within one species; thus, each angel is of a unique species.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why two angels cannot be of the same species?
options: Angels are too perfect to be grouped together in any kind of numerical category.
The diversity of angelic powers creates a difference so large it changes their basic type.
Without matter to distinguish them, they would have to be identical in every way.
Angels are incorporeal, so the material principle that distinguishes individuals is absent.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that things agreeing in species but differing in number are distinguished by matter; since angels lack matter, this distinction is impossible.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that angels differ only by 'more and less' (like intensity), which doesn't change species?
options: He agrees that intensity differences are minor and do not affect the species of angels.
He says that intensity differences are the only way spiritual beings can be distinguished.
He claims that angels do not actually differ in simplicity or intellect at all.
He argues that 'more and less' in angels reflects different forms, not just intensity of one form.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas explains that 'more and less' changes species when caused by forms of diverse degrees, which is how angels are diversified.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether angels are incorruptible?
options: Angels are immortal only because God grants them this favor.
Angels are naturally incorruptible and cannot cease to exist on their own.
Angels are dissoluble by nature but indissoluble because God wills it.
Angels are naturally corruptible but are kept alive by God's will.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that angels are incorruptible by their own nature, rejecting the views that they are corruptible by nature or immortal only by favor.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why angels are naturally incorruptible?
options: Their intellectual operations are everlasting, which proves their physical durability.
They are made of a special divine element that is immune to change.
God constantly preserves them in existence, preventing them from decaying.
Angels are pure forms without matter, so they lack the parts needed for corruption.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that corruption requires the separation of form from matter. Since angels are subsisting forms without matter, they cannot undergo this separation.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that Plato called angels 'dissoluble by nature'?
options: He argues that Plato used the word 'angels' metaphorically for humans.
He agrees with Plato but says God overrides this natural dissolubility.
He states that Plato's view is irrelevant to Christian theology.
He claims Plato was referring to heavenly bodies, not angels.
questions.explanation: In his reply to Objection 2, Aquinas clarifies that Plato's term 'gods' referred to heavenly bodies made of elements, which are naturally dissoluble, not to angels.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether angels have bodies naturally united to them?
options: Angels are composed of body and soul, similar to human beings, to give life to the world.
Angels have bodies naturally united to them because they are described as rational animals.
Angels do not have bodies naturally united to them; they are purely intellectual substances.
Angels have bodies, but only as an accidental feature, not part of their essential nature.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states in his answer that 'The angels have not bodies naturally united to them' because understanding is not an act of a body.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why angels do not have bodies?
options: Angels are too perfect to be burdened with physical matter, which is inherently evil.
God created angels separately from humans, who are the only ones meant to have bodies.
Understanding is a mental act that does not require a body, so pure intellects need no body.
Bodies are only necessary for acquiring knowledge through senses, which angels do not use.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since understanding is not the act of a body, having a body is not part of the nature of an intellectual substance.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that Gregory called angels 'rational animals'?
options: He agrees that angels are animals but argues they are a higher, spiritual type of animal.
He explains that Gregory used the term 'animal' metaphorically to show likeness to rational nature.
He states that 'rational animal' refers only to humans, and Gregory was quoting an older error.
He claims Gregory was mistaken and that angels are purely spiritual beings without any animal traits.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas clarifies that Gregory used the term 'rational animal' metaphorically due to the likeness to rational nature, not literally.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether angels take on physical forms?
options: Angels take on physical forms only when they are angry or fighting.
Angels never take on physical forms; all sightings are just mental images.
Angels are naturally made of physical matter, so they always have bodies.
Angels sometimes take on physical forms to be seen by human eyes.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that angels sometimes assume bodies because Scripture describes them being seen by multiple people, which requires a physical object outside the viewer's mind.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for believing angels assume bodies?
options: Scripture says angels were seen by many people, which requires a visible body.
Angels use bodies to eat and drink with humans during their visits.
Angels need bodies to protect themselves from the harshness of the physical world.
Angels need bodies to travel quickly through the air to different places.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since multiple people saw the same angel, it must have been a bodily vision of a real object, not just a private mental image.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that air is too thin and shapeless for angels to use?
options: He says angels use fire because it is bright and easy for humans to see.
He argues that angels do not use air, but instead create solid stone bodies.
He states that the objection is invalid because angels do not actually appear.
He claims that air can be condensed to have shape and color, like clouds do.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas notes that air can be condensed to take on shape and color, similar to how clouds form, allowing it to serve as an assumed body.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about an angel’s presence in space?
options: An angel can be in several places at once.
An angel is in only one place at a time.
An angel is everywhere like God.
An angel’s location is unknowable.
questions.explanation: Aquinas says an angel’s finite power limits him to one determined place; he is not everywhere.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas say an angel cannot be in multiple places?
options: Because angels are as powerful as God.
Because an angel’s power applies to only one thing.
Because angels are indivisible and occupy a point.
Because angels can move the heavens.
questions.explanation: He argues the angel’s finite power can be applied to only one determined thing, so the angel occupies only one place.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to Objection 1 (that angels, like souls, can be in several places)?
options: He says angels are not like souls, so cannot be in several places.
He agrees, but says souls are different.
He says souls are in one place, not several.
He says souls are in several places, but angels are not.
questions.explanation: Aquinas rejects the objection by stating that, unlike souls, an angel’s finite power limits him to one place.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether multiple angels can occupy the same location at once?
options: Several angels can share the same space because they do not have physical bodies.
Only one angel can be present in a specific place at any given moment.
Two angels can be in the same place if they are working together on a task.
Angels can overlap in space just as human souls do within a body.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states in his answer that 'There are not two angels in the same place.' He rejects the idea that their lack of physical bulk allows them to share space.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for why two angels cannot be in the same place?
options: Angels are too large to fit together in a single location.
The place is already filled by a sensible body, leaving no room for angels.
Angels are spiritual beings that cannot interact with physical locations.
It is impossible for two complete causes to directly produce the same effect.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that an angel's presence in a place is a direct, perfect causal act. Since two complete causes cannot immediately cause the same thing, two angels cannot be in the same place.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that a demon and a soul can be in the same place?
options: He states that the soul leaves the body when a demon enters it.
He claims that demons are not actually spiritual substances like angels.
He agrees, noting that spiritual beings do not take up physical space.
He argues that the soul and the demon relate to the body in different ways.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas explains that the inference fails because the soul is the form of the body, while the demon is not, meaning they do not have the same causal relationship to the place.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether a blessed angel can move from one place to another?
options: No, because movement implies imperfection which angels lack.
Only if the angel is not currently blessed or happy.
No, because angels have no physical parts to move.
Yes, a blessed angel can move locally.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states, 'A beatified angel can be moved locally,' rejecting the objections that claim they cannot due to their nature or blessed state.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, why is an angel's local movement different from the movement of a physical body?
options: Angels move by applying their power to places successively, not by filling space.
Angels move by changing their physical shape to fit new locations.
Angels do not move at all; they only appear in different places.
Angels move continuously through space just like bodies but much faster.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that unlike bodies which are contained by place, angels contain place by 'virtual contact,' so their movement is the successive application of their power to different places.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that movement is an act of an 'imperfect being'?
options: He agrees that angels are imperfect but says they move anyway.
He states that movement is actually a sign of perfection for spirits.
He argues that an angel's movement is an act of power, not a sign of lack.
He claims that only unblessed angels are imperfect and thus move.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas distinguishes between movement due to potentiality (imperfection) and movement by application of energy (actuality), stating the latter is an act of one in act.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether an angel passes through intermediate space?
options: An angel passes through intermediate space only if its movement is continuous.
An angel skips all intermediate space because it is a simpler substance than the soul.
An angel never passes through intermediate space because it has no physical size.
An angel always moves continuously and must pass through every intermediate point.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that if an angel's movement is continuous, it must pass through the middle space, but if the movement is not continuous, it can pass from one extreme to another without going through the middle.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why continuous movement requires passing through intermediate space?
options: Because between any two points, there are infinitely many intermediate places.
Because the soul can think of distant places without thinking of the ones in between.
Because the angel's power extends across the entire distance it travels.
Because a body cannot move from one place to another without taking time.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that continuous movement involves an order of first and last that corresponds to magnitude, and since there are infinite intermediate places between any two extremes, the mover must pass through them.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection comparing an angel's movement to the soul's ability to think of distant places?
options: He says the soul is actually more powerful than an angel in local movement.
He claims the soul's thought is a type of continuous local movement.
He states the soul's essence is not applied to places, unlike the angel's.
He agrees that the soul and angel both skip intermediate steps in the same way.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas distinguishes the two by noting that while an angel's essence is applied to various places during local movement, the soul's essence is not applied to the things it thinks about.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the speed of an angel's movement?
options: It is faster than any physical movement but still occurs over a continuous period.
It happens instantly, with no time passing between the start and end points.
It is impossible to determine because angels do not occupy physical space.
It takes time, because the angel must be in the starting place at some specific moment.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that an angel cannot be in the starting place for the whole duration and then suddenly in the end place, as that would imply rest. Therefore, there must be a specific moment when the angel is still in the starting place, which means time passes.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for rejecting the idea that angelic movement is instantaneous?
options: Light travels instantly, and since angels are spiritual, they must move like light.
Rest requires staying in the same place, so a change of place requires a sequence of moments.
The distance between places is too great for any being to cross in a single instant.
Angels are too powerful to be constrained by the laws of time and space.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that if something rests in a place, it stays there through every instant of that rest. Since movement is a change, the subject must be in different states at different moments, requiring a succession of 'nows' or time.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that illumination is instantaneous and thus angelic movement should be too?
options: He states that angels are not illuminated, so the comparison is logically invalid.
He argues that illumination is a change in state, while angelic movement is a change in location.
He agrees that both are instantaneous because they involve no physical resistance.
He claims that light actually travels over time, just like an angel moving through space.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas distinguishes between the two types of change. He notes that illumination is an alteration (a change in quality) that ends a process, whereas the angel's movement is a local movement (change of place) that is not the end of another movement.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about whether an angel’s understanding is the same as its existence?
options: Understanding is unrelated to existence at all.
Understanding is the same as existence for an angel.
Understanding is a part of existence but not identical.
Understanding is not the same as existence for an angel.
questions.explanation: Aquinas says the angel’s action of understanding is not his existence.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas say the angel’s understanding is not its existence?
options: Because understanding is an inward action that stays within the angel.
Because understanding is an outward action that changes the world.
Because angels cannot understand anything beyond themselves.
Because existence is only a physical property, not an act.
questions.explanation: He explains that understanding is an internal action that remains within the agent, unlike outward actions.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to Objection 1, that understanding is a form of living?
options: He agrees that understanding is a kind of life, but not the same as existence.
He argues that life can be a vital operation, not the existence itself.
He claims that understanding is the only true form of life.
He says life and understanding are completely unrelated.
questions.explanation: In his reply he distinguishes life as a vital operation from existence, showing understanding is not the same as existence.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding an angel's power of intelligence?
options: The power of intelligence is an accident added to the essence.
The power of intelligence is distinct from the angel's essence.
The power of intelligence is identical to the angel's essence.
The power of intelligence is the same as the angel's existence.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that in no creature, including angels, is the operative power the same as its essence.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why an angel's essence is not its power of intelligence?
options: Because a simple form cannot be the subject of any accident.
Because angels are simpler in nature than primary matter.
Because an angel's essence is pure act without any potentiality.
Because an angel's act of understanding is different from its act of existing.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since every power is ordered to an act, and an angel's operation (understanding) is not the same as its existence, the power cannot be the same as the essence.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that angels are called 'minds' because they are simple forms?
options: He claims that the term 'mind' refers to the angel's potentiality, not its act.
He says angels are called minds because all their knowledge is intellectual, unlike humans.
He argues that Boethius was speaking about God, not about created angels.
He agrees that angels are pure acts and therefore their essence is their power.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas explains that angels are styled 'intellects' or 'minds' because their knowledge is entirely intellectual, whereas human knowledge includes sensitive parts.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether angels possess both an active and a passive intellect?
options: Angels have a passive intellect to receive truth, but lack an active intellect to process it.
Angels possess an active intellect to enlighten others, but lack a passive intellect for learning.
Angels have both an active and a passive intellect, functioning exactly as they do in human souls.
Angels do not have distinct active and passive intellects because their understanding is always actual.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that the conditions requiring separate active and passive intellects in humans are absent in angels, so they do not have these distinct powers.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas argue that angels do not need a passive intellect?
options: Because angels always understand their natural objects actually, never merely in potentiality.
Because angels receive all their knowledge directly from God without any internal processing.
Because angels are purely material beings that do not engage in intellectual thought.
Because the concept of potentiality does not apply to any spiritual or immaterial nature.
questions.explanation: The passive intellect exists in humans because we start in potentiality; angels, however, naturally apprehend their objects in actuality, removing the need for a passive power.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that angels enlighten lower angels, proving they have an active intellect?
options: He argues that higher angels use a different power, not the active intellect, to teach.
He clarifies that the active intellect enlightens potential objects, not other intellects.
He agrees that enlightening others is the primary function of an angel's active intellect.
He states that lower angels are not intellects but merely potential objects of knowledge.
questions.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes the function of the active intellect: it makes potential objects actually intelligible, rather than illuminating other minds directly.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the type of knowledge angels possess?
options: Angels have a mix of intellectual and imaginative knowledge.
Angels have both intellectual and sensitive knowledge, similar to humans.
Angels possess only intellectual knowledge, lacking any sensitive faculties.
Angels possess sensitive knowledge but lack intellectual understanding.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that since angels have no bodies, they cannot have powers that rely on bodily organs like sight or hearing, leaving only intellect and will.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why angels do not have sensitive faculties?
options: God created angels to be completely different from human beings.
Sensitive faculties require physical organs, which angels do not naturally possess.
Sensitive faculties are considered inferior to intellectual ones in the divine order.
Angels are too pure to interact with the physical world in any way.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that powers like sight and hearing operate through corporeal organs, and since angels have no bodies, these powers cannot belong to them.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that angels have 'experience' because they learn from many memories?
options: He says angels actually use a sensitive memory faculty to store past events.
He argues the term is used by analogy because angels know single objects, like we do via senses.
He claims Isidore was mistaken because angels only know universal truths.
He rejects the claim entirely, stating angels never know individual specific things.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that 'experience' is attributed to angels by likeness of the objects known (single things), not by likeness of the faculty, since they do not use senses.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether angels know all things through their own nature?
options: Angels know all things directly through their essence.
Angels know all things through a separate mental image.
Angels know all things by becoming the things they study.
Only God knows all things directly through His essence.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that only the Divine essence is infinite and contains all things within itself, so only God knows all things by His essence. Angels have finite essences and require mental images to know things.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why an angel cannot know all things by its essence?
options: An angel's essence is identical to the objects it understands, causing confusion.
An angel's essence is limited to a specific type and does not contain everything.
An angel's essence is material and therefore cannot grasp universal truths.
An angel's mind is too weak to hold the full picture of the universe.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that an angel's essence is restricted to a particular genus and species, meaning it is finite and does not comprise all things within itself, unlike the infinite Divine essence.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that an angel's nature is the medium for its knowledge?
options: The phrase means the angel's essence changes to match every object it studies.
The phrase confirms that the angel's essence is the direct image of the thing known.
The phrase refers to the angel's power to know, not the specific content of knowledge.
The phrase is a mistake because angels do not have a proper nature.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas clarifies that 'according to his own nature' describes the faculty or power of knowing, not the medium (the mental image) used to know specific things.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the question of how angels understand things?
options: They use a stronger version of the human active intellect.
They understand through innate concepts naturally built into their nature.
They receive knowledge directly from other angels through communication.
They abstract mental images from physical objects they observe.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that angelic understanding relies on species that are 'connatural' to them, meaning they are naturally part of their being, rather than being drawn from external things.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why angels do not learn from physical things?
