options: Physical things are too imperfect to provide clear knowledge to angels.
Angels were created after humans and already had all necessary knowledge.
Angels are too powerful to need to study the material world.
Angels exist without bodies, so they do not need to seek perfection through matter.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because angels are free from bodies, they attain their intellectual perfection through an intelligible outpouring from God, unlike human souls which are forms of bodies and must learn from matter.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that angels must move locally to gain knowledge of distant things?
options: He argues that angels move to perform actions, not to acquire new knowledge.
He claims that angelic species are only valid for things that are nearby.
He states that angels can see distant things without moving their bodies.
He says angels do not move at all, so the objection is invalid.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas clarifies that while angelic knowledge is indifferent to distance, their movement is for the purpose of operation (action), not for the purpose of acquiring knowledge.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's conclusion regarding how higher angels understand compared to lower angels?
options: Higher angels use the same number of concepts as lower angels.
Higher angels do not use concepts because they know things directly.
Higher angels use more specific details to understand things more perfectly.
Higher angels use fewer, more universal concepts to grasp many things at once.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that higher angels, being closer to God, know many things through fewer, more universal forms, whereas lower angels need many specific forms.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why higher angels use more universal concepts?
options: They prefer general ideas because specific ones are confusing.
They imitate God, who knows all things through His single essence.
They derive their knowledge from physical objects in the world.
They have a weaker intellect that cannot handle specific details.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that higher angels are more like God, who contains the fullness of knowledge in one thing (His essence), so they know by fewer forms.

questions.q: In his reply to Objection 2, how does Aquinas distinguish between two ways of knowing universally?
options: Knowing only the general nature is imperfect; knowing many things via few forms is perfect.
Knowing specific details is always less perfect than knowing general categories.
Knowing universally is always imperfect because it lacks specific details.
Knowing universally is perfect because it matches God's simple knowledge.
questions.explanation: Aquinas clarifies that knowing only a general nature (like 'animal' for a man) is imperfect, but knowing many things through few forms (as higher angels do) is a sign of intellectual strength.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the question of whether an angel knows himself?
options: Angels know themselves because they are immaterial forms that exist as themselves.
Angels cannot know themselves because a single thing cannot be understood.
Angels know themselves only through their specific powers, not their essence.
Angels do not know themselves because they lack physical senses.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that an angel is a subsisting intelligible form (immaterial), and therefore understands itself by its own form, which is its substance.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why an angel can know itself?
options: Because an angel's form is self-subsisting, so it does not need a separate object.
Because angels are moved by their own thoughts in the same way humans are.
Because the object of knowledge must be separate from the knower to be known.
Because angels are single substances, which makes them naturally intelligible.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that for a self-subsisting form (like an angel), the form is both the knower and the known, so it understands itself without needing a separate external object.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that nothing can be moved or passive to itself?
options: By suggesting that self-knowledge is a transient action rather than an immanent one.
By arguing that angels are physical things, so they can be moved by themselves.
By stating that being passive applies only to the intellect when it is in potentiality.
By claiming that angels do not have an intellect, so the rule does not apply.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas states that the intellect is only passive or moved when it is in potentiality, which is not the case for the angelic intellect regarding self-knowledge.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's conclusion regarding whether one angel can know another?
options: No, because an angel's own nature blocks the perception of external beings.
No, because each angel is a unique species and cannot grasp another's essence.
Yes, because God impressed the forms of all creatures into the mind of every angel.
Only if one angel is the direct cause of the other angel's existence.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that God impressed the intelligible forms of all spiritual and corporeal creatures into every angel's mind, allowing them to know each other.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, what is the primary mechanism that allows an angel to know other beings?
options: The angel observes the other being directly through spiritual senses.
Angels share a collective consciousness that allows instant knowledge transfer between them.
The angel deduces the other's nature by observing its effects in the physical world.
God impressed the intelligible forms of all creatures into the angel's mind at creation.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that God impressed the forms of all things, both corporeal and spiritual, into the angelic mind so they could understand them.

questions.q: In his reply to Objection 2, how does Aquinas explain that one angel can know another even if neither causes the other?
options: Angels cannot know each other unless they are both caused by the same lower angel.
Knowledge requires causality, so angels only know those they directly created.
Knowledge depends on likeness, which exists between angels even without a causal relationship.
Causality is irrelevant because angels communicate telepathically without any mental forms.
questions.explanation: Aquinas replies that while cause and effect imply likeness, likeness itself is sufficient for knowledge, and angels share likeness without necessarily causing each other.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether angels know God using only their natural abilities?
options: Angels cannot know God at all without divine help.
Angels know God perfectly because they are spiritual beings.
Angels know God only by looking at physical objects.
Angels have some knowledge of God through their own nature.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that angels can have some knowledge of God by their own principles, placing this knowledge midway between seeing God's essence and seeing Him in creatures.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for how an angel's natural knowledge of God works?
options: The angel sees God's essence directly in its own mind.
The angel uses physical senses to perceive divine light.
The angel receives a direct message from God every day.
The angel's nature acts as a mirror reflecting God's image.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that the angel knows God because God's image is impressed on the angel's nature, making the angel's nature itself a kind of mirror representing the Divine image.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that God is too far above angels to be known?
options: He says infinite distance prevents any kind of knowledge.
He says they cannot comprehend God but can still know Him.
He agrees that angels cannot know God at all.
He says God is not actually above the angels.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas clarifies that while the infinite distance prevents angels from comprehending God or seeing His essence, it does not mean they have no knowledge of Him at all.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the article's question?
options: Angels know material things only by directly observing them in the physical world.
Angels know material things, but only through physical senses and imagination.
Angels know material things by possessing their intelligible forms in their minds.
Angles do not know material things because they are too perfect for such objects.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that angels know material things because these things exist in the angels through their intelligible species, which are acts of the angel's intellect.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why angels can know material things?
options: Angels have physical bodies that allow them to sense the material world directly.
Material things are perfect enough to serve as the ultimate goal of angelic existence.
Angels are intellectual beings, so material things exist in them as intelligible forms.
God forces knowledge of material things into the minds of all created beings.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because angels are intellectual beings, material things are contained in them in an intellectual manner (as intelligible species), similar to how God knows them.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that angels lack senses and imagination to know material things?
options: He claims that senses are required for all knowledge, so angels must have them.
He suggests that angels learn about material things through direct conversation with humans.
He argues that angels use a superior form of imagination to visualize physical objects.
He states that the intellect alone grasps essences, so senses and imagination are not needed.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas explains that senses and imagination only grasp outward accidents or images, whereas the intellect alone apprehends the essences of things, which is how angels know them.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether angels know individual, specific things?
options: Angels know singulars directly through their single intellectual power.
Angels know singulars only through their universal causes.
Angels only know general categories, not specific individual things.
Angels know singulars only by observing them with physical senses.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that angels, being higher than humans, use their one intellectual faculty to know both universals and singulars, unlike humans who need separate senses for singulars.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for why angels must know singular things?
options: They must know specifics to properly govern and care for the world.
They need to know specifics to compete with human knowledge.
They need to know specifics to move the stars physically.
They must know specifics to prove the existence of God.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that since angels are ministering spirits who administer and provide for the world, they must know the individual acts and things they oversee, as providence applies to specific individuals.

questions.q: In his reply to Objection 1, how does Aquinas explain why the Philosopher's view does not apply to angels?
options: The Philosopher described human intellect, which abstracts from matter; angels do not think this way.
The Philosopher meant that angels know universals, but Aquinas disagrees with this.
The Philosopher was wrong because angels have physical senses like humans do.
The Philosopher's view applies only to God, not to created beings like angels.
questions.explanation: Aquinas clarifies that the Philosopher (Aristotle) was speaking about the human intellect, which relies on abstraction from material conditions, a process that does not fit the nature of angelic understanding.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, do angels know future events with absolute certainty?
options: No, they know nothing about the future except what God directly reveals.
Yes, their intelligence is so powerful they see all future moments clearly.
No, they can only predict likely outcomes based on causes, not chance events.
Yes, because they exist outside of time and see everything as present.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that angels know the future only through causes (predicting likely outcomes), whereas knowing future events in themselves, especially chance ones, belongs to God alone.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas say angels cannot know future events in themselves?
options: Because angelic intellects are limited by the succession of concepts.
Because future events do not yet exist in nature to be known.
Because angels lack the innate universal species required to understand time.
Because only God's eternal perspective sees all time as simultaneously present.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that knowing the future in itself requires seeing all time as present, a capacity unique to God's eternity, which created intellects like angels do not possess.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that angels know distant places, so they should know distant times?
options: Angels only know places where humans currently reside, not all distant places.
Distant places already exist in nature, but future events do not yet exist.
Angels know distant places through physical senses, not intellectual understanding.
Time and space are fundamentally different categories for angelic minds.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 4, Aquinas explains that things distant in place already exist and share in species, whereas future things do not yet exist in this way, making the comparison invalid.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether angels can know secret thoughts?
options: Angels cannot know any secret thoughts because human will is completely hidden from all non-human beings.
Angels know thoughts by seeing the mental images directly, just as we see the shape of a physical object.
Angels can only know thoughts through physical signs, while God alone knows them as they exist in the mind.
Angels can know all thoughts directly because they have no physical bodies to hide them.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that while angels can detect thoughts via bodily effects (like a doctor reading a pulse), only God can know the internal state of the will and mind directly.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why only God can know thoughts as they are in the mind?
options: Angels are too busy attending to their own duties to pay attention to human internal states.
Human thoughts are too complex and chaotic for angelic minds to process or understand correctly.
The human will is the sole agent that chooses to use knowledge, and only God controls this will.
Physical bodies block the transmission of mental information to angels, leaving only God with access.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that using knowledge is entirely up to the will, and since God is the only one who can work in the will as its ultimate end, only He knows what the will is actually doing.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that seeing an angel's mental concepts means knowing their current thoughts?
options: He argues that the objection confuses having the capacity to know with actually using that knowledge at a moment.
He rejects the premise because angels do not possess any mental concepts or intelligible species at all.
He states that angels hide their mental concepts from each other to maintain their individual privacy and rank.
He agrees that seeing the concepts proves the angel is currently thinking about those specific subjects.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas clarifies that while one angel can see the general concepts another possesses, this does not reveal how that angel is currently using them in active thought.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main conclusion regarding the angels' knowledge of the mysteries of grace?
options: They do not know any mysteries of grace because these depend entirely on God's hidden will.
They know some mysteries through divine vision, but not all, and not to the same degree.
They know every mystery of grace by looking directly at God's wisdom without any limits.
They know all mysteries of grace perfectly and equally from the moment they are created.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that angels know mysteries of grace through their vision of God, but explicitly notes they do not know all of them and do not know them equally.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas argue that an angel's natural knowledge cannot grasp the mysteries of grace?
options: Because the mysteries of grace are only revealed to human prophets and are never shared with angelic beings.
Because these mysteries rely on God's free will, which is as hidden to angels as one person's thoughts are to another.
Because angels lack the physical senses required to perceive the events of the Incarnation and other miracles.
Because angels are too weak to understand the complex reasons behind the divine plan for human salvation.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that natural knowledge fails because mysteries depend on God's will, comparing it to how no one can know another person's inner thoughts without that person's spirit.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that angels know the Incarnation because it is the most excellent mystery?
options: He says angels know the Incarnation in general terms as a guiding principle, but not every specific detail.
He claims that the Incarnation is not actually a mystery of grace but a natural event observed by all.
He argues that the Incarnation was hidden from all angels until the time of Christ's birth on earth.
He insists that only the highest angels know the Incarnation, while lower angels remain completely ignorant of it.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas clarifies that the Incarnation is known to angels in a general way as a principle for their duties, distinguishing this from knowing every particular detail.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether an angel's intellect is sometimes in potentiality and sometimes in act?
options: It is never in potentiality at all, as angels possess perfect and unchanging knowledge of everything at all times.
It is never in potentiality regarding natural knowledge, but can be for new divine revelations and when not actively thinking.
It is always in a state of potentiality because angels are constantly learning and desiring to know more about God.
It is only in potentiality when angels are tired, but otherwise it is always in a state of active understanding.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that angels have innate natural knowledge (never potential) but can receive new revealed truths (potential) and do not always actively consider what they naturally know (potential).

questions.q: Why does Aquinas say an angel's intellect is never in potentiality regarding the things it knows by nature?
options: Because angels are purely spiritual beings who do not have physical bodies that limit their understanding.
Because angels choose to ignore potentiality in order to maintain their blessed state of being.
Because God directly implants all natural knowledge into angels, preventing any possibility of ignorance.
Because their natural knowledge is fully present from the start, like heavenly bodies that do not need to move to exist.
questions.explanation: Aquinas compares angels to heavenly bodies, stating that just as celestial bodies have no potentiality to existence, angels have no potentiality to natural knowledge; it is fully actualized by innate species.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that angels are in potentiality because Scripture says they 'desire to look' on God?
options: Their desire is for fresh revelations needed for their tasks, not for something they lack or cannot yet know.
Angels desire to look because they are weary of their current vision and seek a new experience.
The Scripture is metaphorical, meaning angels are curious but already possess complete knowledge of God.
The desire indicates that angels are imperfect beings who are constantly striving to improve their intellect.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas states that angelic desire does not exclude the object (God) but rather seeks fresh revelations to prepare them for specific duties.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion about whether an angel can understand many things at the same time?
options: Angels can only understand one thing at a time, just like human beings do.
Angels cannot understand multiple things simultaneously because their intellect is limited by physical shape.
Angels can understand many things at once only if those things are completely unrelated to each other.
Angels can understand all things simultaneously because they know everything through the single concept of the Divine essence.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that angels know all things at once through their knowledge of the Divine essence, which serves as a single intelligible concept containing all things.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, what is the main reason angels can grasp many distinct things in a single act of understanding?
options: Because understanding is a physical movement that can cover multiple points at once.
Because angels have a special ability to ignore the differences between distinct objects.
Because all these things are contained within one single intelligible concept, specifically the Divine essence.
Because angels use their senses to see all things together before their intellect processes them.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that unity of operation requires unity of object; since angels know things through the one concept of the Divine essence, they grasp all things simultaneously.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that one intellect cannot be informed by many intelligible shapes, just as one body cannot have many shapes?
options: He argues that one internal concept can represent many external objects, just as one shape can resemble many different bodies.
He admits the objection is correct but claims angels are spirits, so physical rules do not apply to them.
He replies that angels do not use an intellect, but rather a higher form of sensory perception.
He states that the intellect is not informed by concepts at all, but by direct divine illumination.
questions.explanation: In his reply to Objection 2, Aquinas clarifies that the intellect holds the species within itself, allowing one concept to mirror many objects, analogous to one shape resembling many bodies.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion about how angels know things?
options: They grasp all truths contained in a principle instantly.
They acquire knowledge through repeated experience and memory.
They learn by moving step-by-step from one idea to another.
They reason from causes to effects to find new truths.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that angels do not use discursive reasoning (moving from one step to the next) but instead see all consequences of a truth immediately.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why angelic knowledge is not discursive?
options: Angels are lower in the order of nature than human beings.
Angels have a weaker intellectual light than humans do.
Angels possess full intellectual light, allowing them to see all conclusions at once.
Angels are spiritual beings who do not interact with the physical world.
questions.explanation: He explains that because angels have the fullness of intellectual light, they perceive the entire range of a principle's implications in a single act, unlike humans who need time to reason.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that demons learn more things by experience?
options: He states that Aristotle was wrong about the nature of experimental knowledge.
He argues that experience is impossible for any spiritual substance.
He says the term is used by similarity, as they know present things without reasoning.
He agrees that demons use experience to build knowledge step-by-step.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas clarifies that saying demons have 'experience' is just a comparison; they know present sensible things directly without any discursive process.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding how angels understand things?
options: Angels understand by using affirmative and negative speech patterns.
Angels understand simply by grasping the essence, without composing or dividing.
Angels understand by actively combining and separating concepts in their minds.
Angels understand by reasoning through a series of logical steps.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that because the angel's intellectual light is perfect, they do not need to compose or divide; they understand the essence directly.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why angels do not understand by composing and dividing?
options: They are pure spirits that cannot handle material or movable concepts.
They lack the ability to process multiple distinct natures simultaneously.
Their speech patterns do not allow for complex logical structures.
Their intellectual light is perfect, so they grasp all attributes of a thing at once.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that human weakness requires composition and division, but angels have a perfect intellectual light that allows them to see all that is contained in a thing immediately.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that angels use affirmative and negative speech?
options: It suggests they are mimicking human reasoning without understanding it.
It indicates that speech is the primary source of their intellectual knowledge.
It shows they know the nature simply, not by the act of composing.
It proves they must be composing and dividing to form those sentences.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas states that using such speech shows they know both composition and division, but they know them by simply understanding the nature of the thing, not by performing the act of composing.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main conclusion regarding whether angels can have falsehood in their intellect?
options: All angels, including demons, are completely incapable of any error or falsehood whatsoever.
Demons are always false in their intellect, while good angels are always perfectly true.
Angels frequently make mistakes because their knowledge is limited compared to God's.
Angels are never false in themselves, but demons can be accidentally misled about supernatural matters.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that falsehood does not exist in angels by nature, but demons can be accidentally deceived regarding supernatural events because they ignore God's special will.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas say that angels do not naturally fall into error when understanding things?
options: They rely on divine revelation for every single fact, so they never have to reason things out.
They only think about simple things and avoid complex ideas that could lead to confusion.
They understand the core nature of things directly, without combining separate parts that might conflict.
Their intellects are so powerful that they can instantly correct any mistake they make.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that human error comes from 'composing and dividing' concepts, whereas angels grasp the essence of a thing directly, which is always true.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that demons have 'perversity' and therefore falsehood?
options: Their perversity means they lie intentionally to trick humans, which counts as intellectual falsehood.
Their perversity proves that all angels are inherently flawed and prone to natural error.
Their perversity is only emotional, so their intellectual understanding remains perfectly accurate.
Their perversity stems from rejecting divine wisdom, leading them to judge supernatural events wrongly.
questions.explanation: Aquinas clarifies that the 'perversity' of demons is their refusal to submit to divine wisdom, causing them to form wrong opinions about supernatural matters like the resurrection.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the existence of 'morning' and 'evening' knowledge in angels?
options: Angels have noonday knowledge instead, which replaces the morning and evening concepts.
Angels only have morning knowledge because they never make mistakes.
Angels possess both morning and evening knowledge as distinct ways of knowing things.
Angels have neither morning nor evening knowledge because they lack darkness.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states in his answer that angels do have both morning and evening knowledge, rejecting the objections that claim they have neither or only one.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, what is the main reason for distinguishing between morning and evening knowledge?
options: Morning is when angels see clearly, and evening is when they see dimly due to darkness.
Morning refers to knowing things as they exist in God's plan, and evening to knowing them in their own nature.
Morning knowledge is about the sun rising, and evening knowledge is about the sun setting.
Morning is for good angels, and evening is for evil spirits who are in darkness.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that morning knowledge is of things in the Word (God's plan), while evening knowledge is of things in their own created nature, marking the beginning and end of their existence.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that there should also be 'noonday' and 'night' knowledge?
options: The objection is valid, so Aquinas agrees that angels also possess noonday and night knowledge.
No, because noonday and night are just other times of day that do not apply to spiritual beings.
Morning and evening belong to the day of good angels, who do not turn to creatures like night does.
Yes, but noonday knowledge is reserved for humans, while night knowledge is for demons.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas clarifies that morning and evening pertain to the 'day' of enlightened angels, who do not adhere to creatures (which would be 'night'), thus excluding noonday and night.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether morning and evening knowledge are the same?
options: Evening knowledge is a lower form that disappears when morning knowledge begins.
They are essentially the same act of knowing, differing only in what is being known.
They are completely different faculties that angels use at different times.
They are distinct because angels draw knowledge from things themselves.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that if we look at the medium of knowing (the Word), the knowledge is essentially one, differing only by the aspect of the object known.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why morning and evening knowledge might be considered essentially one?
options: Angels know things through the Word, which serves as the single medium for both types of knowledge.
Evening knowledge is imperfect and is replaced by the perfect morning knowledge.
Angels always behold God, so their knowledge never changes or shifts focus.
The Bible says 'evening and morning, one day,' proving the knowledge is unified.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since angels know things through the Word, the act of knowing is one, even if the specific aspect of the thing known differs.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that one faculty cannot have two operations at the same time?
options: The intellect perceives principles and conclusions at different times, not at the same instant.
One faculty can have two simultaneous operations if one is referred to the other, like willing ends and means.
Angels do not have faculties like humans, so the rule about simultaneous operations does not apply to them.
Morning and evening knowledge happen at different times, so there is no conflict with having two operations.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas states that one faculty can perform two operations at once if one refers to the other, citing the will and intellect as examples.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the presence of will in angels?
options: Angels have a will only in the sense of natural inclination, like plants.
Angels have no will because they are immovable and cannot be stirred by objects.
Angles possess a will because they understand the general nature of good.
Angels lack a will because they have no reason, only a higher faculty.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that we must place a will in angels because their intellect knows the universal aspect of goodness.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for believing angels have a will?
options: They perceive specific goods through their senses, similar to animals.
They desire things they do not yet possess, which defines appetite.
They are moved by external objects, just like human wills are.
They understand the general concept of goodness, not just specific items.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that will follows the intellect's knowledge of good in general, which angels possess, unlike sensitive appetite which follows knowledge of particular goods.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that will is a 'mover which is moved' and angels are immovable?
options: He argues that this type of movement is an act of a perfect agent.
He says angels are not truly immovable, so the objection is factually wrong.
He claims that will is not a mover at all, so the premise fails.
He states that angels do not understand objects, so they are not moved.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 3, Aquinas explains that the 'movement' of will and understanding is an act of a perfect agent, which can exist in angels.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about the relationship between an angel's will and its intellect?
options: They are distinct powers because one receives knowledge while the other seeks good.
They are the same power because angels are simpler than physical bodies.
They differ only logically, not really, because the good and true are the same.
The will is identical to the angel's essence since it desires its own good.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that intellect and will are different powers in all creatures because the intellect brings the object inside the knower, while the will reaches out toward the good.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why an angel's will cannot be its essence?
options: Angels have no matter, so they cannot have natural inclinations to external things.
Angels are too simple to have multiple distinct powers like humans do.
The will is a material faculty that requires a separate physical body to function.
A creature's essence is finite, so it cannot contain all good within itself.
questions.explanation: He states that essence and will are only identical in God, who contains all good; since created things have limited goodness, their will must be distinct from their essence.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that the good and true are only logically different?
options: He says the difference in how the objects are grasped is enough to separate the powers.
He argues that the good is a specific type of truth unique to the intellect.
He agrees that the faculties are not really different, only conceptually distinct.
He claims that angels do not have a will because they lack material objects.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas explains that the formal distinction in how the good and true are understood is sufficient to differentiate the will from the intellect.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether angels possess free will?
options: Angels have free will, but it is inferior to that of humans.
Angels act purely by nature and therefore have no free choice.
Angels lack free will because they do not need to deliberate or inquire.
Angels have free will, and it is more perfect than human free will.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that since angels have intellect, they have free will, and it exists in them in a higher degree of perfection than in man.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, what is the primary reason angels have free will?
options: They possess an intellect that allows them to judge the common good.
They are not bound by physical bodies like humans are.
They are superior to irrational animals which act only by instinct.
They can choose between good and evil without any guidance.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that free will is tied to intellect because only an intellectual agent can apprehend the general concept of goodness and judge specific things as good.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that angels cannot choose because they do not 'inquire' or 'take counsel'?
options: He claims that angels do inquire, but their inquiry is instantaneous and perfect.
He suggests that angels use a different type of counsel that is not intellectual.
He argues that the definition of choice used in the objection applies to humans, not angels.
He states that choice does not require inquiry for any being, human or angel.
questions.explanation: In his reply to Objection 1, Aquinas says the Philosopher's definition of choice is meant for humans who need to inquire, whereas angels do not need to inquire in the same way.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion about the appetites in angels?
options: Angles have both irascible and concupiscible appetites because they can sin.
Angels possess an irascible appetite but lack a concupiscible one.
Angels have a sensitive appetite that is divided into two parts.
Angels have only a single, undivided appetite known as the will.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that because angels only have an intellective appetite, it is not divided into irascible and concupiscible parts but remains undivided and is called the will.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why angelic appetite is not divided?
options: Angels are purely spiritual and do not have physical bodies to feel emotions.
The intellective appetite aims at good in a general way, not specific sensory goods.
The will in angels is stronger than the sensitive appetite in humans.
Angels are too perfect to experience the confusion of divided mental faculties.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that the intellective appetite seeks good under a common aspect, whereas the sensitive appetite seeks particular sensory goods, which is why only the latter is divided.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that demons have unreasonable fury and wild concupiscence?
options: He agrees that demons have these appetites because they are fallen angels.
He claims Dionysius was mistaken and should not be cited in this context.
He argues that demons actually have a sensitive appetite unlike good angels.
He says these terms are used metaphorically based on the similarity of their effects.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas states that fury and concupiscence are said of demons metaphorically, similar to how anger is attributed to God, due to the resemblance in the resulting effects.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether angels possess natural love?
options: Angles must have natural love because their nature includes an innate inclination.
Angels have neither natural nor intellectual love, only divine charity.
Angels have natural love only if they are in a state of wickedness.
Angels lack natural love since their love is purely intellectual and free.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that we must necessarily place natural love in angels, as every nature has an inclination.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why angels must have natural love?
options: Nature precedes intellect, so intellectual beings retain the natural inclinations of their essence.
Natural love is superior to intellectual love and thus dominates the angelic mind.
Without natural love, angels would lack the capacity for sensory perception.
Angels are created beings and therefore cannot act entirely on their own free will.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that what comes first (nature) is sustained in what comes after (intellect), so intellectual natures retain natural inclinations.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that natural love implies being acted upon rather than acting freely?
options: He claims that angels do not have free will, so they are purely acted upon.
He argues that all created things are moved by something else, except God alone.
He asserts that free will and being acted upon are identical concepts in angels.
He states that natural love is a form of wickedness, which forces action.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas clarifies that all things except the First Agent (God) are moved to act by something else.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether angels possess 'love of choice'?
options: Angels have love of choice but lack any form of natural love.
Angels possess both a natural love and a love of choice.
Angels only have natural love because they lack human reasoning.
Angels have no love of choice since they do not deliberate.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states in his answer that 'There exists in the angels a natural love, and a love of choice.'

questions.q: Why does Aquinas argue that angels can have love of choice despite having perfect intellects?
options: Because angels must deduce conclusions from first principles like humans do.
Because choosing a means to an end is not a sign of intellectual imperfection.
Because their will is imperfect and requires guidance from their intellect.
Because love of choice is identical to natural love in perfect beings.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that seeking one thing naturally as an end and another by choice as a means 'does not argue imperfection in the person desiring.'

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that love of choice is only 'rational' (human) and not 'intellectual' (angelic)?
options: He states that intellectual love is a lower form of rational love.
He denies that angels have any form of love that follows counsel.
He argues that angels actually do use discursive reasoning to make choices.
He claims that not all choice requires the discursive reasoning found in humans.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 1, Aquinas says 'every choice does not follow a discursive act of the reason; but only human choice,' distinguishing it from angelic choice.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the article's question?
options: Angels cannot love themselves because love requires two separate people.
Angels love themselves only when they choose to, not by nature.
Angels love themselves with both natural instinct and deliberate choice.
Angels love themselves only through natural instinct, not through deliberate choice.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that angels and humans naturally love themselves and also love themselves through choice.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why angels can love themselves?
options: Goodness exists in both the being itself and in its qualities, allowing for two types of love.
Natural love and chosen love are identical, so the distinction is unnecessary.
Angels are superior to humans, so they do not need to follow the rules of love.
Love is a movement that must always travel from one person to another.
questions.explanation: He argues that since good is found in both substance and accidents, a thing can be loved as a subsisting good (friendship) and as an inherent good (concupiscence).

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that love is a movement which must tend toward something else?
options: He says that love is not a movement at all, but a static state of being.
He argues that movement can stay within the person and reflect back on themselves.
He insists that the objection is wrong because angels are not physical beings.
He claims that angels do not move, so the definition of love does not apply to them.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, he explains that love is an action that remains within the agent and can reflect back upon the lover, similar to how knowledge reflects on the knower.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main conclusion regarding whether an angel loves another angel with natural love?
options: No, because an angel knows himself better than he knows any other angel.
Yes, because they share the same nature and are united by species.
Yes, but only if the other angel is of a higher rank.
No, because natural love is reserved only for one's own self.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that angels do love each other with natural affection because they are united by sharing the same nature or species.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for why an angel loves another angel naturally?
options: Because everything naturally loves what is united with it by nature.
Because loving others is the only way to achieve personal happiness.
Because angels are created from the same physical matter.
Because God commands angels to love one another equally.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since things are one with what they are naturally united to, they naturally love that which shares their nature.

questions.q: In his reply to Objection 2, how does Aquinas clarify the phrase 'loves another as himself'?
options: It means the love is based on social agreement.
It means likeness, not equal intensity of love.
It means the love is exactly equal in strength.
It means the love is weaker than self-love.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that 'as' denotes likeness, not equality; an angel loves himself more because he is numerically one with himself, whereas he loves others only by species.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding how an angel loves God compared to itself?
options: The angel loves God more than itself because God is the universal good for all creatures.
The angel loves God less than itself because the divine nature is too distant.
The angel loves God and itself equally since both are good in their own right.
The angel loves itself more than God because its own nature is closer to it.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that because every creature naturally belongs to God as the universal good, the angel loves God before itself and with greater intensity.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why the angel loves God more than itself?
options: The angel's intellect is superior to its will, forcing it to choose the higher good.
Angels are commanded by God to prioritize His glory over their own happiness.
Love of God is a supernatural gift that overrides the angel's natural self-interest.
Natural things are more strongly inclined toward what they belong to than to themselves.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that in the natural order, things are principally inclined toward that to which they belong, and since creatures belong to God, they love Him more.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that nature is self-centered and acts only for self-preservation?
options: He claims that angels do not have a nature that acts for self-preservation at all.
He states that nature also inclines toward the common good, which includes the universal good.
He argues that self-preservation is the only true natural goal for any living being.
He says that self-centeredness is a defect that only humans possess, not angels.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas explains that nature is inclined not just to individual preservation but also to the preservation of the species and the universal good.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether angels have a cause for their existence?
options: Angels were mentioned in Genesis but were not actually created by God.
Angels are eternal and have always existed alongside God.
Angels exist on their own and do not need a creator or cause.
Angels were created by God, just like everything else that is not God.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that angels, like all things except God, were made by God because they do not exist by their own essence.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why angels must have been made by God?
options: Angels' nature is different from their existence, so they need a cause to exist.
Angels are mentioned in the Bible, which proves they are created beings.
Angels are less powerful than God, so they must depend on Him.
Angels are made of matter, so they must be formed by an external agent.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that only God is His own existence; in angels, essence and existence differ, meaning they participate in existence and thus require a cause.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that immaterial forms (like angels) have no cause because they have no matter?
options: He agrees that angels have no cause because they are pure forms without matter.
He says angels have no cause that shapes matter, but do have a cause for their whole being.
He claims that the objection is wrong because angels are not actually immaterial forms.
He argues that angels do have matter, just very subtle and invisible matter.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas clarifies that while subsisting forms lack a cause that shapes matter, they still have a cause that produces their entire substance.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether angels have existed forever?
options: Angels have existed from eternity because they are spiritual beings.
Angels existed before God created the physical universe.
Angels have always existed alongside God without a beginning.
Angels were created by God at a specific time after they did not exist.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that God is the only eternal being and that He created creatures 'from nothing,' meaning they did not exist before He made them.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for rejecting the idea that angels are eternal?
options: Only God is eternal, and all other things are made from nothing.
Angels are subject to physical time because they move through space.
God's will is forced to create things at specific moments by necessity.
Angels lack the ability to understand truth, so they cannot last forever.
questions.explanation: The core of his answer is that Catholic faith holds that only God is eternal, and everything else was produced by God from nothing.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that angels must be eternal because they are above physical time?
options: He argues that angels are above all forms of time, including their own existence.
He states that while angels are above physical motion, they still have a beginning.
He says that physical time is the only type of time that matters for creation.
He claims that angels do not exist at all, so time does not apply to them.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas clarifies that angels are above the time measured by heavenly movement but are not above the time that measures their existence after non-existence.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main conclusion regarding when angels were created?
options: Angels were created at the same time as the physical world.
The timing of angel creation is completely unknowable to humans.
Angels were created after the physical world was fully formed.
Angels were created long before the physical world began.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that the more probable opinion, which he supports, is that angels were created simultaneously with corporeal creatures to form a complete universe.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's primary reason for believing angels were created with the physical world?
options: The Bible explicitly states in Genesis that angels appeared on the first day.
Angels are part of the whole universe, and a part is imperfect if separated from the whole.
Angels are divine beings who exist outside of time and space entirely.
God needed angels to help Him create the physical world first.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since angels are part of the universe, they should not be created separately, as no part is perfect when isolated from the whole.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that angels are midway between God and matter?
options: Angels do not stand midway; they are purely spiritual with no relation to matter.
Angels are actually closer to matter than to God in their nature.
God is above the universe and contains all perfection, unlike angels who are parts.
The objection is valid, but God chose to create them later anyway.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas clarifies that God is above the universe and holds its perfection within Himself, whereas angels are merely parts of the universe, so the comparison fails.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about where the angels were created?
options: They were created in a spiritual realm above the physical sky.
They were created in the lower atmosphere near the earth.
They were created outside of any physical location entirely.
They were created in the highest physical place in the universe.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states it was fitting for angels to be created in the highest corporeal place, which he identifies as the empyrean heaven, to preside over all physical nature.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for this conclusion?
options: Angels need a physical body to exist and function properly.
Angels are physically lighter than air and naturally rise to the top.
The Bible explicitly names the empyrean heaven as the angelic home.
Spiritual beings were made to rule over and relate to physical creation.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since the universe includes both physical and spiritual creatures, the spiritual ones were created to bear a relationship to and rule over the physical ones.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that Augustine said angels were created in the upper atmosphere?
options: He states that the upper atmosphere is actually the empyrean heaven.
He says Augustine meant the highest part of heaven, not the air layer.
He claims Augustine was mistaken about the location of the angels.
He argues that only the sinning angels were in the lower atmosphere.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas suggests that by 'upper atmosphere,' Augustine likely meant the highest part of heaven, which has an affinity with the subtle and transparent air.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether angels were created in a state of perfect happiness?
options: They were created without any happiness and had to earn it through long effort.
They were created in a state of confusion and had to choose their own level of happiness.
They were created with natural happiness but not the supreme happiness of seeing God directly.
They were created with the supreme happiness of seeing God directly from the very start.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that angels were created with the happiness they could achieve by their own nature, but not the higher, supernatural happiness of seeing God's essence, which is a gift beyond nature.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas argue that angels did not receive the highest form of happiness immediately upon creation?
options: Because their natural intelligence was too weak to handle the intensity of divine vision.
Because God wanted to test their loyalty before granting them such a great reward.
Because they had not yet completed the work of creating the physical world.
Because this supreme happiness is a goal beyond their natural abilities, not an inherent part of their nature.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that the ultimate beatitude of seeing God as He is exceeds the power of any created intellect; therefore, it is an end to be reached, not a natural starting point.

questions.q: How does Aquinas address the first objection, which claims angels were created in beatitude based on a specific text?
options: He dismisses the text as irrelevant because it was written by a human author, not a divine one.
He argues that the text is mistranslated and actually says angels were created in a state of doubt.
He clarifies that the text uses 'beatitude' to mean the natural perfection they possessed, not the supreme vision of God.
He agrees with the objection but adds that this beatitude was temporary and later lost.
questions.explanation: In his reply to Objection 1, Aquinas explains that the cited passage uses the word 'beatitude' to refer to the natural perfection angels had in their innocent state, not the supernatural beatitude of glory.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about whether an angel needs grace to turn to God?
options: Angels do not need grace because turning to God is a natural human task.
Angels need grace only to overcome internal obstacles that prevent their love.
Angels do not need grace because they naturally love God as their creator.
Angels need grace to turn to God for the sake of seeing His essence.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that angels needed grace to turn to God as the object of beatitude, specifically the vision of His essence, which is beyond their natural power.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why angels need this help?
options: The angel’s will is naturally inclined to turn away from God’s presence.
Angels are too weak to love God without external assistance from other angels.
Grace is required to make the act of loving God less difficult for angels.
Seeing God’s essence is beyond the natural capacity of any created mind.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since seeing God’s essence is above nature, the will cannot be directed toward it without a supernatural principle, which is grace.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that angels naturally love God and thus need no help?
options: He distinguishes between loving God as creator and turning to Him for beatitude.
He claims that the natural love of angels is actually a form of supernatural grace.
He rejects the objection by stating that angels do not naturally love God at all.
He argues that natural love is insufficient because it is not directed at the essence.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas clarifies that while angels naturally love God as the author of their being, the specific turning to God for the vision of His essence requires grace.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main conclusion regarding the state of angels at the moment of their creation?
options: They were created in glory immediately upon their existence.
They were created in sanctifying grace from the very beginning.
They were created without form and only later received grace.
They were created in a natural state and received grace later.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that it is more probable and consistent with holy writings that angels were created in sanctifying grace, not just in a natural state.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for believing angels were created in grace?
options: Augustine explicitly states in Genesis that angels were made of light.
Angels are intellectual beings who cannot sin once they receive grace.
Grace relates to beatitude the way seed forms relate to natural effects.
Grace is the necessary end goal that all rational creatures must eventually reach.
questions.explanation: Aquinas uses an analogy: just as seed forms are implanted in creatures at creation, grace (the seed of God) was implanted in angels at their creation.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that grace would prevent angels from ever turning away from God?
options: He claims that angels do not have a mode of nature involving free inclination.
He explains that grace does not impose necessity, so free choice remains.
He states that grace removes the ability to choose objects of desire.
He argues that grace imposes a strict necessity that overrides free will.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas states that because intellectual natures are inclined freely, grace does not impose necessity, allowing for the possibility of sin.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether an angel merits his beatitude?
options: Angels merit beatitude because they possessed grace before receiving it.
Angels do not merit beatitude because it is their natural state.
Angels receive beatitude without merit, just as they receive grace.
Angels merit beatitude through their current service while in heaven.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that it is best to say angels had grace before entering beatitude, and through that grace, they merited their reward.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why angels must merit their beatitude?
options: Angels experience great difficulty in doing good, which creates merit.
Angels are free agents who choose to work for their reward.
God demands merit from all creatures as a strict legal requirement.
Beatitude exceeds the natural capacity of angels, so it requires merit.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because ultimate happiness is beyond what angelic nature can achieve on its own, it must be attained through merit rather than natural operation.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that angels faced no difficulty in acting rightly?
options: There is no difficulty, so angels do not merit their beatitude.
Angels actually struggle against evil desires just like humans do.
The difficulty is psychological, arising from the weight of responsibility.
The difficulty comes from the good being beyond their natural power.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas states that the difficulty is not from internal hindrance but from the fact that the good work exceeds their natural capacity.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding when angels received their final happiness?
options: They were born with it and did not need to earn it at all.
They received it only after a long period of spiritual growth.
They received it immediately after performing a single good act.
They had to perform many good acts over time to earn it.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that the angel was beatified instantly after the first act of charity, which is the single act of merit.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why angels did not need multiple stages of merit?
options: Angels are smarter than humans and can learn faster.
Angels do not have free will, so they cannot make mistakes.
God decided to be more generous with angels than with humans.
Angelic nature receives its full perfection all at once, not in steps.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that it is proper to the angelic nature to receive perfection at once, rather than passing through various stages like humans do.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that angels should have needed many steps because their final state is so different from their natural state?
options: He argues that merit is not a step between nature and glory.
He says the distance between states does not require multiple acts for angels.
He agrees that many steps are needed but says angels take them very quickly.
He claims angels are not actually far from their natural state.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas states that it is the nature of an angel to instantly attain perfection, so only one meritorious act is required.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's conclusion regarding whether angels receive grace and glory based on their natural gifts?
options: Angels receive grace and glory based on their moral works and actions.
Angels receive equal amounts of grace and glory regardless of their nature.
Angels receive grace and glory in proportion to the degree of their natural gifts.
Angels receive grace and glory solely based on God's arbitrary will, ignoring nature.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states it is reasonable to suppose that grace and glory were bestowed on angels according to the degree of their natural gifts.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why higher-natured angels received greater grace?
options: They performed more moral works than lower-natured angels to earn their reward.
Angels are compounds of different natures that must be balanced by grace.
God's will is completely independent of nature, so nature plays no role.
Their pure nature allows them to turn toward God with full energy, without internal conflict.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because angels are not compounds of conflicting natures like humans, their higher natural powers allow them to turn to God more mightily and efficaciously.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that grace depends on God's will, not nature?
options: Nature is irrelevant because grace comes only from human-like moral acts.
Angels have no nature, so the question of natural gifts is meaningless.
God's will is random and does not follow any order or wisdom.
God's will ordained nature for grace, so degrees of nature match degrees of grace.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 1, Aquinas states that just as God's will ordained nature for grace, it also ordained the various degrees of nature to correspond to various degrees of grace.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding natural knowledge and love in beatified angels?
options: They are replaced entirely by the superior knowledge of beatitude.
They are completely removed because they are imperfect compared to glory.
They cease to exist because the angels' happiness is now complete.
They remain present alongside the higher knowledge and love of glory.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that natural knowledge and love remain in the angels, as nature is preserved in beatitude.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why natural faculties persist in the beatified?
options: Natural love is stronger than divine love and cannot be overridden.
God commands that all original natural gifts must remain unchanged forever.
Angels need natural knowledge to understand the physical world around them.
Beatitude is added to nature, and the foundation must be preserved in what is built upon it.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since beatitude is superadded to nature, nature (the first) must be preserved in beatitude (the second).

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that natural love is removed by the perfection of glory?
options: The perfection of glory only removes hatred, not natural affection.
Natural imperfection supports rather than opposes beatitude, so it is not removed.
Natural love is removed, but replaced by a similar human-like emotion.
Natural love is actually perfect and equal to the love of glory.
questions.explanation: In Reply 1, Aquinas explains that perfection removes its opposite imperfection, but natural imperfection underlies and supports beatitude rather than opposing it.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the ability of a beatified angel to sin?
options: Beatified angels are unable to act at all, so they cannot sin.
Beatified angels cannot sin because their will is fixed on God.
Beatified angels can still sin because their created nature allows for failure.
Beatified angels can choose evil if they exercise their free will.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states in his answer that beatified angels cannot sin because their will is directed solely toward God.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why beatified angels cannot sin?
options: They are physically separated from the world where sin occurs.
Their free will is removed entirely once they reach beatitude.
They have lost their rational powers and can no longer make choices.
They see God's essence, which is pure goodness, making evil impossible.
questions.explanation: The core argument is that seeing God’s essence (which is good) makes it impossible for the angel to will anything else.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that rational powers always incline toward opposites?
options: He argues that beatified angels do not possess rational powers anymore.
He says rational powers do not incline toward opposites when they have a natural tendency.
He agrees that rational powers always incline toward both good and evil.
He claims that the objection is based on a misunderstanding of the Philosopher.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas clarifies that rational powers are not referred to opposites regarding things they have a natural tendency toward.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether angels can increase their happiness?
options: Angels can only increase happiness by helping humans more.
Angels reach a fixed level of happiness and cannot go higher.
Angels can keep rising to higher levels of joy forever.
Angels start with no happiness and earn it over time.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that once an angel reaches the specific degree of beatitude assigned by God, it cannot pass to a higher degree.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why angels cannot advance further?
options: Charity is already perfect in angels, so they cannot merit more.
Advancing would create an imbalance in the spiritual hierarchy.
Angels are too weak to understand the infinite nature of God.
God assigns each creature a specific, fixed limit to its vision of Him.
questions.explanation: He states that God's intention directs each rational creature to a determinate end, fixing their mode of vision at a specific degree.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that angels seem imperfect if they cannot reach the absolute highest place?
options: Angels can still feel joy when they help save other souls.
Angels are actually in the highest degree relative to their own nature.
Angels are not rational creatures, so perfection does not apply to them.
Angels do not care about their rank, only about serving God.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas clarifies that while angels are not in the absolute highest degree, they are in the highest degree for themselves according to Divine predestination.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, is it possible for angels to commit moral faults or sins?
options: No, because angels are purely actual beings with no potentiality for error.
No, because their love for God is natural and therefore cannot be withdrawn.
Yes, because their nature allows for the possibility of deviation from right order.
Only if they are influenced by the evil actions of human beings.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that any rational creature, including angels, can sin by nature because their will is not the ultimate rule of rightness like God's will is.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main reason for saying that created beings, unlike God, can sin?
options: They lack the intellectual capacity to fully understand the nature of good.
Their will must follow an external divine rule, allowing for deviation.
They possess a physical body that is subject to corruption and decay.
Their nature is inherently unstable and prone to changing opinions.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that God's will is the rule itself, so He cannot err, but created wills are measured against God's will and can thus deviate from it.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that angels cannot sin because they lack potentiality?
options: Angels have potentiality in their intellect regarding which object they choose to love.
The objection is correct, but angels sin through ignorance rather than choice.
Angels have no potentiality at all, so they are incapable of any action.
Angels are actually physical beings that can decay like heavenly bodies.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 1, Aquinas clarifies that while angels have no potentiality in their natural existence, they do have potentiality in their intellective part regarding their inclination toward specific objects.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about which sins can exist in angels?
options: Only pride and envy can be found in angels as internal desires.
Angels can feel all sins, including lust and greed for money.
Angels can only commit pride, but not envy or other vices.
Angels are free from all sin because they have no bodies.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because angels are spiritual beings, they can only have spiritual sins. He identifies pride as the first sin and envy as the direct consequence, excluding carnal sins and greed for material goods.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why angels cannot have carnal sins?
options: Angels are too powerful to be tempted by physical desires.
Angels lack bodies, so they cannot experience physical pleasures.
Angels are always focused on God and ignore human actions.
Angels do not have free will, so they cannot choose sin.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that a spiritual nature cannot be affected by bodily pleasures because nothing is affected except by things suited to its nature. Since angels have no bodies, they cannot be moved by carnal delights.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that demons delight in human sexual sins?
options: He claims demons are confused about what sexual sins are.
He states that sexual sins are not real sins for spiritual beings.
He says demons actually enjoy the physical act of lust.
He argues demons only enjoy these sins out of envy of human good.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas clarifies that demons do not have a disposition toward carnal pleasure. Instead, they take pleasure in human sins purely out of envy, seeing them as obstacles to human goodness.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's conclusion regarding whether the devil desired to be equal to God?
options: The devil desired to be equal to God in nature, hoping to become divine.
The devil desired equality with God but was stopped by his own limited wisdom.
The devil did not desire equality because he knew it was impossible and unnatural for a creature.
The devil desired equality only in accidental qualities, not in his essential nature.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that the devil could not desire to be equal to God in nature because he knew this was impossible and would mean ceasing to be himself.

questions.q: How does Aquinas explain the specific sinful desire the devil actually had?
options: He wanted to be subject to no one, effectively wishing for his own non-existence.
He wanted to achieve ultimate happiness through his own natural power, ignoring God's grace.
He wanted to be like God in every way, including being uncreated and eternal.
He wanted to create the universe, a power that belongs only to God.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states the devil sinned by desiring to reach his final goal of happiness by his own natural strength, rather than through supernatural grace from God.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that desiring to be like God is a natural, sinless goal?
options: Desiring likeness is natural, but the devil sinned by wanting it too quickly.
Desiring likeness is only sinless if sought in the proper order, receiving it from God.
Desiring likeness is always sinful because creatures are fundamentally different from God.
Desiring likeness is impossible for angels, so the objection is based on a false premise.
questions.explanation: Aquinas replies that desiring to be like God is not sinful if one seeks this likeness in the right order, meaning by receiving it from God, not by one's own power.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether any demons are naturally wicked?
options: No, demons are neutral spirits that only become evil through external influences.
Yes, demons are naturally deceitful, just as some animals are naturally sly or rapacious.
No, demons are intellectual beings inclined toward good, so they cannot be naturally evil.
Yes, some demons are naturally wicked because they were created by God with flaws.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because demons are intellectual substances, their nature is inclined toward the universal good, making a natural inclination to evil impossible.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why demons cannot be naturally evil?
options: Evil is merely a lack of good, so it cannot exist as a natural property of any being.
Demons lack a physical body, so they cannot have the natural passions that cause evil.
God would not create any creature with an inherent tendency toward wickedness or sin.
Intellectual natures are directed toward the universal good, which excludes any natural connection to evil.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that intellectual natures aim at the universal good, and since no evil can be connected to the universal good, such beings cannot naturally tend toward evil.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that some men are naturally wicked, implying demons might be too?
options: The objection is invalid because men are not created by God in the same way as angels.
Men are naturally wicked only when they reject God's law, which demons do not do.
Men are naturally wicked because they are imperfect copies of angels, who are naturally good.
Human 'natural' malice stems from habit or sensitive passions, not from the intellectual nature itself.
questions.explanation: Aquinas clarifies that when humans are called naturally wicked, it refers to custom or sensitive passions, not their intellectual nature, which remains distinct from the demons' nature.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the devil's sin at the moment of his creation?
options: The devil's nature was evil from the start, forcing him to sin immediately.
The devil could have chosen to sin, but he decided to wait until later.
The devil sinned immediately in the very first instant of his existence.
It was impossible for the devil to sin in the first instant of his creation.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that it was impossible for the angel to sin in the first instant by an inordinate act of free will.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why the devil could not sin immediately?
options: The first operation of a being must come from its creator, not its own will.
