Angels are too powerful to make mistakes during their initial moment of being.
Sin requires a prior state of goodness that does not exist in the first instant.
The act of creation and the act of sinning cannot both end in the same instant.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that the operation beginning with existence comes from the agent's productive cause (God), not from the agent's own free will.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that John 8:44 says the devil was a murderer from the beginning?
options: He argues that the Bible is metaphorical and does not refer to the actual devil.
He says 'beginning' means the start of his sin, as he never returned to goodness.
He suggests that the devil was created as a murderer by God's direct command.
He claims that 'beginning' refers to the start of the world, not the devil's creation.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas cites Augustine to explain that 'from the beginning' refers to the beginning of sin, not the moment of creation.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main conclusion regarding the time between the angel's creation and his fall?
options: It is impossible to know if there was any time between creation and the fall.
The devil sinned immediately after the very first instant of his creation.
There was a significant period of time before the devil chose to sin.
The devil sinned only after a long period of testing his free will.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that the more probable opinion, supported by the Saints, is that the devil sinned at once after the first instant of his creation.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for the devil's immediate fall?
options: Angels reach their final state with one act of free will, so he had no time to delay.
The devil lacked the intelligence to understand the consequences of his actions.
Angels are subject to physical time, which forces them to act quickly.
God punished the devil instantly because he was created without grace.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since angels attain beatitude by one meritorious act, if the devil did not sin in that first instant, he would have immediately received beatitude.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that compares the devil's fall to the delay in human sin?
options: He claims that humans were created in a state of grace, unlike angels.
He states that the comparison is valid and admits there was a delay.
He argues that humans and angels are identical in their capacity for sin.
He says angels have fixed wills after choosing, unlike humans who can change.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 3, Aquinas explains that an angel's free will becomes inflexible after choosing, whereas human will does not work this way.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the rank of the angel who sinned?
options: The sinner's exact rank cannot be determined from the text.
The sinner was an angel from the terrestrial order.
The sinner was the highest angel of all.
The sinner was a lower angel, specifically a Cherub.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that the view identifying the sinner as the very highest of all is more probable because the sin stemmed from pride, which is a motive stronger in higher angels.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas argue that the highest angel was more likely to sin than a lower one?
options: Because higher angels have a greater natural tendency to rebel against God.
Because pride, the cause of the sin, is driven by a desire for excellence found in higher ranks.
Because lower angels are too weak to resist the temptations of the material world.
Because the highest angel was placed in a position of power that encouraged corruption.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that the motive for the sin was pride, and the motive for pride is excellence, which was greater in the higher spirits.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that the highest angel's strong inclination toward God should have prevented him from sinning?
options: The strong inclination did not impose a necessity, so the angel could still choose to turn away.
The angel's inclination was actually weaker than that of the lower angels who remained good.
God forced the highest angel to sin to demonstrate the power of divine justice.
The inclination was so strong that it removed the angel's ability to choose otherwise.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas explains that while the inclination was great, it did not impose necessity, meaning the angel retained the power not to follow it.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's conclusion regarding whether the highest angel's sin caused the other angels to sin?
options: Yes, because the highest angel persuaded them to join him, not by force but by influence.
No, because all the angels sinned at the exact same moment, so one could not cause the others.
No, because each angel sinned out of independent pride without any external influence.
Yes, because the highest angel physically forced the lower angels to commit the sin with him.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that the highest angel's sin was the cause of the others' sinning by inducing them through exhortation, not by compelling them against their will.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, what is the main reason the other angels are now subject to the highest angel?
options: The lower angels naturally had less power and were therefore always destined to serve the strongest angel.
The highest angel earned this authority by being the first to recognize God's supreme power above all others.
Divine justice dictates that those who agree to another's evil suggestion become slaves to that person in punishment.
God punished them collectively because they failed to defend themselves against the highest angel's temptation.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that divine justice requires that anyone who consents to another's evil suggestion shall be subjected to that person in their punishment.

questions.q: In his reply to the objection that all angels sinned simultaneously, how does Aquinas explain that one angel could still cause the others to sin?
options: The highest angel actually sinned slightly before the others, creating a tiny gap in time for influence.
Simultaneous sinning proves that no causal relationship exists, so the objection is correct.
Angels do not need time for deliberation or speech, so persuasion and consent can happen instantly.
The other angels were already weak and needed only a simultaneous signal to fall into sin.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that unlike humans, angels do not require time for deliberation or vocal speech, allowing exhortation and consent to occur in a single instant.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the number of angels who sinned compared to those who remained faithful?
options: The number of sinners and faithful angels was equal.
More angels remained firm than sinned.
It is impossible to determine which group was larger.
More angels sinned than remained firm.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states in his answer that 'More angels stood firm than sinned,' directly rejecting the idea that evil was more prevalent.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for why more angels remained faithful than fell?
options: The devil was only from the lowest order of angels.
Sinning goes against natural inclination, which usually prevails.
Angels are purely intellectual beings without bodily desires.
Goodness is rare in all created beings, including angels.
questions.explanation: He argues that sin is contrary to the natural inclination, and things against nature happen less frequently than those in line with it.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that evil is common in humans, so it must be common in angels?
options: He claims that human reason is stronger than angelic reason.
He argues that humans have infinite fools, but angels do not.
He agrees that evil is common in both humans and angels.
He says humans are driven by physical pleasures, unlike angels.
questions.explanation: In the reply to the first objection, he explains that human evil stems from seeking sensible pleasures, a factor absent in the purely intellectual nature of angels.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the demons' knowledge of truth?
options: They are completely stripped of all knowledge, both natural and supernatural.
They retain their natural intellect but lose the grace that leads to love.
They lose their natural ability to think but retain some knowledge from grace.
They keep their natural powers but are given more divine secrets than holy angels.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that demons keep their natural intellectual powers because they cannot be punished by removing parts of their nature, but they are utterly deprived of the grace that produces love for God.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why demons still possess their natural knowledge?
options: Their nature is simple, so nothing can be subtracted from it to serve as a penalty.
God decided to leave them with some knowledge so they could understand their punishment.
Their intellects are too weak to be fully punished by losing basic mental functions.
Their knowledge comes from experience, which remains available even after their fall.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that because an angel's substance is simple, you cannot punish them by taking away natural parts of their being, unlike a human who might lose a limb.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that demons should know themselves because they are separated substances?
options: He says that separated substances are below humans, so they cannot know them well.
He argues that knowing oneself is the highest form of happiness for all beings.
He claims that demons actually do know themselves perfectly, but they choose to ignore it.
He states that humans can be happy knowing other beings, but their perfect happiness requires knowing God.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas clarifies that while humans can have a kind of happiness by knowing other spiritual beings, their complete happiness depends on knowing God, the first substance.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the will of demons?
options: Their will fluctuates between pride and humility.
Their will is weak and easily swayed by God's mercy.
Their will remains free to choose good or evil.
Their will is fixed and unchangeable in evil.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that the will of demons is obstinate in evil, meaning it is fixed and cannot return to good, unlike human wills.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas argue that demons cannot repent after their fall?
options: Angels grasp truths immovably, so their choice becomes permanent once made.
God's mercy is finite and cannot cover such a grave sin.
Demons lack the intellectual capacity to understand justice.
Their sin was caused by another, making it unfixable.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that angelic intellect apprehends immovably; thus, once they choose, their will adheres fixedly and cannot change.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that God's infinite mercy could save demons?
options: God's mercy only applies to humans, not spiritual beings.
Mercy saves those who repent, but demons cannot repent.
Demons are not saved because their sin is too heavy.
Mercy is greater than malice, so demons are eventually saved.
questions.explanation: In Reply 2, Aquinas argues that God's mercy delivers those who repent, but demons are incapable of repenting because they cling immovably to sin.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether demons experience sorrow?
options: Demons feel no sorrow because they are always joyful in their rebellion against God.
Demons do not feel sorrow because they lack physical bodies and sensory organs.
Demons are incapable of sorrow because sorrow is exclusively a human emotion.
Demons experience sorrow as a deliberate act of their will against their punishment.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that while demons lack physical passions, they possess sorrow as an act of the will resisting the evil of their punishment.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for why sorrow exists in demons?
options: Sorrow is a necessary biological response to the loss of divine favor.
The demons' envy causes them to physically weep over the salvation of others.
Sorrow is inherent to punishment, which is by nature repugnant to the will.
Demons naturally desire happiness but are physically prevented from feeling joy.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that sorrow is part of the very definition of punishment, as punishment is something the will resists.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that demons feel no fear, citing Job 41:24?
options: He claims that demons are too powerful to feel any emotion, including fear or sorrow.
He suggests that the verse in Job is metaphorical and should not be taken literally.
He argues that Job refers only to the fear of God that stops sin, not fear of punishment.
He states that demons do not fear future evil because they are already in hell.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that 'fear no one' refers to the reverential fear of God that restrains sin, not the fear of future punishment which they do feel.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about the location of the demons' punishment?
options: Demons have no place of punishment because spirits are not affected by location.
Demons face two punishments: hell for sin and the atmosphere for tempting humans.
Demons are punished only in hell, not in the atmosphere.
Demons are punished only in the dark atmosphere, not in hell.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that demons have a twofold punishment: hell for their own sin and the dark atmosphere to tempt men.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for demons being in the atmosphere?
options: To ensure the atmosphere remains dark and hostile to human life.
To serve as a trial for humans, helping them grow through resistance.
To allow them to torment humans directly without divine permission.
To keep them away from hell until the final judgment day.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that demons are in the atmosphere to tempt men, which serves as an indirect way to procure human welfare through struggle.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that spirits are not affected by physical places?
options: By asserting that the atmosphere is the only place spirits can exist.
By claiming that demons are not truly spiritual but physical beings.
By stating that the sadness of the will makes the place feel penal.
By arguing that spiritual natures are actually changed by their location.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas explains that a place is penal to a spirit because it saddens the will, not by changing the nature.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's conclusion regarding the origin of physical, visible creatures?
options: They were created by an evil principle, not by God.
They exist independently and were not created by any deity.
They are illusions created by the god of this world.
They are from God, who is the single source of all being.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly rejects the heretical view that an evil principle created visible things, arguing instead that God is the one cause of being for all things, both spiritual and corporeal.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main argument for why God must be the creator of physical things?
options: The Bible explicitly states that God made every visible object in the universe.
Since all things share the common quality of 'being,' they must receive it from one single cause.
Physical things are inherently good, and only God can produce pure goodness.
Physical things are eternal, so they must come from an eternal source.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because 'being' is common to all diverse things, there must be one single principle or cause from which all things derive their existence.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that physical creatures are evil because they can be harmful?
options: He claims that harm is an illusion and physical things are actually harmless.
He says that physical creatures are evil, but God uses them for a greater purpose.
He argues that physical creatures are good by nature, though their good is limited and partial.
He states that God only created good things, so harmful things must be from the devil.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas states that corporeal creatures are good according to their nature, but this good is partial and limited, which leads to opposing qualities.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding why physical things were created?
options: They were created to reflect and display God's goodness.
They were created to serve as tools for human labor.
They were created solely for their own sake and being.
They were created to punish the sins of spiritual beings.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that the entire universe exists to imitate and show forth Divine goodness, rejecting the idea that physical things are merely punishments.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for rejecting the idea that physical things are punishments?
options: It would imply that the physical world's order is the result of chance.
It denies that spiritual creatures have free will to choose good.
It suggests that God is unjust in his dealings with spiritual creatures.
It contradicts the biblical account that God saw each creation as good.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that if physical bodies were punishments for specific sins, the current arrangement of the world would depend on chance events of sin, which is inadmissible.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that spiritual creatures are a greater good than physical ones?
options: He claims that spiritual creatures do not have a higher rank than physical ones.
He states that serving a nearer goal does not cancel out the ultimate goal.
He insists that all creatures are equal in their value to God.
He argues that physical creatures are actually more noble than spiritual ones.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas explains that having a proximate end (serving spiritual beings) does not exclude having an ultimate end (God's goodness).

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main conclusion regarding how God created physical bodies?
options: Physical bodies emerged gradually from a chain of causes starting with God.
God created angels first, and angels then created physical bodies from pre-existing matter.
God created physical bodies directly, without using angels as intermediate creators.
Angels created physical bodies because they have greater power than humans.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly rejects the idea that angels created bodies, stating that only God can create something from nothing (creation), so God created heaven and earth immediately.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas argue that only God can create physical bodies?
options: Because angels lack the wisdom to design complex physical forms like animals and plants.
Because creation involves bringing matter itself into existence, which only the First Cause can do.
Because physical bodies are too simple to be produced by higher spiritual beings.
Because God's infinite power is required to produce any finite effect in the universe.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that creation is the production of a thing's entire substance, including matter. Since matter underlies all things, it must proceed directly from the supreme cause, God, and cannot be produced by a secondary cause.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that diversity in creatures proves diverse creators?
options: God delegates the creation of specific types of creatures to different angelic orders.
God can know many different things while remaining one, allowing Him to create diverse effects.
Diversity is an illusion; all creatures are essentially the same in their relationship to God.
Angels help create diversity by adding different forms to the matter God provided initially.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas states that God, though one, knows many different things. Like an artist who knows many forms, God can cause diverse things without needing multiple creators.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the source of forms for physical bodies?
options: They are caused by physical agents acting on matter.
They are created by the devil differentiating matter.
They exist only in the minds of spiritual beings.
They flow directly from angels as separate spiritual entities.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that forms are not emanations from immaterial beings but are produced when a composite physical agent brings matter from potentiality to act.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for rejecting the idea that angels create physical forms?
options: Angels lack the power to influence physical matter.
Plato and Avicenna were proven wrong by Aristotle.
God creates all forms directly without any intermediaries.
Forms do not exist independently, so their cause must be physical.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that forms only exist as part of a composite whole, not on their own, so their cause must be something that is also composite, like fire creating fire.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that heavenly bodies cause physical changes, so angels must too?
options: He states that angels only influence the mind, not the body.
He says that heavenly bodies do not actually cause any changes.
He argues that heavenly bodies act through movement, not by emitting forms.
He claims that angels are more powerful than heavenly bodies.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas clarifies that heavenly bodies inform earthly things by movement, not by emanation, which distinguishes their action from the rejected view.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about whether matter's formlessness came before its formation in time?
options: Matter existed in a formless state for a period of time before God gave it shape.
Matter and form were created simultaneously, but formlessness is a physical property of matter.
Matter was created already formed; its formlessness is only a logical priority, not a temporal one.
Matter was created formless, but only for a very short instant before being formed.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that matter cannot exist in time without form because existence requires actuality, which is provided by form. Therefore, formlessness is only prior in nature or origin, not in time.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main reason for rejecting the idea that formless matter existed in time?
options: Existence requires actuality, and form provides this actuality; thus, matter cannot exist without form.
God is all-powerful and can create perfect things instantly, unlike nature which takes time.
The Bible says the earth was void, but this refers to a lack of beauty, not a lack of form.
Matter is part of substance and is higher than accidents, so it must always have form.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that to say matter existed without form is to say being existed without act, which is a contradiction. Form is the act that makes matter exist actually.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that nature imitates God, and since nature takes time to form things, God must have too?
options: Nature only imitates God in moral matters, not in the physical process of creation.
God does not imitate nature; rather, nature imitates God, so God's methods are completely different.
God creates actual being from nothing instantly, while nature moves from potentiality to act over time.
God took time to create matter, but He formed it instantly, unlike natural processes.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas explains that nature works by changing potential things into actual ones, which takes time. God creates actual being from nothing, so He can produce a perfect thing instantly.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the matter of all physical things?
options: The underlying matter is identical for both earthly and heavenly bodies.
Matter is the same in all bodies because they share the form of corporeity.
All bodies share one common matter, as proven by their mutual change.
The matter of corruptible and incorruptible bodies is not the same.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that because no form remains subsisting beneath generation and corruption in corruptible bodies, the matter of corruptible and incorruptible bodies must be different.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why the matter differs between body types?
options: Heavenly bodies have a different natural movement than earthly elements.
God's will makes heavenly bodies indissoluble, changing their fundamental nature.
Matter is in potentiality to different forms, and this potentiality differs by type.
The form of corporeity is not the same in all bodies, distinguishing them.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that matter is defined by its potentiality to receive forms; since corruptible and incorruptible bodies have different modes of potentiality, their matter is distinct.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that all bodies are in the same genus of body?
options: He claims that the genus of body is only a logical concept, not physical.
He argues that logically there is one genus, but physically they differ.
He agrees that physically, all bodies share the same genus and matter.
He states that corruptible and incorruptible things are not in the same physical genus.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas distinguishes between logical and physical senses, stating that in a physical sense, corruptible and incorruptible things are not in the same genus due to their different potentialities.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's conclusion regarding whether the empyrean heaven was created at the same time as formless matter?
options: It was not created at all, but exists only as a metaphor for spiritual contemplation.
It was created simultaneously with formless matter to serve as the initial place of bodily glory.
It was created before formless matter to ensure darkness did not precede light.
It was created later, specifically on the second day, after the firmament was made.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that it was fitting for the empyrean heaven to be made from the beginning to provide a starting point for bodily glory, matching the spiritual glory of the angels.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for the existence of the empyrean heaven?
options: To serve as a transparent sphere that separates the earth from the stars.
To govern the lower bodies and influence natural effects in the world.
To provide a corporeal place of rest that is free from corruption and change.
To prevent the Manichean claim that God created darkness first.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that since spiritual glory began with the angels, it was fitting to also create a bodily glory from the start, free from the servitude of corruption.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that all sensible bodies must be movable?
options: He suggests that the empyrean heaven moves too slowly for us to perceive its motion.
He argues that the empyrean heaven is not a sensible body but a spiritual one.
He asserts that the empyrean heaven is invisible and therefore not subject to physical laws.
He claims that movement is only necessary in the current state, not in the state of glory.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 1, Aquinas explains that sensible things are movable now to multiply elements, but in the final state of glory, bodily movement will cease.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, was time created at the same moment as formless matter?
options: No, because time is merely a measure and cannot be a created thing.
Yes, because other holy writers argue matter existed without form for a duration.
Yes, because movement must precede time in the order of creation.
No, because Augustine explicitly states time did not exist until later.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that time was created simultaneously with formless matter, following the view of other holy writers who believe matter was formless for a period of time, which requires time to exist as a measure.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for including time among the first created things?
options: Time is the only thing that can exist without a physical subject.
Time is necessary to measure the movement of the firmament created on day two.
Time is more fundamental than place because it is permanent and unchanging.
Time is a universal measure, unlike movement which is tied to specific objects.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the fourth objection, Aquinas argues that time belongs to the first created things because it acts as a common measure for all things, whereas movement is only related to specific movable subjects.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that time cannot exist without day and night?
options: He argues that day and night are the only valid measures of time.
He rejects the objection by saying day and night are not part of time.
He claims that time existed in an undifferentiated state before being divided into days.
He states that the firmament's movement created time before the light was divided.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas explains that just as matter was formless before receiving its full form, time was in a manner formless (undifferentiated) before it was distinguished into day and night.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether 'light' is used in its proper sense for spiritual things?
options: It is always metaphorical because spiritual things are not physical.
It depends on whether we use the strict definition or the broader, extended meaning.
It is always proper because spiritual light is superior to physical light.
It is never proper because words for senses cannot apply to the mind.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that if 'light' means strictly physical illumination, it is metaphorical; but if it means 'making something known' in a broader sense, it is used properly for spiritual things.

questions.q: What main reason does Aquinas give for this distinction in meaning?
options: Physical light is too weak to describe the brightness of divine truth.
Augustine declared that spiritual terms must always be taken literally to be meaningful.
Words often start with a specific physical meaning and later expand to cover similar abstract concepts.
The Apostle Paul explicitly defined light as a metaphor for all spiritual knowledge.
questions.explanation: He explains that words like 'sight' and 'light' originally referred to physical senses but were extended in common speech to mean intellectual understanding or manifestation.

questions.q: How does Aquinas address the objection that 'light' is a primary name for God and thus must be used properly?
options: He clarifies that even if it is a primary name, it can still be metaphorical in its strict sense.
He agrees that it is a primary name, so it is always used literally.
He argues that Dionysius only meant light in a physical, not spiritual, context.
He rejects the objection by saying Dionysius was mistaken about God's names.
questions.explanation: Aquinas implies that being an intellectual name does not force a literal meaning; if taken in its strict, primary sense (physical illumination), it remains metaphorical even for God.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the nature of light?
options: Light is not a body but something else entirely.
Light is a type of fire that moves through the air.
Light is a body that changes form when the sun sets.
Light is a physical body that exists in the world.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states in his answer that light cannot be a body, rejecting the idea that it is a physical substance.

questions.q: Which argument does Aquinas use to show that light cannot be a physical body?
options: Light does not have a specific shape or size like a rock.
Light has no weight, so it cannot be a material object.
Light is invisible to the naked eye, unlike other bodies.
Light spreads instantly, which physical objects cannot do.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that physical bodies take time to move through space, whereas light illuminates vast distances instantly.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the claim that light is a species of fire?
options: He agrees that light is fire, but in a different form.
He claims that fire is actually a type of light, not the other way around.
He argues that fire cannot exist without air, so light is air.
He says Aristotle was only listing common opinions, not facts.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas explains that Aristotle's statement was just a mention of probable opinions, not a definitive truth.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the nature of light?
options: Light is the substantial form of the sun itself, not just an accident.
Light is a spiritual form that creates substantial forms in earthly bodies.
Light is merely an intentional image of color existing in the air.
Light is an active quality that flows from the substantial form of a luminous body.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that light is an active quality consequent on the substantial form of the sun or other luminous bodies, rejecting the views that it is a substantial form or merely an intentional being.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for saying light is an active quality?
options: Light is visible to the eye, whereas substantial forms are objects of the intellect.
Light remains in the air even after the source of light is removed.
Light produces natural physical effects, such as warming bodies, which mere images cannot do.
Light has a direct opposite, darkness, which proves it is a sensible quality.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because light produces natural effects like warming, it must have a natural being as a quality, since mere intentions or images cannot cause natural changes.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that light is not a quality because it disappears when the source is removed?
options: Light is actually a substantial form of the air, so it should remain when the sun sets.
The objection is wrong because heat also disappears from water immediately when removed from fire.
The endurance of a quality depends on how the subject receives its form; air receives light imperfectly.
Darkness is a positive quality that replaces light, so light does not truly disappear.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 1, Aquinas states that qualities endure differently based on how the subject receives the form; since air receives light imperfectly, it does not remain when the source is withdrawn.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the production of light on the first day?
options: It refers to a temporary cloud of light that later became the sun.
It represents the initial darkness that existed before any creation occurred.
It describes the physical sun being created before the moon and stars.
It signifies the creation of spiritual beings who were formed before physical matter.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that the 'light' of the first day symbolizes the formation of spiritual creatures (angels), which happened before the formation of the physical world.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for placing the production of light first among physical works?
options: Light is the only quality that can exist without any underlying physical matter.
Light is necessary to create the circular movement that distinguishes day from night.
Light is a general quality shared by all bodies, so it logically precedes specific forms.
Light is a subordinate accident that must be established before substantial forms.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that light is a 'common quality' found in both earthly and celestial bodies, and we proceed from general principles to specific ones in creation.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that spiritual darkness did not exist at the beginning?
options: He suggests that Moses omitted spiritual creation because the people were too ignorant to understand it.
He argues that demons were created evil from the start to test the goodness of angels.
He claims that spiritual darkness refers to the lack of physical light in the early universe.
He states that spiritual beings were not created with full glory, but with the grace needed to adhere to God.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the fourth objection, Aquinas explains that spiritual light signifies the perfection of grace given to spiritual creatures, not the perfection of glory they were not yet created with.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main conclusion regarding whether the firmament was made on the second day?
options: The statement can be understood in two ways, depending on whether one refers to its substance or its formation.
The firmament was made on the second day, but only if one accepts Plato's view of fire.
The firmament was not made on the second day because it existed from the very beginning of creation.
The firmament was created in its substance on the first day, not the second.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that the scriptural statement can be understood in two senses: either referring to the starry firmament's substance or its formation, and he outlines different philosophical opinions to explain this.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for allowing multiple interpretations of the scriptural text?
options: Because Augustine taught that all scriptural meanings are equally valid without exception.
To ensure that Scripture is not ridiculed by unbelievers if a specific interpretation is proven false.
To allow scientists to freely change the biblical account to match their own theories.
Because the original Hebrew text is too ambiguous to be translated accurately into Latin.
questions.explanation: Aquinas cites Augustine's second rule: one should hold a specific explanation only loosely, ready to abandon it if proven false, so that Scripture is not exposed to ridicule and obstacles to faith are removed.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that 'heaven' was created in the beginning, before the days?
options: He replies that the 'beginning' refers to a spiritual time, not a physical day.
He states that the objection is invalid because the firmament is not actually called heaven in Scripture.
He claims that the word 'heaven' in Genesis 1:1 refers only to the air, not the firmament.
He argues that Moses first spoke of God's works collectively, then explained them part by part.
questions.explanation: In his reply to Objection 1, Aquinas cites Chrysostom, explaining that Moses initially summarized the works collectively ('created heaven and earth') and then detailed them individually in the subsequent days.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the existence of waters above the firmament?
options: They are purely spiritual beings that praise God, rather than physical material substances.
They exist, because Scripture explicitly states they are there and divine words outweigh human logic.
They do not exist, because water is heavy and naturally falls downward toward the earth.
They are useless and therefore cannot exist, as God does not create things without a purpose.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that the waters exist because he prioritizes the authority of Scripture (Genesis 1:7) over human objections based on natural philosophy.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for accepting the existence of these waters despite logical objections?
options: Human experience is limited and cannot fully comprehend the nature of celestial elements.
The firmament is a sphere that can hold fluids in place through its unique geometric structure.
Scripture has greater authority than human intellectual arguments, so we must accept the text as true.
These waters are necessary for the generation of composite bodies located above the starry heaven.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly cites Augustine to argue that the words of Scripture hold more authority than the most exalted human intellect, forcing acceptance of the waters' existence.

questions.q: How does Aquinas address the objection that water is fluid and cannot rest on a spherical surface?
options: He rejects the objection by saying that fluids can rest on spheres if they are spiritual substances.
He states that water above the firmament is heavy, which allows it to stay attached to the sphere.
He claims that the firmament is not actually a sphere, so the fluidity argument does not apply.
He argues that the waters above are not ordinary elemental water but may be formless matter or a different substance.
questions.explanation: Aquinas does not directly refute the physics of fluids on spheres; instead, he suggests the nature of these waters differs from elemental water, potentially being formless matter or having a different mode of existence depending on the definition of the firmament.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether the firmament divides waters from waters?
options: Yes, it separates lower transparent bodies from higher ones, or lower air from upper air.
No, because the waters below never actually touch the firmament to be divided by it.
No, because all water is of the same species and cannot be separated by a physical barrier.
Yes, but only if we accept the ancient theory that water is an infinite element.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that the firmament does divide waters from waters, interpreting 'waters' as transparent bodies or air, separating the lower atmosphere from the higher.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for interpreting 'waters' in Genesis to include air or transparent bodies?
options: Water is the only element that can exist in infinite quantities above the visible sky.
Ancient philosophers proved that air is actually a form of water that exists above the stars.
The word 'deep' in Genesis literally means a vacuum where no physical matter can exist.
Moses used familiar terms for ignorant readers who might not understand that air is a physical body.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues Moses spoke in simple terms for ordinary people, using 'water' to imply air because not everyone understood air as a corporeal substance.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that the firmament cannot divide waters because the lower waters do not touch it?
options: He replies that the objection is valid and the firmament only divides different species of water.
He claims the lower waters actually rise up to touch the firmament during the day.
He states that the firmament is not a physical object, so contact is not required for division.
He argues that invisible air is included under the name 'water,' so 'waters' exist on both sides.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 3, Aquinas explains that Moses includes invisible air under the term 'water,' ensuring 'waters' are present on both sides of the firmament.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the number of heavens?
options: There are exactly seven heavens, all of which are physical spheres made of fire and air.
There is only one heaven because it is the total sum of all matter above the earth.
There are multiple heavens because the term is used in three different senses in Scripture.
There is only one heaven, and the plural usage is merely a Hebrew grammatical habit.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that the difference between one or many heavens is mostly about language. He explains that Scripture uses the word 'heaven' in three distinct ways, leading to a distinction of multiple heavens.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why there can be more than one heaven?
options: The Bible explicitly lists seven distinct physical layers of the sky in the Old Testament.
The earth is the center of a circle, and a single center can have many different circumferences.
The philosopher Aristotle proved that the sky is made of several separate and distinct parts.
The word 'heaven' is applied to different things based on their height and brightness.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that 'heaven' is used in a threefold sense, primarily based on properties like sublimity and luminosity, which allows for multiple things to be called heavens.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that 'heaven' and 'earth' are paired, so if there is one earth, there is one heaven?
options: He claims that the word 'earth' is also used in multiple senses, just like 'heaven'.
He states that the earth is the center of a circle, which can have many circumferences around it.
He argues that the earth is actually made of many parts, just like the sky is.
He says that the pairing in Genesis is poetic and does not imply a one-to-one physical match.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas uses the geometric analogy that one center (the earth) can have many circumferences (heavens) around it.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's conclusion regarding whether it was fitting for the waters to be gathered on the third day?
options: It was not fitting, because the waters should have been gathered on the first day with light.
It was fitting only if one rejects Augustine's view of spiritual creation entirely.
It was not fitting, because the earth was already named in the beginning.
It was fitting, because different interpretations explain the order as either natural origin or actual time.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that it was fitting, explaining that the order can be understood either as an order of nature/origin (Augustine) or an order of time (other writers).

questions.q: According to Augustine's interpretation, what does the 'third day' represent in the creation narrative?
options: The creation of spiritual beings like angels, which are higher than physical bodies.
The initial creation of formless matter before any shapes or forms existed.
The impression of elemental forms on matter, such as water and earth, in order of nature.
The formation of the firmament, which separates the waters from the sky.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that for Augustine, the third place in the order of nature corresponds to the impression of elemental forms (water and earth) on formless matter.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that the earth was already covered by water, leaving no place to gather it?
options: He states that the earth was not covered, but only partially wet, allowing for gathering.
He argues that the waters were produced in the act of gathering, not moved from elsewhere.
He suggests that the objection is invalid because the earth was created after the waters.
He claims the waters were gathered into the sky, leaving the earth dry and visible.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas cites Augustine to say we need not suppose the earth was covered first; rather, the waters were produced in the very gathering together.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about when plants were created on the third day?
options: They were created only in their underlying causes or potential.
They were fully grown and visible on the surface immediately.
They were created simultaneously with the stars and the sun.
They were created after the sixth day to show God's ongoing work.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that on the third day, the earth received the power or cause to produce plants, rather than the plants being fully formed in act on the surface.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for believing plants were not fully formed on the third day?
options: The production of plants is a work of propagation, which continues after the six days.
Plants are not truly alive because they cannot move from place to place.
Plants are too similar to stones and metals to be considered distinct creations.
The Bible says the earth was cursed before any plants could grow.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that creating new species from existing ones is a work of propagation, which God continues to do, whereas the six days covered the initial creation of causes.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that plants should not be made on the third day because they are fixed to the earth like stones?
options: He states that plants are not fixed to the earth because they can grow upward.
He argues that stones are actually a type of plant in disguise.
He claims that stones were created on the first day along with the light.
He says Moses only listed things that were obvious to human senses, unlike hidden minerals.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas explains that minerals are generated in hidden ways within the earth, so Moses omitted them to focus on things manifest to the senses.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's conclusion regarding whether the lights should have been created on the fourth day?
options: Yes, but only as a spiritual symbol, not as physical bodies.
No, because the lights are incorruptible and existed before time began.
Yes, because the fourth day marks the start of the work of adornment.
No, because the lights were created on the first day with the light.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that the fourth day begins the 'work of adornment,' where lights are produced to beautify the heavens through their movement.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main reason for placing the creation of the lights on the fourth day?
options: God wanted to prevent people from worshipping the sun and moon as gods.
The lights serve as an external adornment for the heavens, similar to clothing for a person.
The lights are necessary causes for plants, so they must follow the earth's formation.
The firmament could not hold the lights until the fourth day of creation.
questions.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes between intrinsic perfection and extrinsic adornment, comparing the lights to clothing that adorns the heavens just as clothes adorn a person.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that plants (effects) were made before the sun (cause)?
options: He claims that plants do not actually depend on the sun for their existence.
He argues that the sun's light on day one was sufficient to grow plants immediately.
He says plants were made first to prevent people from worshipping the sun as a god.
He states that the sun was created on the third day but hidden until the fourth.
questions.explanation: In his reply to Objection 4, Aquinas cites Basil, stating the order was chosen to prevent idolatry among those who believed heavenly bodies were gods.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the reason for creating the heavenly lights?
options: The assigned cause is false because the lights were created only to be signs.
The assigned cause is unreasonable because the lights are too noble to serve the earth.
The assigned cause is reasonable because the lights serve humans in three specific ways.
The assigned cause is invalid because the distinction of days began before the lights existed.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly answers that the cause is reasonable, explaining that the lights serve humanity regarding sight, seasons, and signs for weather.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas say Moses mentions only the usefulness of the lights to humans?
options: To prevent people from worshipping the stars and sun as gods.
To demonstrate that the lights were created before the rest of the universe.
To prove that the lights are physically superior to the human body.
To show that the lights have no other purpose besides helping farmers.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that Moses highlights the service to man specifically to withdraw his people from the error of idolatry.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that the new moon cannot rule the night?
options: The moon does not rule the night, so the biblical text is metaphorical only.
The moon was created in its full, perfect state, allowing it to rule the night.
The objection is wrong because the new moon is the brightest phase of the moon.
The sun actually rules the night, and the moon is merely a reflection of it.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the fifth objection, Aquinas argues that the moon was likely made in its full perfection, which allows it to rise in the evening and rule the night.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether the heavenly bodies are living beings?
options: They are inanimate because they lack the physical traits needed for sensation and nutrition.
They are living because they move themselves, which is a sign of life.
They are living but their souls are of a completely different, angelic nature.
They are living because they possess a soul that allows them to understand and move.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that while heavenly bodies cannot feel or eat, they can understand and move, which are operations of the soul, making them living beings.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why heavenly bodies cannot have senses or a nutritive soul?
options: They are made of elements that are too stable to change or decay.
They are too far away from Earth for their senses to function properly.
They are too noble to be associated with lower forms of life like plants.
They are incorruptible and lack the mix of elements required for touch and growth.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that senses depend on touch, which requires a specific mix of elements, and nutrition requires change, which is impossible for incorruptible heavenly bodies.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that heavenly bodies impart life to animals on Earth?
options: He argues that animals receive life directly from God, not from the stars.
He says they act as instruments moved by a living substance that gives life.
He denies that the sun and stars have any power to influence life on Earth.
He claims that the life in animals is a reflection of the stars' own life.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas explains that heavenly bodies are instruments moved by a living agent, and they impart life through that agent's power.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main conclusion regarding the creation of birds and fish on the fifth day?
options: They were created on the sixth day to complete the cycle of all living creatures.
They were created on the fifth day because they are more perfect than land animals.
They were created on the fourth day alongside the sun, moon, and stars.
They were created on the fifth day to match the water and sky made on the second day.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that the fifth day corresponds to the second day because the fifth day adorns the intermediate bodies (water and air) that were distinguished on the second day.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for placing the creation of birds and fish on the fifth day?
options: Birds and fish are biologically superior to land animals and therefore deserve an earlier day.
Water is the only element capable of generating life without the use of seeds.
The air is too invisible to be named separately, so it must be grouped with water.
The fifth day is the middle day of adornment, matching the middle day of distinction for water.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that the order of adornment mirrors the order of distinction; since the second day distinguished water (the intermediate body), the fifth day (the middle day of adornment) creates its inhabitants.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that birds should be produced from air, not water?
options: He states that air is more perfect than water and therefore creates higher life forms.
He argues that air is not named separately because it mixes with water and heaven.
He claims that birds physically rest on the earth, so they must come from water.
He asserts that all birds are actually fish that learned to fly in the air.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas explains that air is not listed on its own because its lower part is thickened by watery exhalations and its upper part is associated with heaven.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main conclusion regarding the description of the sixth day's work in Genesis?
options: The description is flawed because land animals should have been created before birds and fish.
The description is unnecessary because God created all animals simultaneously on the first day.
The description is fitting because the earth's adornment mirrors the water's adornment on the second day.
The description is symbolic only and should not be taken as a literal account of creation.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that the sixth day corresponds to the third day just as the fifth day corresponds to the second, making the mention of the earth fitting in both contexts.

questions.q: What reason does Aquinas give for this correspondence between the days of creation?
options: Scripture explicitly states that the earth was formed on the sixth day for no other reason.
The earth is the lowest body, just as water is the intermediate body, creating a parallel structure.
The blessing of animals on the sixth day mirrors the blessing of light on the first day.
Land animals are more complex than sea creatures, requiring an extra day for their formation.
questions.explanation: He explains that the sixth day adorns the lowest body (earth) corresponding to the third day, just as the fifth day adorns the intermediate body (water) corresponding to the second day.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that poisonous animals should not have been created by a good God?
options: He compares it to an unskilled person seeing tools in a workshop whose purpose they do not understand.
He states that poisonous animals are actually beneficial for controlling the population of other species.
He argues that poisonous animals were created after man sinned to punish human disobedience.
He claims that God created them to test man's strength and courage against dangerous beasts.
questions.explanation: In his reply to Objection 6, Aquinas quotes Augustine, comparing the situation to an unskilled observer who sees tools in an artisan's workshop and wrongly judges them unnecessary.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about the completion of divine works on the seventh day?
options: It marks the universe's initial structural completeness, not its final end.
It is incorrect because God performed no new actions that day.
It marks the final beatitude of the saints at the world's end.
It is only a partial completion since many species came later.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that the seventh day represents the 'first perfection' (structural completeness), while the final end (beatitude) occurs at the world's end.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for attributing this completion to the seventh day?
options: The initial structural completeness serves as the cause for the final end.
The seventh day is the only day where God directed existing creatures.
God rested to show that all possible creatures had already been made.
The final beatitude requires nature and grace, both given on day seven.
questions.explanation: He explains that the 'first perfection' (completeness of parts) is the cause of the 'second perfection' (the final end/operation).

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that God did not act on the seventh day?
options: He acted by creating new species that were not present before.
He acted by forming Eve from Adam's rib on that specific day.
He acted by directing existing creatures to their proper tasks.
He acted by resting, which is itself a divine operation.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas states God acted by directing and moving His creatures to their proper work, not by creating new ones.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's conclusion regarding whether God rested on the seventh day?
options: God rested by ceasing to create new kinds of creatures and by being fully satisfied in Himself.
God did not rest because He continues to work in the world today.
God rested only in the sense that He caused humans to stop working.
God never rested because He created everything without any physical effort or movement.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that God rested in two ways: by stopping the creation of new creatures and by finding complete satisfaction in His own being, needing nothing external.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for saying God rested 'from' His works?
options: God was physically tired from the labor of creation and needed a break.
God had no need for the things He made to be happy, as He is self-sufficient.
God transferred the burden of creation to humanity, allowing Him to relax.
God's desire for external objects was finally satisfied by the creation of man.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that God rested 'from' His works because He did not need them for His happiness; He was already happy in the enjoyment of Himself.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that God 'works until now' (Objection 1)?
options: God stopped all activity on the seventh day and does nothing in the present.
God's work continues only through the actions of humans, not through His own power.
God works now by preserving and providing for existing creatures, not by making new ones.
God works now by creating entirely new creatures that did not exist before.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 1, Aquinas clarifies that God's current work consists of preserving and providing for what He has already made, not creating new kinds of creatures.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the seventh day?
options: It is neither blessed nor sanctified because God does not change.
It is both blessed and sanctified for specific reasons.
It is only sanctified because God finds rest in Himself.
It is only blessed because God stopped creating new things.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that the seventh day is blessed because of God's ongoing care for creation's growth and sanctified because it points to resting in God.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for the seventh day being blessed?
options: The day marks the completion of the first six days of work.
God’s ongoing care allows creatures to multiply and grow.
God’s goodness is better shown by stopping all activity entirely.
God created new species during that specific day.
questions.explanation: He explains that blessing refers to the increase of creatures through multiplication, which is sustained by God's providence.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that blessing implies a change in God?
options: He agrees that God changes, but only in a spiritual sense.
He argues that God’s rest is a physical need for Him.
He says the change happens in creatures, not in God.
He claims the objection is based on a mistranslation of the text.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas states that nothing is added to or taken from God; rather, something is added to creatures through their growth and rest.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main conclusion regarding the number of days in the creation account?
options: The days are insufficient because creation should have its own separate day.
The days are arbitrary and do not follow any logical order or pattern.
The seventh day is superfluous because no new physical things were made.
The six days are sufficient because they reflect a perfect numerical structure.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that the arrangement corresponds to the perfection of the number six, which is the sum of its parts (one, two, three), making the enumeration sufficient.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for distinguishing the different days of creation?
options: To ensure that fire and air receive their own distinct days from water.
To separate the making of matter from the making of form completely.
To match the production of animals with the specific parts of the world they adorn.
To show that spiritual creatures were made after all physical bodies were formed.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas explains that animal production days are grouped based on which part of the world (heaven, water, or earth) the animals adorn.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that the seventh day should not be counted because nothing new was created?
options: He states that the seventh day is only included for poetic effect.
He claims that the sun and moon were created on the seventh day.
He says the seventh day is actually a mistake in the biblical text.
He argues that God resting in Himself is a distinct act worthy of mention.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the fifth objection, Aquinas cites Augustine to say that God resting in Himself is a distinct action attributed to the seventh day, justifying its inclusion.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether the six days of creation are one single day or distinct days?
options: They are all one single day, as Augustine argued, representing angelic knowledge.
The question is unanswerable because Genesis uses metaphorical language throughout.
They are distinct days only in human perception, but simultaneous in divine reality.
They are distinct days representing a real succession in time and the order of works produced.
questions.explanation: Aquinas rejects Augustine's view that the days are one simultaneous day of angelic knowledge, concluding instead that the days signify a real succession in time and the order of created things.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for distinguishing the days as successive rather than simultaneous?
options: Because the physical elements of the earth required long periods to cool and solidify.
To maintain a proper and orderly sequence in the creation and arrangement of the world.
God needed time to rest between tasks because creating the universe was exhausting.
Because the angels could not understand multiple works happening at the exact same instant.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that the distinction of days is not due to a lack of power in God, but to ensure that a due order is observed in the instituting of the world.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that God created all things together at once, as stated in Sirach?
options: He claims that 'together' means all things were created in a single instant of eternity.
He says God created all substances together, but distinguished and adorned them in successive days.
He argues that Sirach is metaphorical and should not be taken literally regarding time.
He asserts that the objection is wrong because God did not create everything at once.
questions.explanation: In his reply to Objection 2, Aquinas clarifies that God created all things together regarding their basic substance, but did not create them together regarding their final formation and distinction.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the suitability of the words used in Scripture for the six days of creation?
options: The words are suitable only if one accepts that the elements were created with their final forms from the very start.
The words are unsuitable because they do not explicitly state that God saw each individual work as good.
The words are unsuitable because they fail to mention the Word of God in the initial creation of heaven and earth.
The words are suitable because they correctly express the distinct works of creation, distinction, and adornment.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that the Scripture uses suitable words because it distinguishes between the initial creation (where the Son is mentioned as the beginning) and the subsequent works of distinction and adornment (where the Son is mentioned as the Word).

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why the 'Word of God' is mentioned in the later works but not in the initial creation?
options: The Word is mentioned later because it signifies the form given to creatures, whereas the initial creation refers to formless matter.
The Word is mentioned later to emphasize that the Spirit of God moved over the waters to give them shape.
The Word is omitted initially because the Son was not yet distinct from the Father at the moment of the first creation.
The Word is mentioned later because it represents the divine command that creatures could only obey after they were made.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that the initial creation involves formless matter, while the later works involve giving form to the world. The 'Word' is associated with giving form, similar to how an artist's mental concept gives form to a work of art.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that the creation of water is not mentioned in the text?
options: He suggests that the omission is intentional to show that water is less important than the firmament and the land.
He claims that the water was not created until the second day, so it correctly appears later in the narrative.
He states that the water was created by the Spirit of God moving over it, which is why its specific creation is not listed.
He argues that water is not a distinct creation but is part of the general 'heaven and earth' mentioned in the first verse.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas cites Augustine to explain that 'heaven' and 'earth' in the first verse refer to formless spiritual nature and formless matter, respectively, meaning no creature, including water, is actually omitted from the description.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about whether the soul is a body?
options: The soul is both a body and an incorporeal principle.
The soul is not a body, but the act of a body.
The soul is a body that moves other bodies.
The soul is a body that also has a separate incorporeal part.
questions.explanation: Aquinas says the soul is not a body but the act of a body.

questions.q: What main reason does Aquinas give for the soul not being a body?
options: The soul is a body because it is the only thing that can give life to bodies.
The soul is a body because it is the moving principle of the body.
The soul must be a body because it moves the body.
A body cannot be the first principle of life, only a principle of life can be a body.
questions.explanation: He argues that a body can be a principle of life, but the first principle (the soul) cannot be a body.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to Objection 1, that the soul must be a body because it moves the body?
options: He denies that the soul moves the body at all.
He says a mover need not be moved, so the soul can be incorporeal.
He claims the soul is a body because it is the moving principle of the body.
He argues that only bodies can move, so the soul must be a body.
questions.explanation: He replies that a mover need not be moved, so the soul can be incorporeal.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the nature of the human soul?
options: The soul is a physical part of the body that cannot exist on its own.
The soul is a temporary state that disappears when the body dies.
The soul is a vague concept that cannot be defined as existing or not.
The soul is a non-physical entity that exists independently of the body.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that the intellectual principle (the soul) must be incorporeal and subsistent, meaning it exists in its own right apart from the body.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main argument for why the soul must be non-physical?
options: Because the soul can know all physical things, it cannot itself be limited to one physical nature.
Because the soul controls the body, it must be superior to physical laws.
Because the soul is invisible, it must be made of a different kind of matter than the body.
Because the soul feels emotions, it must be separate from the physical senses.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that if the intellect were physical, its specific physical nature would block it from knowing other physical things, just as a bitter tongue cannot taste sweetness.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that the soul needs the body to understand?
options: He claims the body is the source of the soul's power to think and understand.
He argues the body is needed only to provide images, not as the source of the thinking power.
He says the soul understands directly through the eyes without any mental images.
He denies that the soul ever needs the body for any kind of operation at all.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 3, Aquinas states the body is necessary for the intellect only regarding the object (providing phantasms/images), not as the origin of the intellectual action itself.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the souls of non-human animals?
options: They are corporeal principles that move the body from within.
They are independent entities that exist separately from the body.
They are not independent entities because they lack operations of their own.
They are identical to the human soul but with fewer capabilities.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that animal souls are not subsistent (independent) because they have no operations that belong to them alone, apart from the body.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for his conclusion?
options: Sensation always involves a physical change in the body, like the eye reacting to light.
The sensitive faculty cannot perceive objects without the help of the intellect.
Ancient philosophers incorrectly believed that sensing was a purely mental activity.
Animals are of a different species than humans, so their souls must differ.
questions.explanation: He argues that sensing requires a physical change in the body (such as the pupil changing), meaning the soul's action is tied to the body and not independent.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that animals and humans are in the same genus?
options: He claims that the soul of man is not subsistent, unlike animal souls.
He agrees they are the same species but differ only in size.
He states that being in the same genus does not mean being in the same species.
He argues that humans are actually a different genus from other animals.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas clarifies that while humans and animals share a genus, they are different species, and specific differences come from different forms.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether the soul is man?
options: Man is a composite being made of both soul and body.
The soul is the complete definition of what a man is.
Man is merely a soul that temporarily uses a body.
The soul is a distinct person separate from the body.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because sensation requires the body, man cannot be soul alone but must be a union of soul and body.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for rejecting the idea that man is just a soul?
options: The soul is too universal to be identified with a specific person.
Matter is essential to the definition of any natural species.
Scripture clearly distinguishes between the inward and outward man.
Sensation is an operation of the whole man, not the soul alone.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that since sensation is not proper to the soul alone but to the composite, the thing that performs human operations (man) is not just the soul.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that the soul is a 'person' because it is a particular substance?
options: Only substances with the complete nature of their species are persons.
The soul is a universal substance, not a particular one.
Persons are defined by their social roles, not their substance.
A person must be intellectual, and the soul is not intellectual.
questions.explanation: Aquinas clarifies that not every particular substance is a person; only those possessing the complete nature of their species, like a whole human, qualify.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the composition of the human soul?
options: The soul is made of matter but lacks a distinct form.
The soul is a mix of physical matter and spiritual form.
The soul is a pure form with no material component.
The soul is a separate substance that contains both matter and form.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that the soul has no matter and is an absolute form, not composed of matter and form.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for why the intellectual soul cannot contain matter?
options: Matter prevents the soul from being created by God.
Matter prevents the soul from being the form of a body.
Matter makes the soul infinite, which is reserved for God alone.
Matter would limit the soul to knowing only specific individual objects.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that if the soul had matter, it would receive forms as individuals, meaning it could only know specific things rather than universal natures.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that the soul changes from ignorance to knowledge, implying it has matter?
options: He argues that the soul's capacity for change is different from physical matter's.
He agrees that the soul has matter because it undergoes change.
He states that changing from ignorance to knowledge is a divine act, not a natural one.
He claims that the soul does not actually change, only the body does.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas explains that the soul's potentiality for change is distinct from the potentiality of primary matter.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the human soul?
options: The human soul dies when the body dies, like animal souls.
The human soul is a physical form that decays with the body.
The human soul is corruptible because it originates from nothing.
The human soul is immortal and cannot cease to exist.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that the intellectual principle, or human soul, is incorruptible, distinguishing it from the corruptible souls of animals.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's primary reason for claiming the human soul is incorruptible?
options: It exists independently as a substance, not just as a part of a body.
It is created directly by God without any natural process.
It is made of the same eternal material as the heavenly bodies.
It never interacts with the physical senses or the material world.
