questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because the human soul is a self-subsistent form (it exists in its own right), it cannot be corrupted accidentally with the body, unlike animal souls which are merely parts of the body.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that the soul needs the body to understand?
options: He argues that understanding does not require any mental images at all.
He claims the soul understands differently after separating from the body.
He denies that the soul ever needs the body for any operation.
He states that the soul stops understanding once the body dies.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 3, Aquinas explains that while understanding through images is the soul's mode of operation while united to the body, it will have a different mode of understanding after separation.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether the human soul and an angel belong to the same species?
options: They are of different species because incorporeal substances must differ in nature to differ in number.
They are of the same species because their intellectual nature is identical in kind.
They are of different species only because the soul is attached to a physical body.
They are of the same species because both share the ultimate goal of eternal happiness.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that separate forms (like souls and angels) cannot be merely numerically distinct individuals of the same species; diversity in number implies diversity in species and nature.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why angels and souls cannot be of the same species?
options: The human soul is imperfect because it is united to a body, whereas angels are perfect and separate from bodies.
Intellectual nature is too vague to define a species, so souls and angels must fall into different categories.
Separate forms are pure essences, so any difference between them must be a difference in kind, not just individual identity.
Angels are made of matter and form, while souls are pure forms, making their compositions fundamentally incompatible.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that since incorporeal substances are subsistent forms without matter, they cannot have multiple individuals of the same species; thus, distinct beings must be distinct species.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that the soul and angel are the same species because they share the same ultimate end (eternal happiness)?
options: He argues that angels do not seek eternal happiness, only human souls do, so their ends are different.
He states that the end of the soul is earthly virtue, while the angel's end is purely intellectual contemplation.
He distinguishes between the natural end, which determines species, and the supernatural end, which does not.
He claims that eternal happiness is accidental to both, so it cannot define their essential species.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 1, Aquinas clarifies that the argument confuses the proximate natural end (which defines species) with the ultimate supernatural end (eternal happiness).

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the relationship between the intellectual principle and the human body?
options: The intellect is a separate entity that never connects to the physical body.
The intellect is the specific form that makes the human body a living human.
The intellect exists only as an accidental quality of the body, like being white.
The intellect is a part of the body, similar to how the eye is a part for seeing.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly asserts that the intellect, which is the principle of understanding, is the form of the human body, meaning it is what primarily makes the body alive and human.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why the intellect must be the form of the body?
options: Because the intellect is the only part of the soul that can exist without a body.
Because the body acts as a container that holds the intellectual power in place.
Because the soul is the primary source of all vital actions, including understanding.
Because the body needs a separate agent to process sensory information into thoughts.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that whatever is the primary cause of an action is the form of the thing acting. Since the soul is the primary principle of all vital actions, including understanding, it is the form of the body.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that the intellect has independent existence and therefore cannot be a form of the body?
options: He claims that the objection is wrong because the intellect does not actually have independent existence.
He states that independent existence prevents the intellect from acting on the body at all.
He argues that the intellect's existence is shared with the body, creating a single unified existence.
He explains that the intellect exists separately before birth and only joins the body at death.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the fifth objection, Aquinas explains that the soul communicates its own existence to the body, resulting in a unity of existence for the whole composite being.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the number of human intellects?
options: Each human being possesses a distinct, individual intellect.
Intellects are multiplied only when the physical body is destroyed.
There is one single intellect shared by all human beings.
The intellect is a separate substance that does not belong to any specific person.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states it is impossible for one intellect to belong to all men, concluding that each person has their own distinct intellectual principle.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for rejecting the idea of a single shared intellect?
options: It would make all humans identical, leaving no real difference between individuals like Socrates and Plato.
Human souls are made of matter, which prevents them from being shared among different bodies.
Plato and Aristotle both agreed that the intellect must be unique to each person.
If there were one intellect, knowledge could not be transferred from a teacher to a student.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that if one intellect were shared, Socrates and Plato would be the same man, differing only by external things like clothing, which he deems absurd.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that Augustine said there are not many human souls?
options: Augustine only applied this rule to angels, not to human beings who have bodies.
Augustine meant that there are not many different kinds of human souls, not that there is only one soul.
Augustine was wrong because the Bible clearly states that every person has a unique soul.
Augustine agreed with Aquinas that souls are multiplied according to the number of bodies.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the sixth objection, Aquinas clarifies that Augustine denied a plurality of species (kinds) of souls, not a plurality of individual souls within the same species.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's conclusion regarding whether humans have multiple essentially different souls?
options: Humans have a sensitive soul and a separate intellectual soul.
The soul is divided into corruptible and incorruptible parts.
Humans have three distinct souls located in different organs.
Humans have only one soul that performs all vital functions.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that if there were multiple essentially different souls, a human would not be a single, unified being, which contradicts the nature of a living organism.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for rejecting the idea of multiple souls in one body?
options: Different souls would conflict with each other and cause physical pain.
Aristotle proved that only plants have one soul while animals have many.
Multiple souls would prevent the human from being a single, unified entity.
The body is too small to contain more than one spiritual substance.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that unity comes from a single form; having multiple souls would mean a human is not 'absolutely one' but a collection of different beings.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that the sensitive soul in humans must be different from that in animals because human souls are incorruptible?
options: Humans do not actually have a sensitive soul, only an intellectual one.
The sensitive soul in humans is corruptible, unlike the intellectual soul.
Animals also have incorruptible souls, so there is no difference.
The human sensitive soul is incorruptible because it is united with the intellect.
questions.explanation: In his reply to Objection 1, Aquinas explains that the sensitive soul is incorruptible in humans not by its own nature, but because it is part of the intellectual soul.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the presence of other forms in a human being?
options: The human body contains separate substantial forms for each element like fire and water.
The soul acts only as a motor, requiring a separate form to give the body being.
Only the intellectual soul exists as a substantial form, virtually including all lower forms.
The sensitive and nutritive souls exist as distinct, independent substantial forms in man.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that the intellectual soul is the sole substantial form in humans, and it virtually contains the powers of lower forms rather than them existing separately.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for rejecting the idea of multiple substantial forms?
options: The human body is too complex to support more than one substantial form at the same time.
A second form would prevent the soul from giving being simply, contradicting how generation works.
The Platonists incorrectly believed the soul was separate, which leads to logical contradictions.
Aristotle explicitly forbids the existence of multiple forms in a single physical organic body.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that if another form existed, the soul would not be the cause of the body's simple existence, which is false because the soul is the substantial form.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that self-moving bodies must have separate moving and moved parts?
options: He agrees that the soul is a separate part that moves the body as an external engine.
He argues that the body moves itself without any need for a soul or form.
He states the soul moves the body through motive power, not by being a separate part.
He claims that the moved part is the soul and the moving part is the body.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas clarifies that the soul moves the body via its motive power, not by being a distinct physical part separate from the body.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether the intellectual soul is properly united to the human body?
options: No, because the soul is too perfect to be limited by a physical body.
Yes, because the body serves as a necessary tool for the senses, which the soul needs to learn.
Yes, but only because the body provides natural protection like hair or hooves.
No, because the soul is immortal and the body is corruptible, making them incompatible.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that the union is proper because the soul needs a bodily instrument to perform sensory operations, which are essential for acquiring knowledge.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why the intellectual soul must be united to a body?
options: The soul must gather knowledge through the senses, which require a physical organ to function.
The body is needed to keep the soul warm and protected from the elements.
The body allows the soul to interact with other souls through physical touch.
The soul is too weak to exist independently without the support of matter.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that since the human soul learns from individual things via the senses, and senses require a corporeal instrument, the soul must be united to a body suited for this purpose.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that the intellectual soul is one form and thus cannot unite with a body made of parts from different species?
options: He replies that the objection is valid, but God overrides this natural law.
He states that the body is not made of parts, but is a single, uniform substance.
He argues that body parts like eyes or hands are not separate species, but different dispositions of one whole.
He claims that the soul actually divides itself into multiple forms to match each body part.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 3, Aquinas clarifies that individual parts do not constitute species; rather, the entire body constitutes the species, while the parts are merely various dispositions.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the union of the intellectual soul and the body?
options: No accidental dispositions can exist between the soul and the body because the soul is its form.
The soul joins the body through specific accidental dispositions that act as a bridge.
The body must have certain measurable dimensions before the soul can unite with it.
The soul moves the body like an external engine, requiring a power to connect them.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since the soul is the substantial form of the body, no accidental dispositions can intervene between a form and its matter.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why no accidental dispositions can pre-exist in the body?
options: The soul contains all lower forms virtually, so it does not need any external help to perfect the body.
Dimensions and quantity are primary forms that must be established before any other qualities can appear.
Matter must first have actual existence, which is provided by the substantial form, before it can have accidents.
Accidental dispositions are too weak to support the weight of the spiritual soul in a physical body.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that matter cannot have accidents like heat or quantity before it has actual existence, which comes solely from the substantial form.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that spiritual things connect to bodies only through power or virtue?
options: He agrees that the soul uses its power to connect, but denies that this power is an accident.
He states that virtual contact is sufficient for the soul to guide the body without any physical union.
He argues that the soul is united by its very being as a form, even though it moves by power.
He claims that the body has a pre-existing aptitude to be moved, which makes the connection possible.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 3, Aquinas distinguishes between a soul acting as a motor (united by power) and the intellectual soul, which is united by its very being as a form.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's conclusion regarding whether a physical medium connects the soul to the body?
options: The soul relies on heavenly light to bridge the gap to the body.
The soul connects through a special incorruptible body attached to it.
The soul connects directly to the body without any physical intermediary.
The soul uses a subtle body like air or fire to link with the body.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because the soul is the form of the body, it unites immediately to matter as its act, making any mediating body unnecessary and false.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas argue that no physical body can serve as the means of union between soul and body?
options: Because the soul, as the body's form, makes the body actual and unified by its very nature.
Because only an external agent can cause matter to exist, not the soul itself.
Because the soul is too distant from the body to touch any physical medium.
Because physical bodies are too heavy and slow to connect with a spiritual soul.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that form gives existence and unity directly; since the soul is the form, it unites to matter immediately by its own nature, not through another thing.

questions.q: How does Aquinas explain why the soul separates from the body when breathing stops?
options: Breath is not the bond itself, but its loss removes the body's readiness for union.
The cessation of breath proves that air is the primary link between soul and body.
Breath is the subtle body that physically holds the soul inside the body.
The soul leaves because it can no longer move the body without air.
questions.explanation: In Reply 2, Aquinas clarifies that breath is an instrument for movement, not the means of union; its cessation destroys the bodily disposition required for that union to persist.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the soul's presence in the body?
options: The soul is present in the entire body and is fully contained within every single part.
The soul hovers above the body as a separate mover, touching only the head and hands.
The soul exists only in the heart, which acts as the central engine for the rest.
The soul is divided into separate pieces, with each part of the body receiving only a fragment.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because the soul is the substantial form of the body, it must be in the whole and in each part, unlike a mere motor that might only be in one place.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why the soul must be in every part of the body?
options: The soul is a logical form that defines the body's essence without physically occupying any space.
The soul is a potential form that waits to be activated by the body's various sensory organs.
The soul is an accidental form that only organizes the body's external shape and structure.
The soul is the substantial form that gives actual existence and life to each individual part.
questions.explanation: He distinguishes the soul from accidental forms (like the shape of a house) by noting that a substantial form perfects and gives existence to each part of the whole, not just the whole itself.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that all soul powers would be in every body part (e.g., sight in the ear)?
options: He suggests that the powers are mixed together so thoroughly that they cannot be distinguished in any part.
He states that higher powers like intellect and will exceed the body's capacity and are not in any part.
He claims that all powers, including intellect and will, are physically located in every organ of the body.
He argues that the objection is valid, so the soul must actually be divided among the different senses.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 4, Aquinas explains that powers like intellect and will are not in any specific body part because they exceed the entire capacity of the body.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the relationship between the soul's essence and its powers?
options: The soul's essence is a potentiality that becomes a power through action.
The soul's essence is identical to its powers because they are one substance.
The soul's essence is distinct from its powers, so they are not the same thing.
The soul's essence is an accident that depends on its powers for existence.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states it is impossible to admit that the power of the soul is its essence, concluding that they are distinct.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for why the soul's essence cannot be its power?
options: Because the soul is nobler than primary matter, which is its own potentiality.
Because if essence were power, every living thing would always be actively thinking or sensing.
Because the soul is a simple form that cannot have any parts or distinctions.
Because the soul is a substance, and powers are always accidents in substances.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that if the essence were the immediate principle of operation, anything with a soul would always be in actual vital action, which is not observed.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that Augustine says memory and understanding are essentially in the soul?
options: Augustine is speaking about the divine essence, not the human soul, so the quote is irrelevant.
Augustine means that memory and understanding are separate substances from the soul's essence.
Augustine refers to the soul knowing and loving itself, making those acts essential in that context.
Augustine is wrong because memory and understanding are accidental forms, not essential.
questions.explanation: In his reply to Objection 1, Aquinas clarifies that Augustine is describing the soul as it knows and loves itself, where the substance is what is known and loved.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the number of powers in the human soul?
options: The soul must have several distinct powers to perform its functions.
The soul has no powers at all, only a single unified essence.
The soul has fewer powers than angels because it is lower in rank.
The soul has one simple power because it resembles God's unity.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that we must place several powers in the soul, rejecting the idea that it has only one simple power.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for why the human soul needs many different powers?
options: It is the highest form of life and requires no movement to act.
It must achieve perfect goodness through many different operations.
It sits at the boundary between spiritual and physical creatures.
It shares the same simple nature as God, requiring unified action.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because humans are the lowest beings capable of achieving perfect goodness (beatitude), they require many various operations and powers to reach it.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that a higher power must be more unified?
options: He says a diverse power is superior if it covers many different things.
He argues that the soul is not actually higher than other forms of life.
He claims that unity is only important for physical, not spiritual, things.
He agrees that the soul is unified and therefore has only one power.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas explains that a power with many forms is superior if it extends over many things, whereas a unified power is only superior if it covers equal things.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding how the powers of the soul are distinguished?
options: They are distinguished by their accidental properties, such as size or shape.
They are not distinguished at all, as the soul is a single, undivided unity.
They are distinguished by their specific acts and the objects those acts target.
They are distinguished solely by the physical parts of the body they inhabit.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that powers are necessarily distinguished by their acts and objects, rejecting the idea that they are undivided or defined by accidental features.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why powers are distinguished by their objects?
options: Because the nature of an act is diversified by the nature of its object.
Because acts exist in time before the powers that produce them.
Because objects are physically larger than the powers that perceive them.
Because all objects are accidental to the soul and thus change its species.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that we know a power by its act, and the act's nature is diversified by the object, which serves as either the principle or the end of that act.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that a single power cannot have contrary objects (like white and black)?
options: Contraries like white and black are actually the same thing in different lights.
The power targets the common aspect shared by both contraries, such as color.
The power of sight is actually two different powers combined into one.
Contraries do not exist in reality, so the objection is based on a false premise.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas explains that sight does not regard white or black as such, but rather the common aspect of both, which is color.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the arrangement of the soul's powers?
options: The order exists only in time, not in nature or object relations.
The powers are simultaneous and have no natural sequence or hierarchy.
Only the intellectual powers are ordered; the others are independent.
There is a specific order among the powers, including three distinct types.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that there must be some order among the powers and identifies a triple order: two based on dependence and one based on objects.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for why an order must exist among the soul's powers?
options: Because our physical senses naturally operate in a specific chronological sequence.
Because the intellectual power must command the sensitive powers to function.
Because the objects of the senses, like color and sound, are naturally ranked.
Because the soul is a single unity from which many distinct powers proceed.
questions.explanation: He argues that since the soul is one and the powers are many, things proceeding from a single source must proceed in a certain order.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that sight and hearing act independently, so no order exists?
options: He admits that for some powers, like sight and hearing, no dependency order exists.
He argues that all powers, including sight and hearing, depend on each other.
He states that the objection is invalid because all powers share one object.
He claims that sight and hearing are actually dependent on the nutritive powers.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas concedes that the argument holds for powers ordered only by their objects (like sight and hearing), where one does not depend on the other.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, where do the powers of the soul reside as their subject?
options: Only powers that do not need body parts are in the soul; others are in the whole person.
No powers reside in the soul; all reside in the body.
All powers reside in the soul alone, regardless of whether they use body parts.
Powers reside in the soul only when the person is awake and thinking.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that powers like understanding and will, which do not use body parts, are in the soul alone, while powers like sight, which use organs, are in the composite of soul and body.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main reason for distinguishing where these powers reside?
options: The body is less important than the soul, so the soul must hold all the primary powers.
Augustine taught that the soul senses things without the body, which proves the powers are separate.
The soul is immaterial, so it cannot hold any powers that involve physical sensations.
The subject of a power must be the same as the subject of the operation that power performs.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that the subject of operative power is that which is able to operate, and since the same thing that can operate is what does operate, the subject of the power must match the subject of the operation.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that the soul senses things without the body?
options: He says Augustine was merely reporting Plato's view, not asserting it as true fact.
He claims Augustine was mistaken about the nature of sensation and fear.
He agrees that the soul senses without the body, proving all powers are in the soul.
He argues that fear is a bodily function, so it requires a physical organ.
questions.explanation: In his reply to Objection 3, Aquinas explains that Augustine was using Plato's opinion that sensation is proper to the soul, but was relating it rather than asserting it as true doctrine.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the source of the soul's powers?
options: They are created by the body's physical organs alone.
They exist independently of the soul's core nature.
They flow from the soul's essence as their starting point.
They are caused by external agents acting on the soul.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that all powers of the soul flow from its essence as their principle, whether the subject is the soul alone or the composite.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why the soul's essence produces its powers?
options: The essence is potential, allowing it to receive the powers.
The essence is actual, and actuality causes the powers to exist.
The essence is the final cause, making the powers desirable.
The essence is simple, which allows it to generate variety.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because the subject (the soul) is in act, it produces the accidental forms (powers), whereas it is in potentiality only to receive them.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that emanation requires movement, which a simple thing cannot have?
options: He claims the powers are created by an external agent.
He argues the powers result naturally, like light producing color.
He states that movement is not necessary for any existence.
He says the soul moves itself through its physical parts.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 3, Aquinas clarifies that the emanation is not a physical transmutation or movement, but a natural resultance, comparing it to color resulting from light.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main conclusion regarding whether one power of the soul arises from another?
options: One power can arise from another, acting as a principle for less perfect powers.
Only the highest power arises from the soul's essence, never from other powers.
No power arises from another because all powers are created simultaneously.
Powers are strictly independent and never influence or originate from one another.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that in a natural order, the first cause influences what follows, so higher powers act as principles for lower ones.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, why do some powers of the soul proceed from others?
options: Because the soul's essence is divided into separate, non-interacting parts at creation.
Because higher powers act as active and final causes for lower, imperfect powers.
Because all powers are identical in nature and merely appear different to us.
Because lower powers are physically stronger and generate the higher intellectual faculties.
questions.explanation: He explains that more perfect powers (like intelligence) serve as the end and active principle for less perfect ones (like senses).

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that one power cannot arise from another because they are opposites?
options: Opposites can only arise from a neutral middle ground, not from each other directly.
The objection is valid, and Aquinas concedes that opposite powers never originate from one another.
Opposition between perfect and imperfect does not prevent the imperfect from proceeding from the perfect.
The powers are not actually opposites; they are all variations of the same single faculty.
questions.explanation: In Reply 3, Aquinas states that the opposition is between perfect and imperfect, and imperfect things naturally proceed from perfect ones.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about the soul's powers after it leaves the body?
options: All powers remain fully active in the soul just as they were in life.
No powers remain because the soul is destroyed when the body dies.
Only intellectual and will powers remain active; others exist only as potential roots.
Sensitive powers remain active, but intellectual powers disappear completely.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that intelligence and will remain actually, while sensitive and nutritive powers remain only virtually (as potential roots) because their physical organs are gone.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why sensitive powers do not remain active?
options: These powers depend on physical organs that no longer exist after death.
The soul is too weak to support more than one type of power.
Memory and imagination are not true powers of the soul at all.
The soul loses its strength when separated from the physical body.
questions.explanation: He argues that these powers are accidents of the body-soul composite and cannot exist without their corporeal organs, which are destroyed.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that the rich man in hell remembers his past life?
options: He says the rich man is actually using his sensitive memory power.
He argues this memory belongs to the mind, not the sensitive soul.
He claims the Bible passage is a metaphor and not historical fact.
He states that the rich man has no memory because he is in hell.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the fourth objection, Aquinas explains that the recollection mentioned is to be understood as a function of the mind, not the sensitive part of the soul.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the number of distinct types of powers in the soul?
options: There are only three types of powers, corresponding to the three kinds of souls.
There is only one unified power that manifests in different ways.
There are four types of powers, matching the four ways a thing is said to live.
There are exactly five distinct genera of powers in the soul.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states in his answer that 'There are five genera of powers of the soul,' rejecting the objections that argued for fewer distinctions.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, what is the primary reason for distinguishing these five powers?
options: The powers are distinguished because each requires a different physical organ to function.
The powers are distinct because they correspond to different parts of the human body.
The powers differ based on the universality of their objects and how they transcend bodily nature.
The powers are separated because they operate at different times during a person's life.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that powers are distinguished generically by their objects (from the specific body to all being) and by how their operations transcend corporeal nature.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that motive power should not be a separate genus because sense and appetite already cause movement?
options: He suggests that movement is caused by external forces, not by internal soul powers.
He states that appetite is merely a passive response and cannot initiate any action.
He argues that sense and appetite alone are insufficient for movement, as seen in immovable animals.
He claims that only the intellectual power can truly cause physical movement in the body.
questions.explanation: In his reply to Objection 4, Aquinas points out that immovable animals possess sense and appetite but lack the power of motion, proving a distinct motive power is needed.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the three parts of the vegetative soul?
options: They are invalid because generation is common to both living and non-living things.
They are fittingly described as nutritive, augmentative, and generative powers.
They are not distinct powers but all stem from a single unified force.
They should be rejected because they are merely natural forces below the soul.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly answers that the vegetative part has three powers: generative (for existence), augmentative (for size), and nutritive (for preservation).

questions.q: According to Aquinas, what is the main reason the vegetative soul requires three distinct powers?
options: The soul must be stronger than the body to ensure it controls all physical changes.
Generation of living things requires an external source separate from the internal soul.
The body needs three different operations: gaining existence, reaching proper size, and being preserved.
The nutritive power must be distinct to prevent the body from consuming its own humidity.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that the living body requires a triple operation: acquiring existence (generative), acquiring due quantity (augmentative), and preservation (nutritive).

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that generation is common to non-living things and thus not a soul power?
options: He suggests that the generative power is actually a sensitive power, not a vegetative one.
He claims that non-living things do not actually generate, so the comparison is invalid.
He states that the soul's power is higher because it acts through heat rather than cold.
He argues that living generation uses internal semen, unlike inanimate generation which is entirely external.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas distinguishes living generation (which uses internal semen) from inanimate generation (which is entirely from an extrinsic source).

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the number of exterior senses?
options: There are fewer than five senses because taste is just a type of touch.
There are more than five senses because touch covers many different qualities.
The number of senses varies depending on the specific organ involved.
There are exactly five exterior senses, properly distinguished from one another.
questions.explanation: Aquinas answers the article's question by affirming that the five exterior senses are properly distinguished, rejecting the objections that argue for more or fewer senses.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, what is the primary reason for the distinction between the different exterior senses?
options: The different kinds of external causes that affect the sense powers.
The different mediums, such as air or water, through which they operate.
The different natures of the sensible qualities perceived by the senses.
The different physical organs in which the senses are located.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that powers are not defined by their organs or mediums, but are diversified according to the diversity of the exterior causes that naturally affect them.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that taste should not be a separate sense because it is a kind of touch?
options: Taste is a specific variety of touch located only in the tongue, not the whole body.
Taste is completely distinct from touch and shares no biological connection with it.
Taste is not a real sense but merely a spiritual immutation of the tongue.
Taste is a separate sense because it perceives qualities that touch cannot perceive.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the fourth objection, Aquinas states that taste is a kind of touch existing specifically in the tongue, distinguishing it from the general sense of touch spread throughout the body.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the distinction of interior senses?
options: The interior senses are suitably distinguished as separate powers necessary for animal life.
The interior senses are not distinct but are merely different names for the exterior senses.
Only the common sense is a distinct power, while others are just passions of it.
The distinction is unsuitable because the intellect alone handles non-sensory information.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that nature requires diverse powers for diverse actions, concluding that the interior senses are suitably distinguished to handle reception, retention, and estimation.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for distinguishing a power that retains images from one that receives them?
options: Animals need to remember past events to avoid predators in the future effectively.
The exterior senses are too weak to hold onto images for more than a second.
Receiving and retaining are different principles in physical bodies, like moist and dry matter.
The intellect requires stored images to perform logical reasoning and syllogisms.
questions.explanation: Aquinas uses the analogy of physical bodies: moist things receive easily but retain poorly, while dry things do the opposite, proving that receiving and retaining require distinct principles.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that sight cannot distinguish white from sweet?
options: He claims that the common sense mixes all inputs into a single unified perception.
He suggests that the intellect performs this cross-sensory discrimination, not the senses.
He argues that taste is actually a form of sight adapted for flavor detection.
He states that to discern between two things, a power must be able to know both.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas explains that proper senses only judge their own objects; discerning between different senses (like white and sweet) requires a power that knows both.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the relationship between the intellect and the soul?
options: The intellect is the very essence of the soul itself.
The intellect is a specific power or faculty within the soul.
The intellect is the same thing as the human mind.
The intellect is a separate substance from the soul.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that the intellect is a power of the soul, not its essence, because in created beings, the essence is not identical to the act of understanding.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why the intellect is a power rather than the soul's essence?
options: The soul is immaterial, so its powers must be distinct.
Angels are called minds, so humans must have a separate intellect.
Only in God is the act of understanding identical to His being.
The appetitive power is different from the intellectual power.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that for any being other than God, the essence is not the same as its operation; since understanding is an operation, it must be a power, not the essence.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that humans understand with angels, who are called 'minds'?
options: Humans share the same essence as angels because they are both immaterial.
The objection is wrong because humans do not actually understand with angels.
Angels are called minds because they lack a physical body entirely.
Angels have no other powers besides intellect and will, so they are called minds.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas explains that angels are called 'minds' because their entire power consists of intellect and will, unlike humans who have other powers.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether the human intellect is a passive power?
options: The human intellect is purely active because it is the highest power of the soul.
The human intellect is passive because it starts empty and must receive knowledge to become active.
The human intellect is neither active nor passive, but a neutral substance.
The human intellect is passive only in the sense of being corrupted or damaged.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that the human intellect is passive in the third sense: it begins in potentiality (like a blank slate) and receives intelligible forms to move into act.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for saying the human intellect is passive?
options: It is corruptible and therefore subject to the same passions as the body.
It is finite and cannot contain all knowledge at once, so it must receive information.
It is inferior to the vegetative soul, which is purely active.
It is made of matter, which is always subject to change and decay.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because no created intellect is infinite, it cannot be the act of all being; thus, it stands in potentiality to intelligible things and must receive them.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that the intellect is incorruptible, so it cannot be passive?
options: He claims that Aristotle was wrong to link passivity with corruptibility in all cases.
He clarifies that 'passive intellect' in that context refers to the sensitive appetite, not the mind.
He argues that incorruptible things can still be passive in the strict sense of losing qualities.
He states that the human intellect is actually corruptible, contrary to previous claims.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas explains that the term 'passive intellect' used by some refers to the sensitive appetite, which experiences passions, distinguishing it from the intellectual power.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the existence of an active intellect?
options: It does not exist because Plato proved that all forms are naturally intelligible without any active help.
It is necessary to transform potential understanding into actual understanding by stripping away material details.
It is only needed to provide light for the senses, similar to how sunlight helps us see colors.
It is unnecessary because the passive intellect is already immaterial and ready to receive forms.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since we understand things found in matter, which are not actually intelligible on their own, an active power is required to make them intelligible by abstracting them from material conditions.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why an active intellect is required?
options: Plato’s theory of separate forms requires an active agent to connect the soul to the physical world.
Forms in matter are not actually intelligible, so something active is needed to move them from potential to act.
The senses are active, so the intellect must also be active to maintain a parallel structure in the soul.
The passive intellect is too weak to handle the complexity of natural forms without external assistance.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that nothing moves from potentiality to act without something already in act; since forms in matter are not actually intelligible, an active intellect is needed to make them so.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that the passive intellect's immaterial nature is sufficient for receiving forms?
options: He claims that the passive intellect is actually material, so it cannot receive forms without an active helper.
He argues that the recipient's disposition matters only if the agent does not pre-exist, which is the case here.
He agrees that the passive intellect is sufficient if the agent form already exists separately from matter.
He says that the passive intellect receives forms exactly as the eye receives light, making an active part unnecessary.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas explains that the recipient's nature only affects how a form is received if the agent does not pre-exist; since the forms we understand do not pre-exist apart from matter, the passive intellect's nature is not enough.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the number of active intellects?
options: The number of active intellects depends on how many bodies exist.
The active intellect is a separate substance independent of the human body.
There is a single active intellect shared by all human beings.
There is a distinct active intellect for every individual human soul.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because the active intellect is a power belonging to the soul, and souls are multiplied for each person, there must be as many active intellects as there are souls.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for his conclusion?
options: The active intellect causes universal concepts, which are one in many things.
All humans agree on the first intellectual concepts, proving a shared mind.
It is impossible for one single power to belong to multiple different substances.
The active intellect is more noble than the passive intellect according to Aristotle.
questions.explanation: He states that it is impossible for one same power to belong to various substances, so since souls are distinct substances, their powers must be distinct too.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that all men agree on first intellectual concepts?
options: Humans share the action of their species, but the power itself is not identical in everyone.
Agreement on concepts proves that all humans share one identical intellectual power.
First concepts are abstracted from matter, so they do not require a shared intellect.
The active intellect is separate from the body, so it cannot be multiplied by bodies.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas explains that while members of a species share the same action, the power that enables that action is not identical in each individual.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion about whether memory exists in the intellectual part of the soul?
options: Memory exists in the intellect because it can hold ideas without actively thinking them.
Memory is impossible in the intellect because it lacks a physical organ.
Memory is only in the senses because animals also have memory.
Memory is separate from the intellect and belongs to a different faculty.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that the intellect can hold the 'species' (mental images) of things in a state of potentiality, which allows for memory, even when not actively understanding them.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why memory can exist in the intellect?
options: Animals and humans share the same type of intellectual memory.
The past is defined by fixed time, which the intellect can process.
The intellect is more stable than physical things, so it can retain mental images.
The active intellect constantly sends new images to the passive intellect.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that the intellect is of a 'more stable nature' and 'more immovable' than corporeal nature, allowing it to retain things received according to its own conditions.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that memory is common to both humans and animals?
options: He claims animals do not actually have memory, only instinct.
He agrees that human and animal memory are exactly the same.
He argues that memory is only in the body for humans.
He says animal memory is physical, while human memory is not.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas clarifies that memory in the sensitive part (shared with animals) is the act of a bodily organ, distinguishing it from the intellectual part.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether intellectual memory is a separate power from the intellect?
options: Intellectual memory is the same as the active intellect but different from the passive intellect.
Intellectual memory is a separate power distinct from both intellect and will.
Intellectual memory is a distinct power because it deals with past events.
Intellectual memory is not a distinct power but part of the intellect itself.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that memory is not a distinct power from the intellect because retaining information belongs to the nature of the passive intellect.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main reason for claiming that memory is not a separate power from the intellect?
options: The intellect's object is 'being' in general, so it does not split into powers based on time.
The active intellect creates knowledge, while the passive intellect only stores it separately.
Memory and understanding are equal aspects of the soul, so they must be one power.
Sensitive memory is distinct from sense, so intellectual memory must be distinct from intellect.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because the intellect deals with 'being' in a common way, it is not divided by differences like past or present, which would be required for a separate memory power.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that Augustine treats memory, understanding, and will as equal and distinct?
options: He says understanding comes from memory like action from habit, not as separate powers.
He argues that will is distinct, but memory and understanding are the same.
He claims Augustine was mistaken about the equality of memory and understanding.
He agrees with Augustine that they are three distinct powers in the soul.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 3, Aquinas clarifies that intelligence arises from memory as act arises from habit, meaning they are related as activity to capacity, not as separate powers.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the relationship between reason and intellect?
options: Reason is a lower form of intellect found only in humans.
They are the same power, though they perform different actions.
They are two separate powers, like sense and imagination.
Intellect is distinct because it shares eternity with angels.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that reason and intellect cannot be distinct powers in man, but are one and the same power.

questions.q: What is the main analogy Aquinas uses to explain why reason and intellect are the same power?
options: They are like a builder and a house, where one creates and the other exists.
They are like time and eternity, which are fundamentally different states of being.
They are like sight and hearing, which both perceive but in different ways.
They are like movement and rest, which belong to the same nature.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that just as movement and rest are not different powers but states of the same nature, reasoning (movement) and understanding (rest) are actions of the same power.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that lists reason and intellect as separate steps in a sequence?
options: He argues that the sequence reflects the order of actions, not distinct powers.
He claims the source of the quote is too unreliable to be considered valid.
He says that imagination is actually part of reason, not a separate step.
He asserts that the list is incomplete and misses the power of sense.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 1, Aquinas states that the enumeration is made according to the order of actions, not according to the distinction of powers.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the higher and lower reason?
options: They are one single power distinguished by different functions.
They are two completely separate powers of the soul.
The higher reason is a power, but the lower is not.
They are distinct habits that cannot be combined in one act.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that the higher and lower reasons are 'one and the same power' but are distinguished by their different functions or acts.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why the higher and lower reason are the same power?
options: Because the higher reason controls the lower reason like a master.
Because the same intellect moves from known truths to new conclusions.
Because the lower reason is physically located below the higher reason.
Because both reasons rely on the same external sensory inputs.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that reason acts like a movement from one thing to another; since the same intellect passes through the medium to reach the end, it must be a single power.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that the 'scientific' part of the soul is a different power from the 'opinionative' part?
options: He says that the scientific part only deals with eternal, unchanging truths.
He argues that necessary truths exist within temporal things, so no new power is needed.
He agrees that scientific knowledge requires a separate mental power.
He claims that the Philosopher was mistaken about the nature of scientific parts.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas notes that necessary truths are found in temporal things (like math), so the 'scientific' part is not a distinct power from the one handling contingent things.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the relationship between 'intelligence' and 'intellect'?
options: Intelligence is the active process of understanding, while intellect is the faculty that performs it.
Intellect is the act of thinking, while intelligence is the potential to think.
Intelligence and intellect are two completely separate mental powers with different functions.
Intelligence is a higher power than intellect, reserved for angels and God.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that intelligence is not a distinct power but rather the act of the intellect, distinguishing between the faculty (power) and its operation (act).

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for saying intelligence is not a distinct power from intellect?
options: Because intelligence properly signifies the very act of understanding, which is what the intellect does.
Because Damascene listed intelligence as just one step in a sequence of intellectual acts.
Because ancient Greek philosophers always used the terms interchangeably in their writings.
Because Boethius stated that only God possesses true intelligence, not humans.
questions.explanation: Aquinas bases his argument on the definition of terms, stating that 'intelligence' signifies the act of understanding, whereas 'intellect' is the power itself.

questions.q: In his reply to Objection 2 (Boethius), how does Aquinas explain the difference between reason and intelligence?
options: Reason is the passive intellect, while intelligence is the active intellect that illuminates truth.
Reason requires investigation to understand, while intelligence understands all things immediately without inquiry.
Reason is a human power, while intelligence is a separate divine power unrelated to humans.
Reason deals with physical senses, while intelligence deals only with abstract mathematical concepts.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that Boethius uses 'intelligence' to describe an act that transcends reason, specifically the ability to understand without the need for investigation or reasoning steps.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the speculative and practical intellects?
options: They are two separate powers because they handle different types of knowledge.
They are distinct powers because truth and good are fundamentally different objects.
They are the same power, differing only in their final goal or purpose.
The practical intellect is a distinct power because it motivates action.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that they are not distinct powers, but rather the same power directed toward different ends: truth for the speculative and operation for the practical.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why these two intellects are not distinct powers?
options: Truth and good are identical concepts that cannot be separated in any way.
The practical intellect only directs movement and does not actually perform it.
The sensitive powers differ more than the intellectual ones do.
The difference in their goals is accidental to the nature of the object itself.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that whether an object is directed toward action or just consideration is an accidental feature, not a fundamental difference in the object's nature that would require a different power.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that the practical intellect is a 'motive power' while the speculative is merely apprehensive?
options: He states that the distinction between apprehensive and motive powers does not apply to the intellect at all.
He argues that the speculative intellect is also a motive power because it desires truth.
He claims the practical intellect is not a motive power in the sense of executing movement, but only in directing toward it.
He agrees that the practical intellect executes movement directly, unlike the speculative.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas clarifies that the practical intellect is 'motive' only in the sense that it directs toward action, not because it physically executes the movement itself.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion about the nature of synderesis?
options: It is a natural habit, not a distinct power of the soul.
It is reason itself, considered as a natural faculty.
It is a special power higher than human reason.
It is a separate power distinct from the rational mind.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that synderesis is not a power but a natural habit, rejecting the views that it is a higher power or reason itself.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for classifying synderesis as a habit rather than a power?
options: It allows us to judge discovered things without using reason at all.
First practical principles are innate habits, just as first speculative principles are.
Synderesis always incites to good, whereas powers can incite to evil.
It is opposed to sensuality, which is clearly a different type of faculty.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues by analogy: since first speculative principles belong to the habit of understanding, first practical principles (synderesis) must also belong to a habit, not a separate power.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that Jerome's division of synderesis against other powers proves it is a distinct power?
options: Jerome was mistaken because synderesis is actually a part of sensuality.
Jerome meant that synderesis is a power, but Aquinas disagrees with him.
Jerome's division shows that synderesis is a habit, not a power.
Jerome's division is based on different acts, and one power can perform many acts.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 1, Aquinas clarifies that Jerome's list categorizes acts, not powers, and a single power can be responsible for various different acts.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main conclusion about the nature of conscience?
options: It is a spirit that exists independently of the mind.
It is a habit that remains unchanged throughout life.
It is an act where knowledge is applied to a specific case.
It is a permanent power of the soul that guides us.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that conscience is properly an act because it involves applying general knowledge to individual actions, rather than being a static power or habit.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for calling conscience an act?
options: It is the only thing in the soul that can be defiled.
The word implies knowledge linked to a specific situation.
It is distinct from the mind and operates as a separate spirit.
Conscience must exist constantly to guide every decision.
questions.explanation: He analyzes the etymology of the word, which breaks down to 'knowledge with' something, indicating an active application of knowledge to a particular instance.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that conscience is a power because it can be defiled?
options: He claims that only powers can be defiled, so the objection is valid.
He agrees that defilement proves it is a distinct power of the soul.
He says the conscience is defiled only because the person knows they are.
He argues that defilement is a metaphor for losing one's moral habits.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas states that conscience is not defiled as a subject, but rather because the person is aware of their own defilement.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether appetite is a distinct power of the soul?
options: Appetite is merely a natural inclination shared by all matter and does not require a separate soul power.
Appetite is a distinct power because knowing beings desire what they perceive, not just what nature dictates.
Appetite is the same as the power of knowledge since we desire what we know.
Appetite is not a special power because all things, even rocks, desire good.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that while inanimate objects have a natural inclination, beings with knowledge have a superior inclination to desire what they apprehend, requiring a distinct appetitive power.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for assigning a special appetitive power to the soul?
options: Because knowledge allows beings to desire things beyond their fixed natural form, surpassing simple natural inclination.
Because the soul is made of fire and must rise upward, just as physical fire does.
Because the intellect and senses are identical powers that merge into one single appetitive force.
Because inanimate objects lack any form or inclination, making the soul's appetite unique by contrast.
questions.explanation: He reasons that since knowledge exists in a higher mode than natural form, the inclination following it (appetite) must also be higher and distinct from natural appetite.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that appetite is not distinct from knowledge because they share the same object?
options: He argues that the object is viewed differently: as something known versus as something good or suitable.
He states that the object of knowledge is physical, while the object of appetite is purely spiritual.
He replies that we only desire things we have already fully understood with our intellect.
He claims that knowledge and appetite are actually the same power, just named differently by philosophers.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas explains that while the real object is the same, it differs in aspect: apprehended as sensible/intelligible, but desired as good/suitable, which requires different powers.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the sensitive and intellectual appetites?
options: They are the same power because both desire individual things.
They are distinct powers because they respond to different types of knowledge.
They are identical because the motive power follows the same pattern in all animals.
They are not distinct because the object's nature is accidental to how it is known.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that the intellectual appetite is a distinct power from the sensitive appetite, rejecting the idea that they are the same.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for believing these two appetites are distinct?
options: The appetite's nature is defined by its relation to the specific type of knowledge that moves it.
The intellect knows universals while the senses only know individual things.
The sensitive appetite is subordinate to the intellectual appetite in all human actions.
The motive power in humans is fundamentally different from the motive power in animals.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that passive powers (like appetite) are differentiated by the active principles (like knowledge) that move them; since intellectual and sensitive knowledge are different, the appetites are too.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that the difference in how an object is known is merely accidental?
options: He claims that the intellect and senses perceive the exact same individual things.
He argues that the way an object is known is essential to how it moves the appetite.
He agrees that the difference is accidental and therefore the appetites are the same.
He states that the sensitive appetite does not actually move the soul toward anything.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas insists that the manner of apprehension is not accidental but belongs to the nature of the appetible object, as it only moves the appetite when apprehended.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the nature of sensuality?
options: Sensuality is primarily cognitive but also has appetitive aspects.
Sensuality is a cognitive power that directs the bodily senses.
Sensuality is strictly an appetitive power, not a cognitive one.
Sensuality is a mix of both cognitive and appetitive powers.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly concludes that sensuality is the name for the sensitive appetite, distinguishing it from the apprehensive (cognitive) powers.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas argue that 'sensual movement' refers to appetite rather than cognition?
options: Because the bodily senses are physically located in the appetitive organs.
Because appetite involves a striving toward an object, which resembles movement.
Because cognition is too passive to be considered a true movement of the soul.
Because Augustine stated that movement is exclusive to desire and not knowledge.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that cognitive acts are like rest (the object is in the knower), while appetitive acts are like movement (the desirer is borne toward the object).

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that sensuality is cognitive because the serpent (representing sensuality) proposed sin?
options: The serpent represents reason, not sensuality, so the objection is based on a false premise.
The serpent's role was purely informational, proving sensuality is a cognitive power.
The serpent also incited action, which aligns with the appetitive nature of sensuality.
Sensuality is cognitive because proposing sin requires knowledge of what is wrong.
questions.explanation: Aquinas clarifies that the serpent signifies sensuality not just by proposing sin (cognitive) but by inciting its commission (appetitive).

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the division of the sensitive appetite?
options: It is identical to the concupiscible power, with no separate irascible part.
It is a single power that handles both seeking good and resisting harm.
It is divided into three powers based on the types of sensory inputs.
It is divided into two distinct powers: the concupiscible and the irascible.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that the sensitive appetite is divided into two specific powers, the irascible and the concupiscible, which are species of the generic sensitive appetite.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for why two distinct appetitive powers are necessary?
options: Hatred and love are opposite emotions that cannot exist within the same faculty.
Animals need to resist obstacles that hinder the acquisition of suitable things.
The senses perceive black and white as distinct contraries that require separate powers.
The soul must distinguish between things that please the senses and those that do not.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that just as fire must rise to its suitable place and also resist what destroys it, the soul needs one power to seek suitable things and another to resist hindrances.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that hatred belongs to both the irascible and concupiscible parts?
options: He rejects the objection by stating that Jerome was mistaken about the location of hatred.
The objection is wrong because hatred is actually a form of love in the concupiscible part.
Hatred is purely an irascible passion because it involves fighting against vice.
Hatred is fundamentally a concupiscible passion, but its resulting strife can involve the irascible.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas clarifies that hatred belongs simply to the concupiscible appetite, but the strife arising from it may belong to the irascible appetite.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the article's question?
options: The sensitive appetites are independent of both reason and the will entirely.
The sensitive appetites completely resist reason and never follow its commands.
The sensitive appetites obey the will but are totally free from reason's influence.
The sensitive appetites obey reason in their actions and the will in movement.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that the irascible and concupiscible powers obey reason in their acts and the will in execution.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why the sensitive appetites obey reason?
options: The sensitive appetite naturally moves the intellect to make universal decisions.
A particular reason compares individual cases and is guided by universal reason.
The will commands the appetites to move before any reasoning takes place.
Reason forces the appetites to act through a despotic, slave-like power.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that the 'particular reason' (cogitative power) compares individual intentions and is naturally guided by universal reason, thus directing the sensitive appetite.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that we cannot always hear or see when we wish?
options: He claims that the sensitive powers are actually superior to the rational part.
He argues that exterior senses need external objects, which reason cannot control.
He suggests that hearing and seeing are acts of the will, not the senses.
He states that the will must command the senses to function properly at all times.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas notes that exterior senses require external sensible things to be affected, and the presence of these things is not ruled by reason.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether the will desires something out of necessity?
options: The will is always coerced by external forces, making all voluntary actions necessary by force.
The will never desires anything out of necessity because freedom requires the ability to choose opposites.
The will is completely free from any form of necessity, whether natural or related to goals.
The will desires the ultimate end of happiness with absolute necessity, but not the means to get there.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that while the will is not coerced, it necessarily adheres to the ultimate end (happiness) just as the intellect necessarily accepts first principles.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why the will necessarily desires happiness?
options: God forces the will to choose happiness, making it a matter of external coercion.
Desiring happiness is a social convention that humans have agreed upon to maintain order.
Happiness is the ultimate goal, and the will must naturally cling to it just as the mind accepts basic truths.
The will is a rational power that extends to opposites, so it must eventually settle on one option.
questions.explanation: Aquinas compares the will's necessary adherence to the final end with the intellect's necessary adherence to first principles, calling it a natural necessity.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that we are masters of our actions, and thus cannot be necessitated?
options: He argues that mastery applies to choosing means, not the ultimate end, so desiring the end is not a choice we control.
He claims that being a master means we can force ourselves to do anything, including necessary actions.
He states that Augustine was wrong and that necessity always removes our status as masters of our actions.
He says that we are only masters of our actions when they are voluntary and never necessary.
questions.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes between the end and the means, stating that choice (and thus mastery) concerns the means, while the will necessarily desires the end.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the will's desire for specific goods?
options: The will only desires goods that are strictly necessary for survival.
The will must always desire every good it recognizes as good.
The will desires all goods with the same level of intensity.
The will does not necessarily desire every good thing it wants.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that the will does not desire of necessity whatsoever it desires, distinguishing between necessary and contingent goods.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why the will is not forced to desire certain goods?
options: Because some goods are not required for true happiness.
Because the will prefers bad things over good things sometimes.
Because the senses interfere with the will's decision-making process.
Because the will is too weak to follow the intellect's commands.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that individual goods that do not have a necessary connection to happiness (the last end) are not desired of necessity.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that the will's object moves it like a mover moves a movable object?
options: He claims the object is not actually a mover at all.
He states that the will only moves when the object is physically present.
He says the will is too heavy to be moved by any object.
He argues the will's capacity is too broad for any single good to control it.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas explains that the will's capacity regards the universal good, so it is not subjected to any individual good.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether the will is higher than the intellect?
options: The will is always higher because it moves toward the ultimate end of human life.
The intellect is absolutely higher, though the will can be relatively higher depending on the object.
The will is absolutely higher because love is a more powerful force than knowledge.
The intellect and will are equal in dignity and cannot be ranked against each other.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that while the intellect is nobler in itself (absolutely), the will can be considered higher when directed toward objects nobler than the soul itself (relatively).

questions.q: Why does Aquinas claim the intellect is 'absolutely' higher than the will?
options: Because its object, truth, is simpler and more abstract than the will's object, good.
Because the intellect acts first in time, establishing the foundation for willing.
Because the intellect deals with eternal truths while the will deals with temporary desires.
Because the will relies on the intellect to function, making it dependent.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that the intellect's object (the idea of good/truth) is simpler and more absolute than the will's object (the appetible good existing in things), making the intellect nobler in itself.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that the will is higher because its object (the end) is the first cause?
options: He claims that the end is not a cause but merely a result of intellectual activity.
He agrees that the end is highest but says the will does not reach it directly.
He states that the intellect also seeks the end, so both powers are equal.
He argues that truth is more absolute than good, and even good is a form of truth.
questions.explanation: In his reply to Objection 1, Aquinas explains that truth signifies something more absolute than good, and since good is perceived through comparison, truth extends to the idea of good itself.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether the will moves the intellect?
options: The intellect moves the will, but the will never moves the intellect.
The will only moves the intellect accidentally, not directly.
The will does not move the intellect because the intellect is nobler.
The will moves the intellect as an agent directing it to act.
