questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that the will moves the intellect and other powers of the soul as an agent, similar to how a king rules over governors.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for the will moving the intellect?
options: The will aims at the universal good, guiding powers aimed at specific goods.
The intellect is passive and cannot function without the will's physical push.
The will precedes the intellect in time, so it must cause its actions.
The will is physically stronger than the intellect and forces it to work.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that the power regarding the universal end (the will/good) moves the powers regarding particular ends (like the intellect/truth), using the analogy of a king and city governors.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that this relationship would cause an infinite loop of willing and understanding?
options: The loop is impossible because the will and intellect are actually the same faculty.
The process ends when the soul reaches a state of perfect, unchanging knowledge.
The chain stops because understanding always comes before willing, not the other way around.
The objection is invalid because the will can understand without any prior act.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas states that we must stop at the intellect as preceding the rest, because every movement of the will is preceded by apprehension, but not every apprehension is preceded by an act of the will.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the will?
options: The will contains separate powers for desire and anger.
The will is divided into two parts based on intellectual objects.
The will is distinct from the sensitive appetite but has similar divisions.
The will is a single power without distinct parts for desire or anger.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that the will regards good under a common notion, so it is not differentiated into irascible and concupiscible parts like the sensitive appetite.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for this conclusion?
options: Anger and desire are only passions of the body, not the soul.
A power directed to a general idea is not split by specific details.
The will cannot apprehend universal truths, only particular goods.
Intellectual objects are universal, while sensitive objects are particular.
questions.explanation: He explains that a power directed to a common notion (like 'good' in general) is not multiplied by the specific differences under that notion.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that hope is an irascible virtue?
options: Hope is actually a passion found only in the sensitive appetite.
The irascible part exists in the soul before it joins the body.
Hope belongs to the intellect, not the will, so the objection fails.
The will can be called irascible when it rejects evil based on reason.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas states that the will is 'irascible' when it wills to repel evil from a judgment of reason, not from passion.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether humans possess free will?
options: Humans lack free will because their actions are ultimately determined by God's will.
Humans do have free will, as evidenced by the existence of moral laws and punishments.
Free will is an illusion created by our inability to perceive natural causes.
Humans have free will only in trivial matters, but not in serious moral choices.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that man has free-will; otherwise, commands, rewards, and punishments would be pointless.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for why humans have free will?
options: God grants free will to everyone equally to ensure fairness in the afterlife.
Humans act on instinct, which allows for spontaneous and unpredictable behavior.
Humans are physically stronger than animals, giving them more control over their environment.
Humans use reason to compare options, allowing them to choose between different possible actions.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that unlike animals acting on fixed instinct, humans use reason to judge contingent matters, enabling choice among alternatives.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that God controls human will (Objection 3)?
options: Human will is a separate entity that God cannot touch or influence in any way.
The biblical verses cited are metaphors and should not be taken literally regarding will.
Free will is self-moving; being moved by God does not remove our status as cause of our action.
God only influences kings and leaders, leaving ordinary people completely free to choose.
questions.explanation: Aquinas replies that free will is the cause of its own movement; being moved by another (God) does not negate this self-causation.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about the nature of free will?
options: Free will is a power, not a habit.
Free will is strictly an act, not a power.
Free will is a power combined with a specific habit.
Free will is a habit that helps us choose well.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that free will cannot be a habit because it is indifferent to good and evil, so he concludes it is a power.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for rejecting the idea that free will is a habit?
options: Habits are acquired through learning, while free will is natural to humans.
Habits only apply to the intellect, not to the will or emotions.
Habits are lost when we sin, but free will remains after the fall.
Habits make us disposed toward good or evil, but free will is neutral.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that habits dispose us to act well or ill, whereas free will is indifferent to both good and evil choices.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that free will is lost through sin?
options: We lose the ability to choose freely from external coercion.
We lose free will entirely and can no longer make any choices.
We lose freedom from fault and unhappiness, not natural liberty.
We lose the power of reason, which is the basis of free will.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas clarifies that sin removes freedom from fault and unhappiness, not the basic natural liberty from coercion.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about the nature of free will?
options: It is a physical instinct beyond our control.
It is a power of desire that moves us to act.
It is a mix of memory and imagination.
It is a power of reason that helps us think.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that free will is an appetitive power, meaning it is the faculty of desire or will, rather than a cognitive or thinking power.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas argue that free will is primarily an appetitive power?
options: Because choice targets useful goods, which desire naturally seeks.
Because reason alone cannot make a decision without emotion.
Because the will is stronger than the intellect in humans.
Because Aristotle claimed that thinking is always passive.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since the object of choice is the 'useful' good, and good is the object of appetite, choice—and thus free will—belongs principally to the appetitive power.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that free will is cognitive because it involves judgment?
options: Judgment is actually a form of desire in disguise.
Free will ignores judgment and acts on impulse instead.
Reason does not judge; only the will can compare options.
Judgment ends reasoning, but the will must accept it to choose.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas explains that while reason forms a judgment, the appetite must accept that judgment for a choice to be made, linking the act of choosing to the will.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the relationship between free-will and the will?
options: The will is distinct from free-will because they have different objects.
They are two separate powers that work together to make decisions.
They are the same power, distinguished only by their different acts.
Free-will is a passive power that responds to the active will.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that will and free-will are not two powers but one, similar to how understanding and reasoning are the same power.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for saying will and free-will are the same power?
options: The intellect moves the will, so the will must move the free-will.
Just as understanding and reasoning are one power, willing and choosing are one.
Both powers are required to understand the difference between ends and means.
Choice is the act of the will, so they must share the same source.
questions.explanation: He argues by analogy: since understanding and reasoning belong to the same intellectual power, willing and choosing belong to the same appetitive power.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that choice and willing are different acts, proving they are different powers?
options: He states that different acts can belong to the same power, like understanding and reasoning.
He argues that choice is actually just a part of the act of willing.
He claims that the act of choosing is identical to the act of willing.
He agrees they are different powers because their acts are fundamentally distinct.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas explains that while choice and willing are different acts, they belong to the same power, just as understanding and reasoning do.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether the soul knows physical bodies through the intellect?
options: The soul knows bodies by using immaterial concepts derived from them.
The soul knows bodies only through direct sensory perception.
The soul cannot know bodies because they are constantly changing.
The soul only knows separate, immaterial ideas, not physical things.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that while the object of knowledge is the body, the intellect knows it through immaterial, intelligible species (concepts), not through material forms.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas reject Plato's view that we only know separate 'ideas' rather than physical things?
options: Separate ideas are too complex for the human mind to grasp.
Plato did not believe that physical bodies actually exist.
Physical bodies are more real than immaterial ideas.
It makes scientific knowledge of change and matter impossible.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that if we only knew separate, immovable ideas, we could not have science about movement or matter, which are central to understanding the physical world.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that the intellect deals only with unchanging things, while bodies are changeable?
options: Change always involves something unchanging, like matter or substance.
Bodies are actually unchanging if you look at them closely enough.
The intellect can change its focus to suit the object.
Only spiritual things are truly unchanging, not bodies.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 3, Aquinas explains that every change presupposes something that remains unmoved, such as the underlying substance or matter.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about how the soul understands physical things?
options: The soul understands physical things by having their forms exist in it without physical matter.
The soul understands physical things only through the senses, never through the intellect.
The soul understands physical things by physically becoming the same material substance as them.
The soul understands physical things by using its own essence as a direct physical mirror.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that knowledge is inversely related to materiality, so forms must exist in the knower immaterially, not physically.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main reason for rejecting the idea that the soul knows bodies through its own essence?
options: Materiality limits a form to one specific thing, but knowledge must reach external things generally.
Physical objects outside the soul would also have to possess knowledge if the soul did.
The soul is too superior to contain the lower nature of physical objects in any form.
The soul is only potentially related to things, not actually composed of them in any way.
questions.explanation: He explains that matter determines a form to a single specific thing, whereas the act of knowing extends to things outside the knower.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that Aristotle said the soul is 'everything'?
options: He argues that Aristotle meant the soul is physically composed of all four elements like Empedocles said.
He states that the soul knows everything because it is superior to all corporeal creatures in a complete way.
He says the soul is potentially open to all things through senses and intellect, not actually made of them.
He claims that the soul is actually everything because it shares the same physical nature as all bodies.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas clarifies that Aristotle meant the soul is in potentiality to all things, not actually composed of them.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding how the human soul understands physical things?
options: The soul understands through innate ideas present from birth.
The soul understands only what angels have already revealed.
The soul has no innate ideas but learns them through experience.
The soul understands through a mix of innate and learned concepts.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that the intellect starts as a potentiality without innate species and is reduced to act through instruction and discovery from sensible objects.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for rejecting the idea that we have innate knowledge?
options: Primary matter requires form to exist, unlike the intellectual soul.
People born blind cannot know colors, proving knowledge comes from senses.
Angels understand differently than humans, so human knowledge must differ too.
Plato's view that the body hinders the soul is logically inconsistent.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that if knowledge were innate, a person born blind would still know colors; since they do not, knowledge must come from sensory experience.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that humans share understanding with angels, who have innate knowledge?
options: Angels do not actually have innate species, contrary to what the objection claims.
Human understanding is entirely separate from angelic understanding and shares nothing.
Humans share intelligence with angels, but not in the same degree of perfection.
Angels learn through senses just like humans, so the comparison fails.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 1, Aquinas states that while humans share intelligence with angels, they do not share the same degree of perfection.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the source of the mind's ability to understand?
options: The mind relies on an external active intelligence to inject knowledge into the soul.
The mind copies pre-existing, independent forms that exist without any physical matter.
The mind uses a power within itself to process sensory data into understanding.
The mind receives understanding directly from separate, independent spirits outside the body.
questions.explanation: Aquinas rejects the idea that understanding comes from separate external forms or spirits. Instead, he argues that the active intellect is a power of the soul itself that helps the passive intellect understand.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for rejecting the view that separate forms cause our understanding?
options: It incorrectly assumes that physical objects are actually intelligible in the same way they are sensible.
It ignores the role of the first principle, God, as the ultimate cause of all knowledge.
It fails to provide a sufficient reason for why the soul is united to the body.
It contradicts the proven fact that all knowledge is innate and present from birth.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that the opinion holding that intelligible species come from separate forms cannot assign a sufficient reason for the soul being united to the body.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that the mind must be moved from potential to actual state by an external, always-actual intellect?
options: He agrees that a separate intelligence acts as the immediate cause of our understanding.
He claims that the mind is always in actuality and never in potentiality.
He states that God acts as the proximate cause to move the mind to act.
He argues that the active intellect is a power of the soul, not a separate intelligence.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas clarifies that the passive intellect is moved to act by the active intellect, which is a power of the soul, not by a separate intelligence as the proximate cause.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion about how the human soul knows material things in the eternal types?
options: The soul knows them directly as objects, like seeing images in a mirror.
The soul cannot know them at all in its current state of life.
The soul knows them only through the divine light that acts as a principle of knowledge.
The soul knows them by participating in the forms themselves as independent substances.
questions.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes between knowing something 'in' another as an object (like a mirror) and as a principle (like the sun). He concludes we know things in the eternal types as a principle, because our intellectual light is a participated likeness of the divine light.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why the soul knows things in the eternal types?
options: Because Plato proved that all knowledge must be derived from separate, existing ideas.
Because the eternal types are visible to the naked eye just like physical objects.
Because the human intellect's light is a share of the uncreated divine light containing these types.
Because the Bible explicitly states that we see God's invisible things through the types.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that the intellectual light within us is a 'participated likeness' of the uncreated light in which the eternal types exist. This shared light is the mechanism that allows us to know things through those types.

questions.q: How does Aquinas address the objection that knowing things in eternal types leads back to Plato's error?
options: He agrees with the objection and rejects the idea that the soul knows things in types.
He argues that Augustine invented the concept of eternal types to replace Plato's ideas.
He states that the objection is invalid because Romans 1:20 proves the types are known first.
He claims Plato was wrong because he thought forms exist separately from matter, unlike divine types.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that Plato erred by thinking forms subsist apart from matter. Augustine corrected this by substituting 'types in the Divine mind' for Plato's independent ideas, making the concept compatible with Christian faith.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether intellectual knowledge comes from sensible things?
options: Intellectual knowledge is independent of the senses and operates entirely on its own.
Intellectual knowledge comes directly from images discharged by physical bodies.
Intellectual knowledge is not derived from sensible things, but from separate forms.
Intellectual knowledge is derived from sensible things, following Aristotle's middle path.
questions.explanation: Aquinas rejects Plato's view that intellect is separate from senses and Democritus's view that images enter the soul. He adopts Aristotle's middle course, agreeing that sense is affected by sensible things, which serves as the basis for intellectual knowledge.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for accepting that intellectual knowledge originates from sensible things?
options: He asserts that all truth must be verified by direct sensory experience.
He believes the soul is purely material and cannot function without physical input.
He argues that the senses are affected by external objects, influencing the composite human being.
He claims that the intellect is too weak to generate knowledge without physical triggers.
questions.explanation: Aquinas follows Aristotle in holding that sense perception is an act of the 'composite' (soul and body). Since external sensible objects affect this composite, they cause the operation of the sensitive part, which is the starting point for intellectual knowledge.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that intellectual knowledge extends beyond what the senses can perceive?
options: He states that sensitive knowledge is not the sole cause of intellectual knowledge.
He argues that the senses are actually capable of perceiving all intellectual truths.
He claims that intellectual knowledge is merely a stronger version of sensory data.
He suggests that the objection is valid and intellectual knowledge is independent.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 3, Aquinas explains that while sensitive knowledge is not the entire cause, it is a partial cause. Therefore, it is not strange that the effect (intellectual knowledge) extends further than this partial cause (sensitive knowledge).

questions.q: According to Aquinas, can the human mind understand something right now without looking at mental images?
options: No, because mental images are only needed when we first learn something new.
No, because our minds are tied to bodies and need mental images to think actively.
Yes, but only for abstract ideas that do not exist in the physical world.
Yes, because once we learn a fact, our mind holds it and can use it independently.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that in our current state, the intellect is united to a body and must always turn to mental images (phantasms) to understand anything actually, not just when learning.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main reason for saying we need mental images to think?
options: Our minds are designed to know universal natures as they exist in individual physical things.
God created humans to rely on senses, so thinking without images is sinful.
The brain is too weak to process information without visual aids to help it.
Mental images are the only source of truth, so we cannot think without them.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that the human intellect's proper object is the nature of things found in matter, and we only grasp individuals through senses and imagination.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that we can understand spiritual things without images?
options: Spiritual things are actually physical, so we can form images of them directly.
We understand spiritual things by comparing them to physical things we can imagine.
Angels show us visions of spiritual things, so we do not need to imagine them.
Once we reach a high level of wisdom, we no longer need physical references.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 3, Aquinas states that we know incorporeal things by comparison with sensible bodies, using examples like knowing God as a cause.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the article's main question?
options: The intellect's judgment remains fully active even without sense input.
The intellect's judgment is hindered when the senses are suspended.
The intellect does not depend on the senses at all.
The senses can only hinder the intellect if the person is awake.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly answers that it is not possible for the intellect to form a perfect judgment while the senses are suspended.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for this conclusion?
options: Sleep causes the brain to stop processing logical arguments entirely.
Our understanding relies on comparing ideas to things we perceive with our senses.
The intellect is physically located inside the sensory organs.
The senses are superior to the intellect in terms of power.
questions.explanation: He argues that in our current state, we know things by comparison to sensible things, so perfect judgment requires sensory knowledge.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that people sometimes reason while asleep?
options: He says that syllogizing is a sensory act, not an intellectual one.
He claims that sleeping people are actually using their eyes to see.
He denies that people ever reason while they are asleep.
He argues that sleep only partially suspends the senses due to bodily changes.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, he explains that senses are suspended to varying degrees based on evaporation, implying they are not fully gone.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding how our intellect understands material things?
options: It understands them by participating in separate, immaterial ideas.
It understands them by directly receiving the form as it exists in matter.
It understands them by separating their form from the specific individual matter.
It understands them by having the form impressed upon it like sight.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that we must say our intellect understands material things by abstracting the form from the phantasms, which represent individual matter.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why the human intellect uses this method?
options: It is identical to the active intellect, which only receives abstracted species.
It is the act of a physical organ, so it can only know individuals.
It is not a physical organ but is united to the body, placing it in the middle.
It is completely separate from the body, so it must know immaterial forms.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues the human intellect holds a middle place: it is not the act of an organ (unlike senses) but is united to the body (unlike angels), requiring it to know forms in matter but not as in that specific matter.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that the active intellect only illuminates phantasms without abstracting?
options: He states the active intellect abstracts the species by its own power, not just illuminating.
He claims the passive intellect is actually responsible for performing the abstraction.
He argues that abstraction is impossible because the phantasm is too material.
He agrees that the active intellect only provides light and does nothing else.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the fourth objection, Aquinas explicitly states that the active intellect does more than throw light; it uses its own power to abstract the intelligible species from the phantasm.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about the relationship between the mental image and our understanding?
options: It is the actual object that our mind understands.
It is the tool our mind uses to understand things.
It is a copy of the thing outside the soul.
It is the result of the mind reflecting on itself.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly rejects the idea that the mental image is what is understood, stating instead that it is the form or means by which the intellect understands.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for rejecting the view that we only know our own mental impressions?
options: It would mean science only studies ideas inside the soul.
It would make all contradictory opinions equally true.
It would imply that external things do not exist.
It would make it impossible to use words to communicate.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that if we only judged our own impressions, then both healthy and corrupt tastes would be equally correct, leading to the absurd conclusion that all opinions are true.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that words are signs of soul passions, so those passions must be what we understand?
options: He claims that the senses only receive impressions, not images.
He states that the soul has no passions that can be signed by words.
He argues that imagination creates images of absent or unseen things.
He says words actually refer to the external things themselves.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas distinguishes between the sense receiving an impression and the imagination forming an image of something that is not currently present.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, which type of concept do we grasp first in our intellectual process?
options: Abstract principles before any sensory experience of the world
Complex definitions before the simple parts that make them up
Specific individuals like 'Socrates' before general categories like 'man'
Broad, general categories like 'animal' before specific ones like 'man'
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that we know the more universal (like 'animal') before the less universal (like 'man') because our intellect moves from a confused, general awareness to distinct, specific knowledge.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's primary reason for claiming we know universals before particulars?
options: Our mind starts with vague, confused knowledge and gradually clarifies it into distinct details
Senses perceive individual objects, so the intellect must immediately analyze their parts
We learn causes and principles directly, without needing to observe their effects first
Universal concepts are simpler in nature and therefore easier for the brain to process
questions.explanation: He explains that the intellect proceeds from potentiality to actuality, first grasping the whole confusedly (the universal) before distinguishing its specific parts (the particulars).

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that we know causes before effects?
options: Causes are always known through their effects, which proves universals are known last
Universals are not causes in the relevant sense; they are results of our mental abstraction
We actually know effects before causes, so the objection is based on a false premise
The objection is valid, but Aquinas concedes that principles are known secondarily
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 4, Aquinas states that the universal, considered as a principle, is actually a result of the intellect's mode of understanding by abstraction, not a prior cause.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's conclusion regarding whether the intellect can understand multiple distinct things simultaneously?
options: The intellect can understand many different things simultaneously because it exists outside of time.
The intellect can understand many things at once if they are grasped as a single unified concept.
The intellect can understand many things at once just as it perceives color and smell together.
The intellect can understand many things at once because they are not opposed to each other.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that while we can understand many things as 'one' (a unified whole), we cannot understand them as 'many' (distinct items) at the same time because that requires multiple mental forms.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas claim the intellect cannot hold multiple distinct concepts simultaneously?
options: Because the intellect is too weak to handle the complexity of multiple ideas at once.
Because time prevents the intellect from processing more than one idea in a single moment.
Because distinct concepts are always opposed to each other, making simultaneous holding impossible.
Because the mind is like a body that cannot have two different shapes or colors at once.
questions.explanation: Aquinas uses the analogy of physical forms: just as one body cannot be red and blue at the same time, the intellect cannot be perfected by two different mental forms simultaneously.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that we must know two things at once to compare them?
options: We know them together only in their relation to each other, not as separate distinct items.
We use a different part of the brain for comparison that operates outside of time.
Comparison is an illusion; we only ever truly understand one thing at a time.
We actually know them one after the other, but so fast it feels like simultaneous knowledge.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 4, Aquinas states that when comparing, we know both things only in relation to their difference or comparison, similar to how parts are known within a whole.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding how the human intellect understands?
options: It understands by combining and separating concepts through a step-by-step process.
It understands only by looking at physical objects in the present moment.
It grasps the complete truth of a thing all at once without any steps.
It does not use composition or division because those are only for many things.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that the human intellect must understand by composition and division because it acquires knowledge gradually, unlike the divine intellect which knows everything at once.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas say the human intellect necessarily uses composition and division?
options: Because all things in reality are made of separate parts that must be analyzed.
Because angels and God also use this method to understand the world.
Because the human mind is too weak to understand simple essences directly.
Because human knowledge grows in stages, moving from basic definitions to complex relations.
questions.explanation: Aquinas compares the human intellect to generated things that attain perfection by degrees, starting with simple apprehension and moving to comparing things through reasoning.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that the intellect abstracts from time, and thus cannot use time-bound composition?
options: He states that the intellect completely ignores time and images when understanding truths.
He says the intellect still relies on mental images, which involve time, even when abstracting.
He claims that composition and division happen in eternity, not in human time.
He argues that time is an illusion created by the human mind's confusion.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas explains that although the intellect abstracts from images, it must still turn to them to understand actually, and this turning involves time.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about whether the intellect can be false?
options: The intellect can be false when it connects things in ways that do not match reality.
The intellect is never false because it is always directed to its proper object.
The intellect can only be false when it judges the basic nature of a single thing.
The intellect is always false because it relies on physical senses that are easily deceived.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that while the intellect is correct about the basic nature of things, it can err when combining or separating concepts, such as in reasoning or definitions.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why the intellect can make mistakes?
options: The intellect is naturally inclined to doubt the truth of first principles and scientific facts.
The intellect fails to grasp the simple, unchanging nature of material objects.
The intellect can mistakenly combine incompatible ideas or apply wrong definitions to things.
The intellect uses a physical organ that can be damaged by disease or bad humors.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that errors occur in the 'surroundings' of a thing's essence, specifically when the intellect composes or divides concepts incorrectly, such as defining a triangle as a circle.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that sin involves falsehood, so the intellect can be false?
options: He claims that sin is a physical defect that prevents the mind from seeing the truth.
He argues that sinners are actually correct in their judgments but choose to act wrongly.
He denies that sin involves any error, stating that evil actions are always based on true beliefs.
He says the sinner errs in the practical judgment of what is desirable or appetible.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas specifies that the error of the sinner lies in the practical judgment regarding the object of appetite, not in the theoretical intellect's grasp of truth.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether one person can understand a thing better than another?
options: No, because understanding a thing differently means you do not understand it at all.
Only one person can understand a thing, and that is the person with the best body.
Only people of different species can have different levels of understanding.
Yes, one person can understand a thing better than another can.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that while the truth of the thing understood is the same for everyone, the act of understanding can be better in one person due to greater mental power or better physical disposition.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why one person might understand a thing better than another?
options: Because the person is using a different language to describe the thing.
Because the person has memorized more facts about the specific thing.
Because the person has a stronger desire to learn the subject matter.
Because the person has a more perfect intellectual power or better mental faculties.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that a person with a more perfect intellect or better-disposed lower mental powers (like memory and imagination) can understand the same thing better, similar to how someone with better eyesight sees more clearly.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that different levels of understanding would mean people are of different species?
options: He agrees that people with different understanding levels belong to different species.
He claims that all humans have exactly the same intellectual power, so no difference exists.
He argues that species are defined by how well a person understands, not by their body.
He says that differences in understanding only create a numerical difference, not a specific one.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas states that variations caused by the physical body (matter) result in numerical differences between individuals, not specific differences that would change their species.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, which does the human intellect understand first: indivisible things or divisible things?
options: Divisible things are understood first because they are the primary objects of our senses.
Neither is known first; we understand both simultaneously through intuition.
Indivisible things are always understood first because the intellect is simple.
It depends on the type; divisible wholes are known first, but points are known later.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that continuous divisible things are known first, but indivisible points are known secondarily through the absence of parts.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main reason for saying that indivisible points are known after divisible lines?
options: Points are too small to be perceived by the senses, which are the source of all knowledge.
The intellect is naturally attracted to complex forms before it can simplify them into points.
Plato taught that forms are known first, but Aquinas rejects this as irrelevant to geometry.
Points are defined by the lack of parts, and we grasp absence only after grasping presence.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that points are known through 'privation of divisibility,' meaning we understand them as lacking parts, which requires prior knowledge of things that have parts.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that a point must be known first because it is part of the definition of a line?
options: He states that definitions are always known after the things they define, regardless of content.
He claims that points are actually divisible, so they do not belong in the definition of a line.
He argues that Euclid's definition applies only to finite lines, not to lines in general.
He agrees with the objection but says the intellect skips definitions when learning geometry.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas clarifies that Euclid defines a finite straight line, which has limits (points), whereas an indefinite line does not essentially contain points.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, what is the primary way our intellect knows individual material things?
options: It knows them directly by abstracting universal concepts.
It knows them directly because the sense organs provide the data.
It knows them indirectly by turning back to mental images.
It knows them directly and primarily through individual matter.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that the intellect knows singulars 'indirectly, and as it were by a kind of reflection' by turning to the phantasms (mental images) after abstracting the species.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why the intellect cannot know singulars directly?
options: Singular things are too complex for the human mind to grasp.
Singular things are material, and the intellect is purely spiritual.
The senses are superior to the intellect in knowing specific details.
The intellect abstracts from individual matter, leaving only universals.
questions.explanation: He argues that the principle of singularity is individual matter, but the intellect understands by abstracting from this matter, which results in knowing the universal.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that the intellect understands itself, and thus must know singulars?
options: Self-understanding is a direct act that bypasses the need for abstraction.
The intellect is a universal, not a singular, so it cannot know itself.
The intellect is a singular thing, but it is immaterial, so it is knowable.
The intellect does not actually understand itself, only its actions.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas explains that while intelligibility is incompatible with material singularity, an immaterial singular like the intellect can be intelligible.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether our intellect can know the infinite?
options: We cannot know the infinite in any way, actual or potential.
We can know the infinite fully and all at once.
We can know the infinite as a single, complete whole.
We can know the infinite only by considering it step-by-step.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because the infinite is not a complete whole, we cannot grasp it all at once. Instead, we know it potentially by moving from one part to another in a sequence.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why we cannot understand the infinite all at once?
options: The infinite is too large for the human brain to process.
Our intellect is a physical faculty that limits our capacity.
The infinite exists only in the future, not in the present.
The infinite lacks a definite end, so it cannot be a single complete unit.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that to know something actually, it must be represented as a whole. Since the infinite has no final limit, it is never a complete whole and thus cannot be grasped in a single act of understanding.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that our intellect is an infinite power and therefore can know infinite objects?
options: He claims that our intellect's power is actually finite and limited.
He argues that infinite power only applies to God, not to humans.
He denies that our intellect has any infinite power at all.
He says our infinite power allows us to know the infinite only potentially.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the fourth objection, Aquinas agrees that our intellect has an infinite power because it is not limited by matter, but he clarifies that this means it knows the infinite only potentially, not actually.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether the human intellect can know the future?
options: Only God can know the future because humans lack the necessary mental power.
Humans can only know the future by understanding the causes that produce it.
Humans can directly perceive future events in the same way they see present ones.
Humans can know the future through dreams and animal instincts.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that while we cannot know the future 'in itself' (only God can), we can know it 'in its cause' by understanding the principles that lead to future results.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why humans can have some knowledge of future events?
options: Because we can understand the causes that lead to specific future results.
Because humans are superior to animals and thus have better predictive powers.
Because our minds are free from the distractions of the physical senses.
Because future events are universal and not tied to specific moments in time.
questions.explanation: The text states that the future can be known by us 'forasmuch as it exists in its cause,' allowing for scientific or conjectural knowledge based on causal connections.

questions.q: How does Aquinas explain the ability of animals to predict weather, which was raised as an objection?
options: Animals' imaginations are entirely influenced by heavenly bodies, unlike human reason.
Animals possess a special spiritual power that allows them to see time clearly.
Animals use their superior intelligence to analyze patterns better than humans do.
Animals know the future because they are closer to God than humans are.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas states that animals lack reason to regulate their imagination, so their imagination follows the influence of heavenly bodies, allowing them to react to future weather.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, how does the human soul know itself?
options: By abstracting a likeness from its own incorporeal nature.
By perceiving its own act of understanding, not its essence.
By using the same method as angels to understand themselves.
By directly grasping its own essence as a pure act.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that the human intellect knows itself not by its essence, but by its act, meaning it recognizes itself through the activity of understanding.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why the human soul cannot know itself by its essence?
options: The human soul lacks the light of the active intellect entirely.
The human soul is a potentiality, not a pure act like God or angels.
The human soul is material and therefore cannot be known directly.
The human soul is too complex to be understood by its own essence.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that the human intellect is a potentiality, similar to primary matter, and thus only becomes actual when it understands something, unlike angels or God who are acts.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that Augustine says the mind knows itself because it is incorporeal?
options: He argues Augustine meant the mind knows itself through its own act of understanding.
He suggests that Augustine only applied this rule to angels, not humans.
He claims Augustine was mistaken about the nature of the human mind.
He states that incorporeality alone is sufficient for self-knowledge by essence.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas explains that Augustine's point is that the mind knows itself by means of itself, being led to self-knowledge by its own act of understanding.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, how do we know if we possess a specific mental habit (like faith or knowledge)?
options: We know it through external signs like body language.
We know it because it is the cause of all our thoughts.
We know it only by observing the actions it produces in us.
We know it directly by seeing its essence inside our soul.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that habits are not perfect acts themselves, so we cannot know them by their essence; we only know them by the acts they enable us to perform.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main reason for saying we cannot know habits by their essence?
options: Habits are causes, and causes are never known directly.
Nothing is known except as it is actually in operation.
The soul's object is always the nature of material things.
Habits are material things that exist outside the soul.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that 'nothing is known but as it is actual,' and since a habit is a medium between power and act, it is only knowable through its actual exercise.

questions.q: In his reply to Objection 1, how does Aquinas explain that we know we have faith?
options: We know it because faith is a material thing in the heart.
We know it because conscience proclaims its presence clearly.
We know it by seeing the external movement of our body.
We know it by perceiving the interior act of believing.
questions.explanation: Aquinas rejects the idea that faith is seen by external movement; instead, he says it is perceived by the subject through the 'interior act of the heart,' meaning the act of believing.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether the human intellect knows its own act of understanding?
options: It knows its own act only through a separate, distinct act of self-reflection.
It cannot know its own act because the act is distinct from the object of knowledge.
It knows its own act secondarily, after it has first understood external material things.
It knows its own act directly and primarily, before knowing any external objects.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that for the human intellect, the first object known is the nature of a material thing. The act of understanding is known secondarily, through the act by which that external object is known.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why the human intellect does not know its own act first?
options: The intellect lacks the power to perceive its own operations without the help of the senses.
The intellect's essence is identical to its act of understanding, making self-knowledge immediate.
Knowing one's own act would lead to an impossible infinite regress of further acts.
The primary object of human understanding is the nature of material things, not the intellect itself.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that the human intellect's first object is the nature of a material thing. Since the intellect is not its own act nor is its essence the first object, it knows its own act only after knowing external objects.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that the intellect should not know its own act because proper senses do not feel their own acts?
options: He argues that the intellect is superior to sense and therefore can perceive its own activity directly.
He claims that the common sense perceives the act of proper senses, just as the intellect perceives its own.
He states that the objection is invalid because the intellect and sense share the same relation to their acts.
He explains that material objects cannot change themselves, so sense acts are perceived by another faculty.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas explains that proper senses are perceived by the common sense because material objects cannot change themselves; one thing is changed by another. This distinguishes the case from the intellect.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's conclusion regarding whether the intellect understands the act of the will?
options: The intellect knows the will only by guessing, not by direct understanding.
The intellect understands the will because the will's act exists intelligibly within the intellect.
The intellect cannot know the will because they are distinct powers with different objects.
The will is known only through external images, similar to how we perceive physical bodies.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since the will is rooted in the intellect, its act is present there intelligibly and is therefore understood by the intellect.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why the intellect understands the will?
options: The will and intellect are completely separate faculties that happen to agree on most matters.
The will is an inclination that follows understanding, so it resides in the intellect as its proper subject.
The object of the will is identical to the object of the intellect in every respect.
The intellect copies the will's actions exactly like a mirror reflects a physical object.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that the will is an inclination consequent on the form understood, meaning it exists intelligibly within the intelligent subject.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that the will and intellect are distinct powers?
options: He claims the objection is valid, but says God bridges the gap between the two powers.
He replies that the intellect ignores the will's distinctness to focus only on truth.
He argues that while distinct, both powers share the same soul substance, allowing one to know the other.
He states that the will is actually just a weaker version of the intellect, not a distinct power.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 1, Aquinas notes that the argument would hold if they were in different subjects, but since both are in the same soul substance, the intellect can know the will.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's conclusion regarding whether the human soul can understand immaterial substances in its current state of life?
options: Yes, because the human soul is itself immaterial and therefore naturally knows immaterial things.
No, because immaterial substances are too complex for the human mind to process.
Yes, but only if the soul unites with a separate active intellect to gain this knowledge.
No, because our intellect currently depends on sensory images to understand anything.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that in our present life, the intellect must turn to sensory images (phantasms) to understand, which is impossible for immaterial substances that do not exist in matter.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why we cannot directly understand immaterial substances now?
options: The human soul is too weak and corrupted by the body to perceive pure forms.
Immaterial substances are constantly changing, making them impossible to grasp clearly.
Our intellect is naturally tied to material things and requires sensory images to function.
God has hidden the nature of immaterial substances from human knowledge entirely.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that our intellect has a natural relationship to material natures and understands by turning to phantasms, which immaterial substances do not provide.

questions.q: In Reply to Objection 2, how does Aquinas refute the claim that 'like is known by like'?
options: He states that Empedocles was right, and the soul does need the nature of all things.
He argues that sharing a nature is not enough; the knower must possess the form of the known thing.
He claims that the soul is actually more similar to material things than to immaterial ones.
He says that knowledge comes from external teaching, not from any natural likeness between knower and known.
questions.explanation: Aquinas replies that natural likeness is insufficient; instead, the likeness of the thing known must be in the knower as a form, not just by shared nature.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding our ability to understand immaterial substances through material things?
options: We cannot understand them at all because God is the only cause that cannot be known.
We can understand them fully since science provides clear definitions for angels and other spirits.
We can understand them perfectly because our minds naturally rise from the physical to the spiritual.
We cannot understand them perfectly because material things do not properly reflect immaterial ones.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that while we may have some knowledge, we cannot understand immaterial substances perfectly because there is no proper proportion or likeness between material and immaterial things.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why we cannot perfectly understand immaterial substances?
options: Our intellect cannot abstract a quiddity from matter that is akin to an immaterial substance.
Immaterial substances are infinitely distant from their effects, making them impossible to comprehend.
The human soul is the only immaterial substance that can be understood through its own acts.
Platonic philosophy incorrectly assumed that immaterial substances are the forms of material things.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since immaterial substances differ entirely from the essence of material things, abstracting from matter will never yield anything similar to an immaterial substance.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that we have sciences and definitions for immaterial substances like angels?
options: He argues that Damascene's definitions are incorrect because angels do not exist in reality.
He claims that philosophy is superior to theology in defining the nature of heavenly beings.
He agrees that these sciences allow us to know the exact essence of immaterial beings.
He states that such sciences know these things mainly through negation, not by defining their essence.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas explains that science treats higher things principally by denying them inferior properties, meaning we do not know their true essence.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, is God the very first thing the human mind knows in this life?
options: No, because God is too simple to be understood by humans.
No, because we know God indirectly through created things.
Yes, because God is the light that enables all knowledge.
Yes, because the human soul bears the image of God.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that God is not the first object known; rather, we know Him through creatures, as stated in his main answer.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for why God is not our first known object?
options: The human mind is too weak to handle spiritual concepts.
Our intellect in this life cannot grasp the essence of the uncreated substance.
God hides His nature from humans until they reach heaven.
Material things are more real and therefore easier to understand.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since we cannot even understand immaterial created substances, we certainly cannot understand the essence of the uncreated God directly.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that God, as the cause of knowledge, must be the first thing known?
options: We know God first, but only because He causes all other things.
The rule about causes applies only to things in the same order of being.
God causes our ability to know, but is not the first object we actually know.
God enlightens the mind, but this light is not an object of knowledge.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas clarifies that God is the first cause of our faculty of knowledge, not the first object known.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the ability of the soul to understand after death?
options: The soul understands by turning directly to intelligible objects without using mental images.
The soul cannot understand anything because its natural connection to the body is destroyed.
The soul understands only through innate ideas that were written on it at creation.
The soul understands by using mental images it retained while alive in the body.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that while the soul naturally uses mental images (phantasms) in the body, after separation it understands by turning directly to intelligible objects, similar to other separate substances.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, what is the main reason the soul's mode of understanding changes after death?
options: The soul loses its senses, forcing it to rely on pure reason instead.
The soul has a different mode of existence when separated from the body.
The soul's nature is fundamentally altered by the event of death.
The body was always an accidental hindrance that the soul finally escapes.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that the soul has one mode of being when in the body and another when apart from it, and its mode of action follows from its mode of existence.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that the soul has no innate ideas or abstracted species to understand with?
options: He claims the soul understands through species arising from divine light.
He insists the soul uses innate species that were present from the start.
He says the soul understands by abstracting new species from the afterlife.
He argues that the soul uses species retained from its time in the body.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas states that the separated soul understands by means of participated species arising from the influence of the Divine light.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about the separated soul's ability to know angels?
options: It knows angels perfectly only through its own body.
It has imperfect knowledge of angels due to its lower nature.
It cannot know any separate substances at all.
It has perfect, complete knowledge of all angels naturally.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that the soul's mode of existence is inferior to an angel's, so its natural knowledge of angels is imperfect and defective.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for the soul's ability to know separate substances after death?
options: It becomes more perfect because it is no longer part of the human whole.
It receives direct presence of God, which allows it to know all things.
It abstracts new ideas from angels, which are simpler than the soul.
It no longer relies on physical images and turns directly to intelligible objects.
questions.explanation: He argues that without the body, the soul understands by turning to simply intelligible objects rather than physical images (phantasms).

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that happiness should not depend solely on separation from the body?
options: Knowledge of separate substances provides the final and ultimate happiness.
Separation from the body is the only way to achieve any kind of happiness.
Ultimate happiness comes from knowing God by grace, not just separate substances.
The body's weight actually increases the soul's capacity for perfect knowledge.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, he clarifies that ultimate happiness consists in the knowledge of God, which is seen only by grace, not merely in knowing other separate substances.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about the knowledge of natural things possessed by a soul separated from the body?
options: It knows nothing about natural things because it lacks a body.
It knows all natural things, but only in a general and confused manner.
It knows only the specific details of things it studied while alive.
It knows all natural things perfectly, just like the angels do.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that separated souls know natural things not with certain and proper knowledge, but in a general and confused manner, unlike angels who know them perfectly.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why the separated soul's knowledge is imperfect?
options: God intentionally hides the details of nature from human souls after death.
The soul is naturally inferior to angels, for whom such knowledge is natural.
The soul relies on memory, which fades away after separation from the body.
The soul loses its ability to think clearly once it leaves the body.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because the soul is by nature inferior to an angel, it does not receive perfect knowledge through the divine species, unlike angels for whom this knowledge is natural.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that knowing separate substances implies knowing all natural things?
options: He argues that even angels understand natural things through specific concepts, not just their substance.
He states that natural things do not actually exist within separate substances at all.
He claims that separate substances are too complex for any created mind to comprehend fully.
He admits the objection is correct but limits it to angels only, not human souls.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 1, Aquinas notes that angels do not understand natural things through their substance but through certain species, so the same logic applies to souls.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, what is the separated soul's ability to know specific individual things?
options: It knows some specific things, but not all of them.
It cannot know any specific individual things at all.
It knows specific things only through physical senses.
It knows every single individual thing that exists.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that separated souls know some singulars, but not all, limiting their knowledge based on prior connections or divine order.

questions.q: How does Aquinas explain that a separated soul can know specific individuals?
options: The soul uses its memory of physical experiences from life.
The soul deduces individuals from general universal concepts.
God infuses knowledge directly, similar to how angels know things.
The soul abstracts details from mental images of the body.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that souls know singulars through species infused by God, which act as a participated likeness of the Divine Essence.

questions.q: In his reply to the third objection, why does Aquinas say the soul does not know all singulars?
options: God intentionally hides most information from the soul.
The soul lacks the intellectual power to process all data.
The soul only knows what it physically saw in life.
The soul has different relationships to different individuals.
questions.explanation: Aquinas replies that the soul does not have the same relation to all singulars, but rather one relation to some and another to others.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about the knowledge we gain during our earthly lives after death?
options: All knowledge acquired in this life is completely destroyed when the body dies.
Knowledge remains entirely intact because the soul is immortal and unchanged by death.
Knowledge is replaced entirely by a new divine light, erasing all previous learning.
The part of knowledge stored in the intellect remains, but the part tied to bodily senses is lost.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that knowledge resides partly in the intellect (which survives) and partly in sensitive powers like memory (which depend on the body and perish).

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main reason for believing that some acquired knowledge survives death?
options: The intellect is an incorruptible faculty that cannot be destroyed by the death of the body.
The Apostle Paul explicitly stated that knowledge will never be destroyed in any form.
Knowledge is a physical quality that becomes stronger when the body is gone.
Divine light preserves all human memories perfectly in the afterlife.
questions.explanation: He states that the intellect is incorruptible, so the intelligible species within it cannot be corrupted by the destruction of the body.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that 'knowledge shall be destroyed' (1 Corinthians 13:8)?
options: He asserts that the verse was mistranslated and originally meant knowledge will be renewed.
He says the verse is metaphorical and does not apply to intellectual habits.
He argues the verse refers to the active process of knowing, not the stored habit of knowledge.
He claims the verse only applies to knowledge gained through bodily senses.
questions.explanation: In his reply to Objection 1, Aquinas clarifies that the Apostle speaks of the act of knowing (which is partial here), not the habit itself.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's conclusion regarding knowledge acquired in this life after the soul separates from the body?
options: The knowledge remains exactly as it was, using the same mental processes as in earthly life.
The knowledge remains, but the soul must still use physical images to understand it.
The knowledge is completely lost because the soul can no longer remember or love anything.
The knowledge remains, but the soul understands it in a different way than it did when embodied.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that while the intelligible species (the content of knowledge) remain, the mode of understanding changes because the soul is no longer united to the body.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why the soul can still understand what it learned in this life?
options: The mental images of the known objects remain in the soul, though the method of using them changes.
The soul's intellectual power increases significantly after death, allowing it to grasp new truths.
The habits formed in life produce acts that are identical in every respect to those in life.
The body's corruption does not affect the soul's ability to turn to physical phantasms.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that the 'intelligible species' (similitudes of objects) remain in the separated soul, enabling it to understand former knowledge, albeit without turning to phantasms.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that habits produce acts similar to those by which they were acquired?
options: He states that the objection is valid, but the separated soul has a special exception to this rule.
He explains that the objection confuses the species of the act with the power of the agent.
He claims that the habit of knowledge is unique and does not follow the general rule of habits.
He argues that acts are similar in their essential type, but not necessarily in their manner or mode.
questions.explanation: In his reply to Objection 3, Aquinas distinguishes between species and mode, noting that acts producing a habit are like those caused by it in species, but not in mode.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's conclusion regarding whether physical distance hinders a separated soul's knowledge?
options: Physical distance hinders knowledge because senses are absent.
Physical distance hinders knowledge just as time distance does.
Physical distance hinders knowledge only for distant events.
Physical distance does not hinder the soul's knowledge.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that knowledge in the separated soul is not hindered by local distance because it relies on divine light, not sensory proximity.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas argue that physical distance does not impede the separated soul's knowledge?
options: The soul retains its senses and can perceive nearby objects.
The soul knows things through divine light, which ignores distance.
The soul only knows things that are temporally close to it.
The soul moves rapidly to overcome any physical separation.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that the separated soul understands singulars through species derived from divine light, which is indifferent to whether things are near or far.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that demons' speed implies distance hinders knowledge?
options: Augustine assumed demons had bodies and senses requiring proximity.
Augustine was mistaken about the nature of demonic knowledge.
Speed is irrelevant because demons do not need to move.
Demons are actually closer to us than separated souls are.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas clarifies that Augustine's statement reflects the view that demons have naturally united bodies and sensitive powers, which would require local proximity.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, do separated souls naturally know what is happening on earth?
options: No, they are naturally ignorant of earthly events.
Yes, but only if the living pray to them.
Only if they were saints during their lifetime.
Yes, they see everything clearly through divine light.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that by natural knowledge, separated souls do not know what passes on earth because they are separated from the living by their mode of existence.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main reason for saying separated souls do not know earthly affairs?
options: God has blocked their vision to prevent interference.
They are united to spiritual beings and distant from fleshly life.
They have forgotten their earthly memories completely.
They are too far away in space to perceive us.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that souls are joined to the world of spiritual substances and are separated from the life of the flesh, making them ignorant of corporeal matters.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that dead people appear to the living to tell them news?
options: He states that the living are hallucinating due to grief.
He claims the stories are lies told by demons.
He says these appearances are miracles caused by God's special will.
He argues the dead naturally watch us like angels do.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas states that such appearances are either by the special dispensation of God and are to be accounted as miraculous.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the origin of the human soul?
options: The soul is an eternal part of God's divine essence.
The soul is a created thing, not part of God's own substance.
The soul is identical to God because both are simple forms.
The soul is a physical body formed from earthly matter.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that it is false that the soul is of the substance of God, concluding instead that it is a created entity.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's primary reason for rejecting the idea that the soul is part of God?
options: The soul is composite, while God is entirely simple and indivisible.
God is a physical body, whereas the soul is purely spiritual.
Scripture says God breathed into man, which implies creation, not division.
God is pure act with no potentiality, while the soul learns and changes.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that the soul has potentiality (it acquires knowledge), which is incompatible with God's nature as pure act who receives nothing.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that 'breathing' implies God sent part of Himself?
options: God's substance is infinite, so losing a part makes no difference.
The text means God physically exhaled his own body into Adam.
Humans breathe out air, which is external, so God must do the same.
Breathing is metaphorical for creating a spirit, not sending physical substance.
questions.explanation: In Reply 1, Aquinas clarifies that 'breathing' refers to the act of making a spirit, not sending forth a part of one's own substance.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding how the human soul comes into existence?
options: The soul is drawn out of the potentiality of physical matter.
The soul is created directly by God, not formed from pre-existing matter.
The soul exists eternally and was never made or created.
The soul is a material form generated like other physical objects.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that the rational soul is a subsistent form that cannot be made from matter, so it must be produced by creation.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas argue that the rational soul must be created rather than generated?
options: Because matter cannot hold any form without being destroyed first.
Because the soul is purely spiritual and has no connection to the body.
Because it is a subsistent form that exists in its own right, unlike accidents.
Because all forms, including the soul, are created directly by God.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that only substances properly exist and are made; since the soul is a subsistent form (a substance), it is made by creation, unlike non-subsistent forms which are made only as part of a composite.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that the soul, being an act of matter, must be drawn from matter's potentiality?
options: He claims that matter has no potentiality until God acts upon it directly.
He agrees that the soul comes from matter but is then separated by God.
He argues the soul exceeds matter's capacity and does not depend on it for existence.
He states that the soul is not actually the act of any physical matter.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas states that the rational soul is subsistent and exceeds the capacity of corporeal matter, so it does not depend on matter for its existence.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, who directly creates the human rational soul?
options: Angels create it using the power granted to them by God.
God alone creates it directly, without any intermediary agents.
It emerges naturally from the formation of the physical body.
Higher spiritual beings produce it to guide lower physical bodies.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that the rational soul is produced immediately by God and that the view of angels producing it is impossible and against faith.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main reason for rejecting the idea that angels produce souls?
options: Only God can create something entirely new without using pre-existing matter.
The Bible explicitly forbids angels from interacting with human souls.
God is the only being capable of changing physical matter into spirit.
Angels are too imperfect to handle the complexity of human minds.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that creating a soul requires creation ex nihilo (from nothing), which only the First Agent (God) can do, whereas all other agents presuppose existing matter.

questions.q: How does Aquinas refute the objection that higher beings should produce lower ones?
options: He argues that producing like from like always involves changing existing matter.
He states that God does not allow any hierarchy among spiritual substances.
He explains that souls are physical and thus cannot be produced by spirits.
He claims that angels are not actually superior to rational souls in power.
questions.explanation: In his reply, Aquinas clarifies that while higher things do lead lower ones, this process involves transmutation (change) of matter, which is impossible for the creation of a spiritual soul.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about whether it belongs to man to act for an end?
options: Human actions are never for an end.
No, only some actions are for an end.
Only irrational actions are for an end.
Yes, all human actions are for an end.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that all human actions must be for an end.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas say all human actions are for an end?
options: Because irrational animals act for ends, so humans must too.
Because the end is always the last step in any action.
Because the end is the first in the agent’s intention, making it a cause.
Because ends are unrelated to human will.
questions.explanation: He argues the end is first in the agent’s intention, thus a cause of the action.
